en: The First Vilāsa:
*Camatkāracandrikā*, composed by the moon among poets, Viśveśvara.

May the Goddess of Speech manifest in my mouth—she who shines forth as the essence of *dhvani* (suggestive sound) and subsequently assumes the form of articulated phonemes through the various places of articulation and efforts.
By designating entities with the names of words, it effects a threefold delineation; having attained the status of a Great Sentence, it bestows a continuous stream of bliss upon the wise.

Resplendent with a body whose meaning is delightful, whose life-breath consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), shining with poetic qualities, coloring the heart, endowed with the modes of expression (*vṛtti*) and stylistic maturity (*pāka*),
radiant with various ornaments, and full of *rasa*— the poetry of some fortunate soul attains flawlessness everywhere, like a beautiful woman ascending her bed.
If this composition is skillful in achieving its intended purpose and exalted by the noble qualities of a clever and magnanimous hero,
then I shall compose this jewel of a work on literary characteristics as an illustration of the virtues of the illustrious King Siṅga.

Just as the world continues to follow the traces of the scent of the wondrous tales of Rāghava and Pāṇḍava, so too shall this work composed by me attain the esteem of the wise, for although I am not such a person, this king Śrī Siṅga is indeed possessed of such virtues— just like those works composed by that sage.
Instruction regarding both the ritual procedure and the Lord is the purpose of poetry;
and when that instruction is imbued with aesthetic charm, once awakened, it shall attain stability.
But the wonder of the learned consists in bringing about a flow of bliss;
[it perceives] the quality (guṇa), the style (rīti), the aesthetic flavor (rasa), the mode (vṛtti), the maturity (pāka), the diction (śayyā), and the ornament (alaṅkṛti).
The wise declare that these seven are the causes of wonder,
through their connection with similarity in producing the beauty of a sentence, such as qualities and so forth.
Kubjaka and others have stated that poetry possesses only a single constituent element;
however, King Bhoja has declared that there are three constituents: the qualities (guṇas), the ornaments (bhūṣās), and the aesthetic flavors (rasas).
Poetry endowed with its seven constituent parts shines like a universal empire; this work, complete in all its parts, is presented by me for the delight of those of cultivated intellect.

In this matter of poetic ornamentation, the prayer that "the wise may be affectionate" is superfluous; for those whose minds reach the very depths of devotion to Bharata and others, they experience joy precisely through their knowledge of the essence. As for those who remain unclear due to doubt, they themselves strive to establish fortitude in their hearts in order to dispel that doubt.
Those who know poetry understand that poetry consists of word and meaning endowed with aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
"Vāk" and "śabda" are synonyms; by means of words, Śiva is remembered as the meaning. (Cvc 1.11)
That speech is traditionally said to be threefold, in order: phonemes, words, and sentences.
The phonemes, beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, are called the *mātṛkā*.
They are considered to be of two kinds: those with few breaths (*alpaprāṇa*) and those with great breaths (*mahāprāṇa*).
Among these, the wise say that the four *ūṣman* sounds are those with great breaths.
Some maintain that within the groups [of consonants], those with similar vowels have similar vowels;
however, the others are considered to have weak breath, as are the *ś* and *s* sounds when followed by other [consonants].
Both of these are also said to be of two kinds: smooth (snigdha) and rough (rūkṣa).
Those that possess few vital breaths (alpaprāṇa) and are joined with their own kind are known as smooth.

Those [consonants] joined with their own or other *mahāprāṇa* [aspirated] letters are said to be rough (*rūkṣa*); furthermore, those joined with *para* [unaspirated] letters are *alpaprāṇa*. Those joined with *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are also said to be rough.
Even harsh sounds sometimes attain smoothness through the presence of an anusvāra;
the wise should understand its distinctions in cases such as *saṃkhyā*, *vandya*, and *vandhya*. (Ckc 1.17)
These phonemes, employed at the beginning of poetry as appropriate for the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and other elements, are the very forms of their respective deities.
They attribute good and evil to the doer, the one who causes it to be done, and the one who hears it;
the syllable "A" should be a giver of joy, whereas its opposite occurs in negation.
Although this [state] bestows joy and possesses three walls, it is not appropriate in times of anger, affliction, and the like;
however, the group of four beginning with *i* (the vowels *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*) brings about contentment and the fulfillment of desires.
The four vowels beginning with *ṛ* are the causes for the stability of the continuum;
the four beginning with *e* bestow desire, speech, liberation, and prosperity.
The *ka*-group brings fortune; the letter *ca* destroys fame. The letters *cha* and *ja* remove fear and disease, while *jha* and *ja* bring about death. (Ckc 1.22)
The letters *ṭa* and *ṭha* cause exhaustion; *ḍa* is auspicious; *ḍha* produces ugliness; *ṇa* brings about the acquisition of objects; and *ta* destroys obstacles. (Ckc 1.23)
The letter *tha* is a doer of strife; *dha* and *dhā* bestow fortitude. The letter *na* causes distress, yet it is remembered as auspicious when used in a sense other than negation.
The syllable *pa* bestows protection; the syllable *pha* grants fearlessness;
the syllable *ba* brings about health; and the syllable *bha* produces memory and good fortune. (Ckc 1.25)
The letter *ma* causes agitation; the letter *ra*, the bestower of glory, causes burning;
the letter *la* causes dullness; and the letter *va* is a mine of speech, health, and longevity.
The *ūṣman* consonants are, in sequence, the treasury of happiness, distinction, glory, and nirvāṇa;
however, when joined with a harsh [consonant], they should be avoided like food mixed with poison, even if they are gentle. Ckc 1.27.
But the union of two defects is better than the bestowal of prosperity;
furthermore, syllables are of two kinds: heavy and light. (Cvc 1.28)

Those ending in an *anusvāra* or a *visarga*, those with long vowels, and those followed by a conjunct consonant are heavy (*guru*); others are known as light (*laghu*). These [syllables] are further classified into three groups.
The prosodic feet (gaṇas) are known as ma, ya, ra, sa, ta, ja, bha, na, and sa; each subsequent one arises from the preceding.
Here, the effect (janya), being near its cause (janaka), does not produce an inauspicious result, just like a son [does not act independently of his father].
Having established that the *magaṇa* is the root of all and that every *gaṇa* is auspicious,
I shall now declare their characteristics and divine results as taught by the ancient masters.
The *magaṇa*, whose deity is the Earth, bestows security;
the *yagaṇa*, whose deity is Water, brings about all goals, beginning with lightness. (Ckc 1.32)
The *ragaṇa*, light in the middle, bestows fear and has Agni as its deity;
the *sagaṇa*, heavy at the end, brings about destruction and has Vāyu as its deity.
The *tagaṇa*, heavy at the end, has Īśa as its deity;
it causes disease. The *jagaṇa*, heavy in the middle, has the Sun (Bhānu) as its deity.
The *ādiguru* (the first syllable long) bestows happiness; its presiding deity is the lunar mansion Bhagaṇa.
The *dhanaṅkara* (the second syllable long) brings wealth; the *sarvalaghu* (all-light) *nagaṇa* has Yajña as its presiding deity.
These eight are said to occur within the [first] eight syllables, while three are traditionally taught to occur within the *mātrā*.
In this [meter], the *gaṇa* consists of either four light syllables, two heavy syllables, or two light syllables followed by one heavy syllable;
and as before, the fruits of fate arise from the all-light, the all-heavy, and the single-heavy [syllable].
One should place auspicious syllables at the beginning of a poem, and never an inauspicious *gaṇa* or letter.
In the north, there is a certain example cited as "the word and its meaning are lovely" (*vāgarthau kaucit kāntau*);
this should be understood to apply to the three [works] of Kālidāsa, where both the *gaṇas* and the *varṇas* are auspicious. (Ckc 1.39)
In the phrases "the glory of the Kurus" (*śriyaḥ kurūṇām*) and "the lord of glory" (*śriyaḥ patiḥ*),
the recollection of Śrī and Śrīpati is intended to ward off the fault of a *jagaṇa* [in the meter].
Alternatively, due to the proximity of the *tagaṇa*, the *jagaṇa* produced thereby is auspicious;
however, in this case [of the verse], because of the connection with the *magaṇa* at the end, it is not so for poets.
Whether for the sake of auspiciousness, in the act of naming, or even in the marking of a deity's name,
the group [of letters] is not to be censured, just as a caste [is not defiled by contact with] a stone presided over by a deity.

In the opening of the *Caturmukha* and similar works, even the *ca*-vowel and the *jagaṇa* are auspicious, owing to their being marked with the name of Brahmā; this holds true even at the beginning of a *kāvya*.
Furthermore, in the opening of this work, *Śṛṅgāravīrasauhārda*,
even the letter *śa* occurring within the vowel *ṛ* is specifically distinguished as being for the sake of auspiciousness.
Because it expresses excellence in words such as *praśasti* and *pātra*, the letter *pa*, even when joined with the letter *ra*, is clearly auspicious at the beginning of a poem. (Ckc 1.45)
When a faulty syllable or metrical foot occurs in the opening of an ancient poem that maintains its authoritative status, the wise person should indeed conduct this kind of investigation.
Generally, the words of the ancients are profound;
therefore, the established system of grammatical characteristics cannot be disregarded by moderns merely on the basis of citing them.
Some maintain that this restriction concerns only the praise of the present leader and does not have as its object those who existed in the past.
That [criticism] is either to be reflected upon or abandoned; what is the use of such courtesy?
For even in a literary composition based on ancient events, there is a restriction regarding what is to be concluded.
Because the author, the instigator, and the listener are motivated by a desire for results,
and because of the power of the faultless poem itself to produce those results.
Because there would be no restraint, leading to the consequence of speaking as one pleases,
and because faults are heard in such a position, this is certainly not the view of the wise.
If even a single fault is seen, ten thousand vows may be destroyed;
such is the innate power of a fault—what indeed can we do?
Therefore, it is certain that a poet who desires dharma, wealth, and other goals must abandon even the slightest trace of a fault with every effort.
The quality is the sweetness of the phonemes; the defect of the phonemes is its opposite.
Thus concludes the analysis of the castes.
That word ending in a case-suffix is declared by those who know the system of *dhvani* to be threefold: denotative (*vācaka*), indicative (*lakṣaka*), and suggestive (*vyañjaka*). Ckc 1.55.

That which makes the meaning understood according to convention is considered a denotative word (*vācaka*). It is of two kinds: etymological (*yaugika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*); among these, the etymological is as follows. (1.56)
That which illuminates its own object by depending upon the analysis of its constituent parts.
Just as the sense organs of people that perceive form find their purpose in the moon, in sandalwood essence, and in the king named Śrī Siṅgha.

In this context, words such as *candra*, *candana*, and *saras* possess denotative power only by virtue of their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) from roots such as *āhlādayati* (to delight); thus, they are derivative (*yaugika*). On the other hand, a conventional (*rūḍha*) word is independent of the etymological analysis of its constituent parts.
Just as Karṇa was renowned for his generosity, Dilīpa for his compassion, Kāvya for his statesmanship, and Rāma for his humility—
if Śrī Siṅghabhūpa is celebrated for possessing all these qualities, he is truly famous.

In this context, words such as *karṇa* and others possess conventional meaning (*rūḍhatva*) because they convey their sense even without an etymological derivation from their constituent parts. That [conventional word] functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) by setting aside its conventional referent in order to denote a thing related to it; and that [indication] is of two kinds: based on convention (*rūḍhi*) or based on a motive (*prayojana*). (Ckc 1.59)
Among these, an example of a conventional (rūḍha) indicative [metaphor] is as follows:

"O King Śrī Siṅgha, kings who are enemies worship your two feet with the rubies on the tips of their crests—rubies that humble the pride of the beauty of fresh *śakragopa* insects—since they have attained a wealth of proficiency through service to you, who are skilled in the art of protection and whose minds are known to be well-trained. (Ckc 1.3)
In this regard, he is thoroughly bathed in the words *niṣṇāta*, *kuśala*, and *pravīṇa*; he takes up the *kuśa* grass; and his lute (*vīṇā*) is excellent (*prakṛṣṭā*).

In the case of the expression "it protects Śakra" (*śakraṃ gopāyati*), since the primary meaning is not intended, the basis is simply the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) denoting the insect *indragopaka* (the cochineal beetle), characterized by its cleverness;

there is nothing else that causes delight to the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). This is therefore "indicative based on convention" (*rūḍhalakṣaka*). An example of "indicative with a purpose" (*saprayojanalakṣaka*) is as follows:

In the time of the illustrious King Siṅgha, at every moment, palanquins together with auspicious golden jars and parasols arrive instantly to serve you, who have entered the assembly hall, for the delight of the people.

In this context, it is impossible for insentient golden jars, umbrellas, and palanquins to arrive for the purpose of service; therefore, one infers that there are men who hold the umbrellas and kings or learned scholars who occupy the palanquins.
By this, the author intends to convey that there is an extreme abundance of umbrellas and palanquins in the courtyard of the assembly hall due to their specific purpose.
And by that, the conveyances such as palanquins and so forth, as well as riches, belong to those who have taken refuge in the Leader;
thus, this [treatise] is the means for attaining the purpose.
Whether through a secondary or a primary mode of expression, once the meaning has been established, [the purpose is achieved].
For that which suggests another meaning for the sake of excellence is indeed a suggester (vyañjaka).
Oh, how great is the literary fortune of the illustrious Lord of Siṅga,
for whose praise the words of me, Viśveśvara, are prepared!

In this context, the specific referent of the word "I" (*asmadartha*), which is the resting place for the skill of poetic composition in its full flavor, is indicated by the word "mine" (*mama*), whose literal meaning has been transferred to another sense.
By this, it is suggested that [this skill] produces aesthetic wonder for no one other than those who possess an innate affinity for literature.
Through the word "prepared" (*saṃnaddhāḥ*), the expressed meaning is entirely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).
It is observed that [the work] is composed with devotion to that [subject].

Here, by this [statement], the fact that the literary artistry of the hero (*nāyaka*) surpasses all similar works is illuminated; thus, this is an instance of *pada-vyañjaka* (suggestiveness at the level of the word).
Just as Siṅghaprabhu was the primary Alaṅkārī, while Rāvaṇa was the Alaṅkārī again;
the difference in their respective classes is heard of and accepted by all.
When the primary denotation (*mukhyā vṛtti*) is established upon the literal meaning— that "varṇa" refers to the difference or distinction between two things by way of color or syllable—

the phrase "difference of caste" (*varṇāntara*) is suggested by the word *varṇāntara* as the mutual exclusion (*vyatireka*) between the hero and the Lord of the Raghus, namely that there is a difference in their caste, the Vaiśya class;
thus, this is an instance of suggestion by a word (*padavyañjaka*).
Or like Narasiṃha, the Lord of Śrī, who shattered the pillar made of kṛtāya, nourished Prahlāda with food, and shines as the crest-jewel of kings.
He who has performed—that is, executed—the breaking down or removal of the iron pillar of dullness regarding auspicious rites is *kṛtāyastambhanirbhedaḥ*;
the meaning is that he is skillful in accomplishing what is favorable to destiny.
He is *rājaśekharaḥ*, the crest-jewel of kings; *narasiṃhaḥ*, the lion among men; and *bhaktaprahlādapoṣakaḥ*, one who nourishes the joy of his devotees and increases the contentment of his servants.

When the contextual meaning— that "the illustrious King Siṅgha shines"— is established through the *asiddhi* (non-establishment) [of the literal sense], there arises the cognition of the Lord Śrī Nṛsiṃha, who bears the crescent moon, who broke the iron pillar, and who nourishes the devotee named Prahlāda;

by means of this, which is rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*), the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the figure of simile (*upamālaṅkāra*) between the hero and the deceptive lion is perceived— thus, this is an instance of the suggestive (*vyañjaka*).
Now, the defects of words:
a defective word is one that is corrupt, unidiomatic, meaningless, contradictory in meaning, redundant, unintelligible, or uncertain. (Cvc 1.61)
It is said to be afflicted, censurable, of indirect meaning, contradictory, inexpressive, loathsome, unwholesome, and shameful. (Ckc 1.62)
In that regard, the unrefined and corrupt [usage] is as follows:

"O King Siṅga, by the Goddess of Speech— who is about to prevail, who prevails, and who prevails intensely through the weight of the ripening of her excellence— [you have attained] the crest-jewel of those who know the true state of beings."

The Creator brought you forth as a conqueror; otherwise, this world would not exist, for it would perish under the curse of those whose lives are fruitless despite their efforts at spiritual discipline.
In this context, the use of the middle voice (ātmanepada) in "jīvet" contradicts the grammatical rule;
therefore, "jīvet katham" is the superior reading.
Even that is a merit when it is imitated.
With the hope that the king is affectionate toward those who speak Sanskrit, we have become his servants; may we prosper by the dust of his feet resting upon our heads.
Thus, out of compassion, the venerable Siṅganārāyaṇa renders intelligible for them the poorly composed speech of those kings who consider themselves wise.

In this passage, the suffix *tral* in *bhṛtyatna* is applied to the word *bhṛtya*, which is not a pronominal; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in *bhavāmahe*; the vowel *a* at the end of *padarajaiḥ*; and the active voice (*parasmaipada*) of the root *edh* in *edhema*—these are Apabhraṃśa forms.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as these are imitations of the speech of uneducated people.
That which, though prescribed by the learned, has not been employed and is disregarded by poets.
Just as the lotuses were abandoned by the Fortune who went to the mouths of kings,
so too these [lotuses] do not share a dwelling with the ill-fated water-lilies.

Here, although there is the grammatical rule stating "padma and nalina [may] be used in the masculine," poets generally do not employ them in the masculine gender; thus, this usage of *padmāḥ* is unidiomatic.
In the first half-verse, the word *padmam* has been omitted.
If this is not the case, then the reading "gataśrīkaiḥ" in the second half-verse is more pleasing.
That [quality] is intended as a merit even for that which is known [as such] in cases such as *yamaka* (rhyme).
Just as all the deities bestow blessings upon the assembly of the foremost Brahmins,
so may all the deities bestow blessings upon the illustrious King Siṅga.
In this case, although the word *daivata* is masculine and thus disregarded by poets [in such contexts], its use in a *āvṛtti-yamaka* (repeated alliteration) is not faulty because it is avoidable.
That which serves merely to fill out a line and which does not provide any distinction has been called "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) by those who know how to embellish words. (Cvc 1.66)

Just as the lotus goddess Lakṣmī, fearing the disappearance of her lotuses, dwells during the cold seasons and other times upon the face of King Siṅga— she who is indeed worthy of universal veneration.

In this context, the word *vai* serves merely as a metrical filler (*pādapūraṇa*). Furthermore, the qualifier *sarvavandyā* (worshipped by all) does not provide any specific distinction regarding the act of sitting (*adhyāsana-kriyā*) when that act is already accompanied by doubt; thus, those two [words] are redundant. [For example: "He always occupies the delightful [place]."
Thus, the second reading of the *argha* verse is charming;
the wise declare that it also possesses meaning within the context of *yamaka* and other poetic figures.

Just as in the previously cited example, "yathā yā praṅktiḥ brāhmaṇendrāṇām āśāste," although the particle *eva* here is devoid of meaning and serves merely to fill the metrical foot, it possesses significance precisely because it facilitates the formation of the *yamaka* (rhyme).
[Otherwise, there would be] a contradiction in meaning.
For that is indeed a contradictory meaning, wherein a contradictory meaning is perceived.
This King of Pāṇḍya, whose enjoyment is like that of Indrāṇī’s lord and who resembles the Lord of the Guhyakas in splendor, shines with a majesty equal to that of Gopāla.
Even that which was spoken by ancient poets would not lead to any fault.

Just as the enemy kings attained a likeness to the Lord of Ambikā by wearing matted hair and garments of skin upon their bodies— having been stripped of their own royal status by Siṅga Bhūpālaka, who possessed the prowess of the hero of Janaka’s daughter at the bow— so too did they come to resemble him.

In this regard, although the intended meaning is that Raghu’s son is Rāma, the son of Janaka, and while the term *pitṛsutāpati* (husband of the father’s daughter) would indeed convey a contradictory sense;

and although in the case of *ambikānātha*, when the intended meaning is "husband of Pārvatī," the understanding arises that he is the "husband of [his own] mother"—nevertheless, there is no contradiction.
Now, one might object: if the perception of a contradictory meaning is common [to both cases], why is it that terms such as *ambikānātha* are considered a poetic excellence (*guṇa*)?

If it is asked, "How is the status of [words] such as *indrāṇīnātha* established as being defective? it is said: [It is established] solely by the acceptance of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) through their predominant usage. But who, then, are the learned in this context?
The position of those who reject [the authority of the Vedas] is that only those who first teach the path are the learned (*śiṣṭa*);
the ancient lords of poets alone are the learned, not those who consume even grass. Therefore: "This son of Janaki is a jewel of the solar dynasty."
"Thus was the daughter of Janaka instructed"; "In the meritorious waters of the bath of Janaka’s daughter";
"May that beloved of Ambikā protect you."
"Her lotus-hands were greedy to touch the orb of Ambikā’s hips," and "He made Ambikā drink the beverage"—
such are the applications of poetic qualities (guṇa) accepted by the great poets.

The quality of being a poetic excellence (*guṇatva*) belongs to [characters] such as Janaka’s daughter, Nāyaka, Ambikā, and Rāmaṇa; conversely, there is a lack of beauty due to the introduction of [characters] such as Indreṇī and Nātha, which are merely imagined from one's own fancy. This is the "Royal Road" (*ghaṇṭāpatha*) approved by those who have reached the further shore of flavorful literature (*sarasasāhitya*).
That which has a trivial meaning and is overly prolix is said to be "insubstantial in meaning."
O illustrious King Siṅga, just as enemy monarchs possess a fitness for sovereignty that is the very opposite of the majesty and sovereignty of Īśāna, so do they [possess] such [a state].

In this context, where one ought to say "fitness for lightness" (*lāghavayogyatām*), the phrase "sovereignty over the meanings of words through their weightiness" (*garimaiśvarthapratīpaiśvaryam*) involves verbal prolixity (*śabdagauravam*).
In certain cases, when there is an intention to express excellence and so forth, even this [defect] may function as a poetic quality (guṇa).
Just as on the lineage-banner of the Leader himself,
there arose from his lotus-feet a stainless complexion,
which attained the status of being a sibling to the fruit of Bhagīratha’s ascetic penance.
Here, in the sense of "O Gaṅgā," the word *bhagīrathatapaḥphalam* ("the fruit of Bhagīratha’s asceticism") is redundant;
nevertheless, because it indicates her act of purifying the sons of Sagara, it confers a state of excellence upon the word *Gaṅgā*, and thus constitutes a poetic merit (*guṇa*).
That which is renowned only in the Vedas and Śāstras is called *apratīta* (unintelligible) in this context. (Cvc 1.71)

O glorious Siṅgha, protector of the earth, by means of you— who are like a sacrificial wooden sword (sphyam)— the pride and arrogance of your enemies have been utterly destroyed by the counsel of Mitraśrī Rāma.
In this context, the fact that the word *sphya* denotes an object shaped like a sword is well-known only in the Veda; that the word *manu* denotes a mantra is known only in the Āgamas;

and that it denotes the exclusion of *vṛddhi* is established only in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*); thus, [the meaning of *manu* as "one who possesses knowledge"] is unfamiliar [to ordinary people].
When one engages in the practice for the accomplishment of that knowledge, this very [discipline] is a virtue.
Just as one who,
having closed the openings of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* and bound the *triśṛṅgāṭikā*, causes [the breath] to ascend through the *suṣumnā* and pierces the six knots along with the wind,

and having driven back the lunar digit (*candrakalā*) by means of the radiance of the inward-facing light, becomes saturated by the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) emitted from that— such a yogi lives for a long time.

In this context, although terms such as *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* are unfamiliar because they are well-known only within the science of Yoga (*yogaśāstra*), they possess the quality of being "virtuous" (*guṇatva*) because the method of the yoga of practice (*abhyāsayoga*) is successfully carried out in every respect.
On the other hand, where that [method] is uncertain, doubt leads to a lack of excellence. (Ckc 1.73)
Just as the lineage of vassal kings, proud of their devotion to serving the lotus feet of the illustrious King Siṅgha, acted as a wish-fulfilling tree for the enjoyment of the earth.
In this context, because there arises the doubt as to whether *dhātrī* means "a nurse" or "the earth," this [reading] remains uncertain;
however, the reading *bhūmibhogāya* is more pleasing.
This is so even though the specific meaning may be understood from the context and other factors.
In cases of superiority or non-contradiction, one does not enter the realm of faults.
O Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla, crest-jewel of the Recarla lineage, how can the greatness of your sword of dense luster be described in this world?
For at its mere trembling, the circle of the kings of the battlefield continuously attains the state of being mentioned alongside [the gods] in their celestial chariots, together with their friends.

In this context, regarding the term *ghanadyuteḥ*, there is no fault because there is no contradiction even if one entertains the doubt as to whether it means "one whose luster (*dyuti*) is dense (*ghana*) and thick (*sāndra*)," or "one whose luster is like that of a cloud (*ghana*).

Regarding the phrase *vimānavartanakathām*, there is no defect even if one entertains the doubt as to whether it refers to "the conduct of one free from pride (*abhimāna*)" or "the movement of celestial chariots (*vyomayāna*"), because of its extreme excellence.

In the phrase "of the kṣoṇībhṛts," where there is a doubt as to whether it refers to kings or mountains, there is no fault because the specific meaning is understood from the context of describing the hero's sword and from the specific characteristics of a king.
This should likewise be observed in cases where the specific meaning is understood through association, dissociation, and so forth.
Because the object is extremely remote, that is called "afflicted."

Or just as the forest land became the royal capital for the wives of King Śrī Siṅgha, who were enemies of King Arāśimitra— the progenitor of the Janaka lineage— along with Asahāya, Keyūra, Vetanaka, Yāna, and Vilocana.
In this matter, Maināka is the friend of the ocean;
Himavān is his progenitor,
and Pārvatī is born from him.
Maheśvara is his companion;
the serpents are his armlets;
and the wind is their wages, the cause of their sustenance.
"Those whose eyes are like the eyes of the deer, which is his vehicle or mount"—
this is *kliṣṭa* (obscure) because the meaning is excessively remote.

Furthermore, when the progression [of the narrative] is brought to completion, or when indicating the degradation of great beings, that which is employed in poetry as "obscure" (kliṣṭa) may instead become a merit. (Ckc 1.76)
An example of the successful completion of the sequence is as follows:
"In wealth, in archery, in policy, in physique, and in winning over others, King Śrī Siṅga surpasses Arjuna;
his son surpasses that son’s friend; and that son’s son surpasses that [grandson’s] friend. (Ckc 1.22)
In wealth, he conquered Devendra;
in archery, his son Devendraputra Arjuna;
and in statesmanship, Devendraputramitra Vāsudeva.
In the passage "pradyumnam" (referring to Pradyumna) as the son of the friend of Indra’s son [Kṛṣṇa],

and "candram" (referring to Candra) as the friend of the friend of the son of Indra’s son [Pradyumna], although the referents are difficult to discern due to the intervening words, they are treated as merits because the sequence of those specific terms is successfully maintained.

Regarding the indication of the insignificance of great men: while the arms of the Lord of Fortune, which are shaped like long golden bars, cause his enemies to have arms that are likewise long golden bars,
it is a marvel, O King Siṅga, that even though your arms are indeed long like the bolts of a city gate, they do not produce long golden bars [in others].

In this context, "āyatasuvarṇakara" means one whose hand (kara) is long (āyata), beautiful (su), and golden (varṇa); thus, it refers to a boar (sūkara). Because of the fear of stating that Viṣṇu possesses the form of an animal, the word was employed with its meaning distanced from the mouth [of the speaker], which constitutes a poetic merit (guṇa). Furthermore, through the perception of a forced meaning, as for example:
Situated within the jewelry casket of Śambhu, shimmering as a rival to Śrī,
and entering the middle station of Viṣṇu, the fame of King Siṅga shines resplendently.
In this context, the chest containing Śambhu’s ornaments is Pātāla,
his illustrious consort is the Earth,
and Viṣṇu’s intermediate station is the Sky; because these meanings are not difficult to understand, they cause no strain, and thus constitute a merit (guṇatva).
That which is well-known in a particular region and devoid of etymological derivation is called "regional" (deśya).

O Śrī Siṅghabhūpa, during your pleasure-hunts, what woman could follow you like a Yavana female attendant— she whose lovely hips are encircled by a girdle, and whose cheeks are doubly flushed with the intoxication of wine?
In this context, *pekā* refers to a carrying-bag (*paridhānabhastrā*), while *halā* and *madirā* are regional dialects (*deśya*). Surely,
because of the similarity between a bag (*bhastrā*) and a basket (*peṭikā*), the word *peṭikā* [is formed] by eliding the middle syllable.
If it is argued that the beloveds of plowmen, such as Pekkā and Halā, are not indeed local women;
In the expression *kandāduṭṭīkata*, the form *kandāṭṭa* and so forth should not be considered an object of censure;
thus, this etymological justification is praised as being within the bounds of propriety.
Therefore, this [teaching] should not be taught at first to those who have abandoned the itching pain of wisdom regarding the agitation of the path, for it would result in their censure.
A *aṅka* is a title of honor (*biruda*).
For example:
"Victorious is King Calamartigaṇḍa-biruda, the Terrifier of Rival Gaṇḍas."
Even Paraśurāma, the axe-wielder of the Saumaka clan, and Gopāla, the sun of the Pāṇḍya dynasty, were likewise praised.

In this case, because [the mention of] calamities, death, Gaṇḍa, and so forth serves as a regional characteristic (deśyatva), it possesses the status of a poetic excellence (guṇatva) due to its being a source of contradiction (birudatva).
Regarding the critique: "What is the use of the harsh *koṃkaravaṃkara* [sound], or what is the use of the *cīṃgirimāṃgira* [sound] of the clothing?
For the wise, a single mastery of learning is the aid for beholding the illustrious King Siṅghabhu. Ckc_1.27.

In this context, the phrase "by Koṅkaravaṃkara" should be explained as meaning "by such a dreadful palanquin. The phrase "cīṃgirimāṃgireṇa," [meaning] variegated with various colors, should be explained.
"With such a garment" means with a silk cloth (*paṭṭāṃśuka*).

Here, someone— having acquired a grand display of palanquins, silken garments, and the like through excessive expenditure, and having entered royal courts in various distant regions— finding that he could not even recover his expenses and suffering from the burden of debt, beholds the hero even without such luxury.

When people ask how you, who possess various splendors brought together by the convergence of your compassionate glances, have achieved such prosperity while remaining free from ostentation, you offer an answer preceded by the mockery of external displays such as palanquins, silk cloths, and garments— merely for the sake of expenditure.
In this matter, since [the lack of substance] is the ground for reproach from those such as Koṅkara and Vaṅkara, it constitutes the quality of being censurable (*deśyatva*).
And it possesses beauty as well.
As in the genealogy of the leader himself:
"To those two were born three sons, who were like wish-fulfilling trees for the earth, heroes who terrified their enemies with the sound of their swords:
Siṅga-prabhu, Vennama-nāyaka, and Reca-mahīpati, the foremost of warriors."
In this case, although the words *siṅgama*,
*vennama*,

and *recaya* lack etymological derivation (*avyutpatti*) and thus constitute the objects of description (*deśyatva*), they do not constitute a defect in the word (*aduṣṭapadatva*) because they function as nominal words (*nāmapada*).
That which is a conceptual construction fashioned by oneself is declared to be of interpretable meaning.
Just as the enemies of the protector of the earth, deprived of their overturned vessels,
flee into the wilderness teeming with returning cuckoos— alas!— so do they vanish.
In this context, the word *pātra* denotes shame (*trapā*) through the reversal of its phonemes;
likewise,
the word *kapir* for a cuckoo (*pika*) is not subject to doubt because it has been established by its own conventional usage.
In riddles and similar contexts, this [use of the vocative] is permitted by the wise.
O Lord of the Earth, he who does not know what is desired by yogis and worldly enjoyers alike has misunderstood Hara; he perceives him in a contrary way.

In this case, when the question "What is dear to yogins and serpents? is asked, although the answer that ought to be given is "solitude" (*rahaḥ*), the word "Hara" (*haraḥ*) is stated instead; though this is a term coined by the speaker's own convention, it is not considered faulty because it functions as a riddle (*prahelikā*).
The means for achieving knowledge of the words of one's own synonyms is the "counter-hand" (pratihastaka).
O illustrious King Siṅgha, just as enemies were cut to pieces by you with a sword whose fang-like blade was dark and formidable, so too were they [consumed] by camphor.
Here, the word *śyāma* indicates its synonym *kāla*;
by that, [it indicates] *yama*.
And the word *karpūra* indicates its synonym *ghanasāra*.
Therefore, the term *adhisāra* is obtained.
Consequently, because the words *śyāma* and *karpūra* merely indicate their own synonyms—namely *kāla* and *ghanasāra* respectively—they possess the status of *pratihasta*.
In works such as secret letters and the like, this quality generally does not lose its beauty.

Just as when the assembly of the gods was obscured by the spreading of Rāhu, King Siṅga issues letters to his ministers from Haridrā, which are adorned for the purpose of battle against those who have lost their wings, stating: "The sun has departed; strike! and he proclaims to his officials that the hour of combat has arrived.
In this context, *haridrā* means *niśā*, that is to say, night;
*rāhu* means *tamas*, that is to say, darkness;
and *icchā* means *āśā*, that is to say, direction.
The term *prayuktālaṅkṛti* refers to a blow;
[it is directed] at the enemies whose wings have been severed.
*Kujarī* refers to the city.
The army (*sārkā*) is the host (*camūḥ*); the attack (*praharaḥ*) is the march (*yāmaḥ*), as in "we go.
Thus, although turmeric and the like are considered "counter-hands" (*pratihasta*) because they indicate only their own synonyms, they are nevertheless employed by the generals.

Having deliberated on the task at hand for the purpose of destroying the fortress, we have set out accompanied by an army; "we shall go to the enemy's fortified city to strike them during the night when the ten directions are shrouded in darkness"— this message, sent to the king in the form of a secret letter due to the fear of a breach of counsel, does not constitute a fault.
It is incapable [of conveying meaning] because it is merely employed as a formal conjunction and thus lacks expressive power.
Just as the horses neighed melodiously and the noble elephants trumpeted in the courtyard of the royal palace of the Lord of the Earth, so too did they rejoice there.

In this context, "ruta" refers to the cry of animals; "vāsita" refers to the sound of ornaments; and "siñjita" refers to the sound of a bell. Regarding the limits of usage: the root *vāśṭ* is used in the sense of contemptuous sound, and *śija* is used for indistinct sound.
Thus, when employed merely for the sake of poetic ornament (*yogamātra*), the words *vāśita* and *śiñjita* are not expressive of the sounds of neighing and braying;
yet their status as a poetic quality (*guṇatā*) should be understood in cases such as those accepted by the authorities of that [poetic] science.
Just as when the illustrious Siṅgabhūmiramaṇa, whose valor is full, is present, no other kings appear on the battlefield;
or rather, when the Pāñcajanya conch resounds, do the warbling of young women even imitate his playful sound?

In this context, since the authors of the treatises on erotics (kāmaśāstra) record the various vocal modulations of the swan, partridge, quail, and other such birds during the intervals between lovemaking among passionate women, the term *kūjita* possesses expressive power even when it denotes something other than the mere cry of a bird.
Because the mind feels revulsion [toward itself], that which is reviled is threefold:
for the sake of what is to be abandoned, for another purpose related to what is to be abandoned, and as the cause for the mindfulness of what is to be abandoned. (Ckc 1.87)

For the sake of what is to be abandoned, those who follow the path opposed to the King of Virtue—enemies wandering on a road hostile to the Sovereign of Excellence—perish in the courtyard of misfortune. They are like great flies emerging from a cave through the mouth of effortless exertion, joined with the experience of the burden of foul vomit, and driven by the desire for initiation as food for themselves. Because they lack the internal dental firmness required for what is to be abandoned, they sink into the courtyard of the difficult.
In this context, because substances such as the filth of the eyes and the like are objects of direct disgust, they are to be abandoned.
An example of the meaning being "other than what is intended" (heyārthāntaratva) is as follows:
"O auspicious king, your sword is an untimely Rāhu for your enemies—those whose splendor is hidden by the tears of the women of the cities whom you have cherished with your hand. (Cvc 1.36)

In this context, because the words *viḍ* and *gūḍhavarcas* denote both feces and, by extension, semen and fire respectively, they possess a secondary meaning of loathsomeness due to their primary signification of excrement.
An example based on the cause of recollection (*heyasmṛti*) is as follows:
"Those enemies, whose bodies are stained by the dust raised by their armies, are purified by immersion in the edge of the auspicious sword. (Ckc 1.37)

In this context, because of the phonetic similarity between the words *pūyante* ("are purified") and *majjanena* ("by immersion"), the word *pūya* (pus) evokes a sense of disgust due to its association with the meaning of pus (*pūya*) and its similarity to the root *majj* (to immerse).
Their subordinate status as objects of apprehension is accepted in cases such as *vka-jit-aṅgīkṛta* and others. (Cvc 1.88)
O King Siṅga, just as the minds of noble, proud women— with palms as tender as new shoots and breasts with high, fleshy nipples— become intensely devoted to you.

In this context, although words such as "flesh," "blood," and "tender" possess a loathsome sense, or a different meaning that suggests it, they are regarded as a poetic excellence (guṇa) because they have been accepted by great poets despite their loathsomeness.
As an example of [words] having an inauspicious meaning:
"By the sounds of the trumpets signaling the preparation for the victorious march of the illustrious King Siṅgha, the enemy kings—the joints of whose bodies were suddenly shattered—perish. (Ckc 1.39)
In this context, the phrase "they die" (*parimriyante*) is directly inauspicious;
the reading "the rival kings sleep long" (*nidrānti dīrghaṃ paripanthibhūpāḥ*) is more pleasing.
An example of a term with an inauspicious secondary meaning:

"By the enemies standing before him, who were agitated by the onset of the battle-arrays of the army-hosts of the illustrious King Siṅga, their own boasts were rendered [meaningless] by their realization [of defeat]. (Ckc 1.40)
By the phrase "by those remaining here," death is understood just as much as a correct state of abiding.
The reading "by those rising" (uttiṣṭhamānaiḥ) is more pleasing;
for example, [the former] is a cause for recollecting inauspiciousness.
Those lords of men whose bellies are protected by the strength of the offering prescribed for the son of Kātyāyana become the supreme lenders of the earth.
In this context, regarding the word *kukṣayaḥ*, the recollection of inauspicious meanings arises from its final two syllables;
furthermore, in cases such as *gupta* and others, their status as subordinate members (*guṇabhāva*) is generally taken into account.
He who was born from the feet of Brahmā upon the birthplace of kings, who is devoted to the Supreme Keśava, the Lord of the Cosmic Egg,

and by whom this [lineage] was protected— removing the manifestation of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done— he now shines as a descendant of the Recarla clan, skilled in the destruction of his enemies.
Although *atroccheda* (the destruction of enemies) directly signifies an inauspicious meaning, it is rendered auspicious by being concealed by the word "enemy" (*śatru*).
Although *kṛtyā* (sorcery) has an inauspicious meaning, it is concealed by its association with *akṛtya* (non-sorcery), as in the pair *kṛtyākṛtye* (what should and should not be done).
Although the final two syllables of the name *Keśava* serve as a cause for recollecting an inauspicious meaning, they are concealed by the majesty of the Blessed One.

Although the final two syllables of the name "Keśava" serve as a cause for recollecting inauspicious meanings, they possess concealment (*guptatva*) due to the majesty of the Blessed One; thus, these [names] have concealment. That which causes shame and is indecorous is also threefold, as previously stated. (Ckc 1.90)
Let there be thousands of other lineages devoted to the genitals and the belly;
this one lineage of Recara alone is virtuous, being dedicated to the protection [of others].
In this case, the word *śipūrvam* refers directly to an indecorous meaning.
The reading *nijodare* is more elegant. An example of another indecorous meaning is as follows:

Some enemies, their foundations of devotion shattered by the force of the river of the excellent king Siṅghabhuva, flee to the quarter protected by Yama; others, however, go to the direction presided over by Guhyakeśa.
In this context, the word *guhyakeśa* suggests not only Kubera but also the sense of "one with contemptible hair," thereby possessing an indecent secondary meaning.
The reading *yakṣarājakalita* (embraced by the king of the Yakṣas) is more elegant. An example of that which calls to mind indecency is as follows:
Having been granted the enjoyment of sovereignty as a favor for their service to the lotus-feet of the illustrious King Siṅgha,
these vassal kings sport at the edge of the forest like bees hovering restlessly around the *śephālikā* flower.
In this case, the first pair of syllables of the word *śephālikā* causes the recollection of an indecent meaning.
The reading "vāsantikācañcala" is more appropriate.
And their status as subordinate elements is observed in the cases of the indicated (lakṣya) and so forth.
Just as in the previous example, "yasya druhiṇacaraṇaḥ" (whose [father] is Druhiṇa),
although the word *yoni* has an indecent meaning, it is not considered faulty because it is used figuratively (*gauṇavṛtti*) in the sense of "one who is like a source" (*yonir iva yoniḥ*).
Although the words *janmabhūmi* (birthplace) and *bhagavat* (Lord) have other indecent meanings, they are treated as non-faulty because they are well-known in common usage (*lokasaṃvītatvāt*).

Furthermore, although the final two syllables of the word *brahmāṇḍa* cause the recollection of an indecent meaning, they are considered a minor fault because the term is protected through metaphorical usage (*gauṇavṛtti*), in that "the egg-like" is called "an egg" (*aṇḍa*).

One should not assert that all of these are either with qualities or without qualities merely on the basis of their similarity in being objects to be abandoned and so forth; such [assertions] belong only to those who are harsh in logic.
He attained the state of being both supreme and other than supreme within the single [reality] of quality and honor,
through those means appropriate for the direct realization of the Brahman of Sahitya, which is full of aesthetic wonder.
Some wise ones have permitted the use of the *kumārī* lotus and so forth;
however, such was not the case in ancient times regarding the *śraviṣṭhā*, the *saṃsthāna*, the *śiprā*, the *pūrvaśnā*, and other such things.
By whatever means the ancient boundary must not be transgressed even by the learned; examining virtues and faults solely along the path prescribed therein, one should proceed.
One should compose poetry that endures until the end of an aeon and remains free from corruption.

Thus concludes the first chapter, titled "The Analysis of Phonemes and Words," in the *Camatkāracandrikā*, which is cooled by the essence of the nectar of King Siṅga and composed by the moon-like poet Śrī Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the mastery of elegant literature.
The Second Vilāsa of *Camatkāracandrikā*, composed by the poet-moon Viśveśvara; now, the second section:
*Vākya* (Sentence).
A sentence consisting of well-connected words is both indicative and suggestive.
An example of an indicative sentence (*lakṣakavākya*) is as follows:

"O Lord of the Earth, Siṅga, that you are sung of as one who is high-minded, affectionate toward those who seek refuge, and a speaker of truth—this has now been fully realized by you. My fortunes have reached their peak; thus, for a long time, I have truly ascended to the status of being an object of your compassionate regard amidst my rival wives."

In this case, because the flattering words [uttered] toward the beloved who has committed an offense against the proud woman are incoherent, a meaning contrary to the literal sense—such as "you are a deceiver"—is indicated.
An example of a suggestive sentence is as follows:
"His feet are lovely when fashioned cool upon the breasts of the mountain-dwellers; his hand caresses the dark stone; his limbs are dear to the eyes."
On Mount Rājācala, which is exceedingly great and favorable with joy, the king shines resplendent for the delight of the virtuous.

Here, by means of every sentence, there is perceived a suggestion through resonance (*anuraṇanadhvani*) in the form of a simile between the hero and the celestial heroine, rooted in the power of the words (*śabdaśaktimūla*); thus, this [verse] is a suggester (*vyañjaka*).

Now, as for the defects of a sentence (*vākyadoṣa*): they are incorrect usage (*apaprayukta*), faulty euphonic combination (*dussandhi*), inversion of order (*vyutkrama*), and tautology (*punaruktimat*).
And [speech that is] difficult to follow, confused by the components of the sentence, or containing an embedded sentence.

A sentence is said here to be defective when it possesses two discordant genders or numbers, or when its comparison is deficient or excessive; it is also called defective when it is either incomplete or redundant.
Where there is a lack of grammatical correctness in the joining of words, it is called *apaprayukta*.
Just as another king, having thoroughly oppressed his subjects, bestows wealth day after day upon throngs of courtesans, libertines, servants, bards,
and actors; this illustrious protector of Siṅga, however, gives away even more riches— wealth acquired through righteous means— to the people of the earth who are learned in the Vedas.
In this case, regarding the expression "stomāya," since it is the usage of one who is not learned (anāśiṣṭa), the instrumental case ought to have been used in the sense of the dative.
Nevertheless, the form "caturthīkṛtiḥ" is thus an incorrect usage (apaprayoga) and constitutes a fault of the sentence.

Those who discern between merits and defects say that even this [the aforementioned fault] may sometimes be considered a merit by virtue of the speaker's intention; others, however, regard it as a merit simply because of its natural beauty.
"May the wish-granting cow swallow the leaves of our *kalpa*-creepers; may my *cintāmaṇi* jewel be transformed by the pedestals [of the gods]; and may the great elephant be led away from afar!
Thus do the gods, mounted upon the railings, cry out as King Siṅha prepares to give away the *kalpa*-tree, the fragrant cow, the elephant, and other gifts.

In this context, although one should have said *kāmagavī*, the fact that *kāmagau* was stated is not an incorrect usage, because the rule for the compound-final suffix *ṭa*—namely, "after *go*, when no *taddhita* suffix follows" (*gorataddhitaluki*)—is non-mandatory; thus, by virtue of its non-mandatory nature, it is employed here with the intention of clarifying the meaning.
Likewise, there is the usage of a great poet in the great poem titled *Tīrthakarakramottaṃsana*:

O Lord of Darśan, in these abodes of the learned, whose heads touch the bright clouds and who shine with eloquent speech, the wish-fulfilling trees bear fruit even without the time of childbirth through the mere touch of a drop from the glance of Your compassionate eye; and the row of wish-granting cows flows most abundantly even without calves.

Thus, the Teachers have said: "For those whose minds are indolent in perceiving the majesty of such scriptures as these, [the teaching] appears like a corrupt dialect, yet it does not abandon its inherent excellence. (Ckc 2.6)
Thus,
it is sung as being unconnected, harsh, vulgar, and so forth, with faulty euphonic junctions (*sandhi*).

Just as the two ears of Kalyāṇasena— possessing a luster equal to the sun and the moon, bearing the splendor of guileless valor, joined with the flash of a sword that strikes down the pride of enemies, and wide with steadfastness—

bear a pair of powerful earrings, so too does this composition of the poet, charming with its excellent joints, endure the connection of a difficult joint within its broad and radiant primordial poetic art, which is otherwise not meant to be heard.
In this context, *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is intended; thus, in the first quarter (*pāda*), there is "bad euphony" (*duḥsandhi*) because the words lack a smooth junction.
In the word *vidviḍḍhrībhara*, etc., there is "bad euphony" because the junction is harsh in form, being *śrutikaṭu*.
In the phrase *dhṛtyā atanvyā uror*, there is "bad euphony" because the junction is harsh due to the frequent omission of the visarga (*visarga-lopa*).
In the third quarter (pāda), there is a state of difficult sandhi because of the presence of many *pragṛhya* vowels and harsh sandhis.
An example of an improper junction (*aślīlasandhi*) is as follows:

"Look, my dear! With her hair standing on end and emitting a stream of *sīt* sounds, she has plunged into the ocean of the terrified heart [of the king] due to the falling of the blade of the sword of the noble monarch.

For one who is thus afflicted, how can there be discernment? In this verse, the word *sītkṛta* (emitting *sīt* sounds) is used in a double sense; while it refers to the sound made by a woman in the throes of passion, it also refers to the *sīt* sounds produced by a person in extreme distress. Because these two meanings are joined together in a way that is indecorous, it is an instance of an improper junction.
In the case of *citrapata*, one should grasp [the object] all at once; at the beginning, the stage of the subordinate [factors] belongs to the first two.
Just as this ocean, a treasury for the lotus-lake of King Śrī Siṅgha, whose arms have terrified the forests of rival kings, provides a refuge for the earth;
so too, alas, alas! do the deeds of the great ones remain intent on dispelling the saffron-marked beauty from the jar-like breasts of women blinded by passion and hatred.

In this case, although the sandhi in "kamalardheḥ" is difficult, it possesses the merit of being a single instance [of such usage], as its purpose is to establish the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) meaning "the prosperity of Kamalā and of the lotus. An example of a *pragṛhya* vowel occurring only once is:
"Your wisdom, like your eyes, grasps subtle meanings."
Like the military expedition of the illustrious King Siṅga, his fame transcends the king of mountains.
In this case, although there is a difficult sandhi in the phrase *locane iva*, because it is a *pragṛhya* vowel, it is considered a merit (guṇatva) precisely because it occurs only once.

One should always avoid a vulgar euphonic junction (*sandhyaślīla*), just as one avoids a wicked person; furthermore, even when this [euphonic junction] becomes pleasant to hear, the sight of nakedness should not be accepted.
Where the sequence of either the word or the meaning intended for application becomes inverted from what is appropriate,
that is called *vyutkrama* (inversion).
Just as Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla is formidable through the power of his strength, just as Darpaka and Kīcaka are [formidable],
and just as Rāghava and Bhārgava are in the execution of the multitude of instructions from their gurus, so are you.

In this context, since it is logical to state the two subjects of comparison in the same order as the enumeration of their common attributes—namely, "strength" and "power"—the expression *kīcakadarpakārī* (the one who humbles Kīcaka) should have been stated in that sequence; however, because it is stated in reverse order, this is a "deviation of word" (*śabdavyutkrama*). In this very instance, since Bhārgava is more venerable than Rāghava, the expression *bhārgavarāghavau* should have been used; yet, by disregarding that order, this is a "deviation of meaning" (*arthavyutkrama*).
In both cases, the reading "the son of Bhṛgu and Rāghava, who humbled the pride of Kīcaka," is more elegant;
for it serves to dispel unfounded suspicions when no distinction is intended to be made,
and facilitates the ease of expression.
This [Buddha] also is worthy of being worshipped.
If you intend no distinction between them, then whether it be a jar, your own city, priceless jewels, or even the entire earth, there is no other course for the great but to abandon them.
O dear one, you must not harbor enmity toward King Siṃha; do not disregard our words, which are appropriate for those who love us.
In this context, because the city, the country, the elephant, and the horse are more highly esteemed [than the preceding], they are mentioned in order from the most important to the least.
Alternatively, it should not be argued that because of their connection with the act of relinquishing, those who are less esteemed must be mentioned first.
This being the case, even if one were to transgress the stated rule, one should protect one's life by surrendering all wealth to its owner, O Lord of Life.
The fault [of the verse] lies in its being spoken by the beloveds of the enemy with the intention of making a distinction between those who are worthy of honor and those who are not.
Regarding the removal of such doubt, it is as in the genealogy of the hero himself:

"The first of whom is known as Kumāratilaka; the illustrious Yaśovigraha [is the second], distinguished by his virtues; and the elder brother of one [is the third], and the elder brother of two in the splendor of his own form."

He triumphs over the elder of the three when his arms, irresistible as durvā grass, display their prowess; he triumphs over the elder of the four in truthful speech, and even over the elder of the five in generosity.

In this context, although one ought to say "the eldest of five, the eldest of three, the eldest of two, and the eldest of one" because Karṇa and the others are more venerable, the fact that the sequence is nonetheless highly beautiful— even though it involves a decrease— is considered a merit (guṇa). This is because, by superimposing an increase in number upon the decrease, the poet avoids the perception of dishonor suggested by the diminishing numbers and instead highlights a progressive intensification.
Regarding the ease of constraining one's speech, for example: "O King Śrīkiṅga, it is evident that Rāmas are the four parts of Hari;
among them, two are equal—noble and generous—while the other two are unequal—excessively haughty. (Ckc 2.13)

In this regard, it has been stated that during the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas, there were four partial incarnations (aṃśas) of Lord Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the world: Bhārgava Rāma, Rāghava Rāma, Yādava Rāma, and Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla.

Among these four, while it should have been said that the first is *uddhata* (boastful/arrogant), the second *udātta* (noble), the third *uddhata*, and the fourth *udātta*, they are nonetheless described as "equal" (*samau*) even though the order is reversed according to the manner in which they are recited; this refers to the two portions [of the lineage] originating from Daśaratha and Navota, which correspond to the second and fourth [incarnations].

The term *viṣamau* (unequal) refers to the first and third portions (*aṃśa*) born from the wombs of Reṇukā and Rohiṇī; because it reflects the correspondence between their shared qualities of being *dhīrodātta* and *dhīroddhata*, beauty unfolds even through the simplicity of the concise expression, and thus it constitutes a merit (*guṇa*). On the other hand, where a word is used for a meaning that is not distinct from its own [conventional] meaning, that is *punaruktimat* (redundant). (Cvc 2.12)
O King Siṅha, this elephant force of yours, worthy of being served by those who hold right views and capable of intimidating the wicked, remains as a mere display of thundering threats;
its rutting ichor is but the deceptive trickery of Śambara.

In this case, because the syllables *ḍa* and *ma* as well as *ba* and *ra* are identical in form, there is a repetition of words; however, when one intends to express an excellence of state (*bhāva*), even this [repetition] is to be respected.
Just as you are an ocean of compassion, protect us, protect us, O ocean of mercy!
We are those to be nurtured, not those to be hated; O King Siṅga, protect us!
In this context, "o ocean of compassion" (*karuṇāmbudhe*) and "o ocean of mercy" (*dayodadhe*) constitute a repetition of meaning;

"protect us, protect us" (*pāhi naḥ pāhi naḥ*) constitutes a repetition of sound. Neither of these two is a fault when intended to express the extreme dejection of the person making the request, as they relate to the one who is being addressed; rather, they possess the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*), for they nourish the intensity of their own respective meanings.
That in which there is a distance between those things that ought to be connected is called "difficult to connect" (duranvaya).

Just as on the battlefields of King Śrī Siṅgha, the bards— having seen the limbs of the enemies’ elephants scattered on all sides by the tumultuous *kila-kila* cries following the blows of fierce swords— become terrified and, amidst the swarms of herons, both increase and diminish their praises.

In this passage, between the two phrases "in battles crowded with flocks of herons" (*kaṅkakulākuleṣu saṅgareṣu*) and "terrified by the fear of these two," and between the two phrases "terrible due to the *kilakila* clamor" (*kilakilārāveṇa ghorāḥ*) and "the bards, having seen these two," and between the two phrases "desiring extreme proximity" (*atipratyāsattikāṅkṣiṇoḥ*) and "separation at a very great distance" (*dūradūrā vighaṭanā dṛśyate*), a disjointedness (*vighaṭanā*) is observed. Since this causes mental distress during the occasion of a connection (*anvaya*), it is a faulty case of "bad connection" (*duranvaya*).
The encircling of the sphere of qualities is seen in this [consciousness] as well, in some cases.
Just as certain milkers protect cows in a pen,
so was that Earth rendered fruitful by King Siṅga.

In this context, although one should have said "pālayāñcakrire" (they protected), some say "pālayāṃ cakrire gopālāḥ" (the cowherds performed the act of protecting); thus, even though there is a remote connection (*dūrānvaya*), some accept such usage despite the intervention. Because it does not deviate from the specific [rule], it is considered a merit (*guṇa*), being a mixture of the components of one sentence while connected with the components of another sentence. (Cvc 2.16)
Just as enemies of King Siṅga depart after asking for leave from their swords, they pull up their brides, shake them off, abandon heaven, and go to the earth.

In this case, where it ought to be stated that "the brides depart after taking leave, draw their swords, shake the earth, release [the sky], and go to heaven," there is a mutual commingling of words between the two sentences; thus, this sentence is one in which the components of the sentences are intermingled, and that [intermingling] is rendered subordinate. (Cvc 2.17)
O Lord of Speech, O Lord of the Gods, O Teacher of the Devas, it is said that King Anavataptasiṅha indeed surpassed even you in wisdom; we have surpassed those very Airāvatas in truth;
and we have surpassed these Kalpavṛkṣas in generosity. Now, since you, our Master, have been surpassed in enjoyment—just as the king is, so indeed are his subjects.
In this case, "O Lord of Speech, O Teacher of the Gods, you too have been defeated by me" is one sentence; "O Lord of the Suras, we have been conquered" is another, the counter-sentence.
Even though there is a commingling of the vocative words which constitute parts of those two, there is no fault, because they function as a sentence and a sub-sentence (upavākya).
That which contains another sentence within its own sentence is called *tadvākyagarbha*. 2.18.
O King, what doubt can there be regarding your sword, which is as cruel as the fangs of Death? For kings who are enemies remain standing [only] because they are blinded by pride.

In this instance, within the sentence "O Hero, the enemy kings stand before your sword," another complete sentence—"What doubt can there be for those blinded by pride?"—remains intact; thus, this is an example of *vākyagarbhita* (an embedded sentence), which delights the connoisseurs and is used for indicating one's own state of being and so forth. (Cvc 2.19)
"O friend Candramukha, sprinkle sandalwood paste from the Mandākinī upon his feet; O friend Padmākṣa, you who possess lotus-eyes, cool him with a lotus; O Madhukarī, extinguish the heat with a lotus!
O Smeraśrī, take the chatterbox Śārikā far away; O Caturikā, [take] Durālāpinī far away! O Śrīsiṅga, my heart’s beloved is here—what is the use of further fabricated words?"

In this context, although the statement "O friends, the moon-faced, lotus-eyed, smiling, and beautiful hero is the one who has entered my heart" is inherently repetitive (*garbhita*)— being expressed through three distinct sentences such as "water your feet," "O friend Padmaka, mine," and "lead Śārikā"— it nonetheless delights the hearts of the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), because it indicates the heroine’s extreme state of passion characterized by the succession of praising the hero's virtues and the resulting surge of feverish longing and agitation.
Regarding the quality [of gender and number]:
where the simile possesses different genders, that is called "dissimilar gender" (bhinnaliṅga);
where it possesses different numbers, that is "dissimilar number" (bhinnavacana) simile.
O Protector of the Earth, Siṅha, just as wisdom derived from the scriptures is white like a swan, so is your fame pure; and just as the moon is radiant, so is your body beautiful.

In this case, the difference in number and the difference in gender between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) are evident; however, where these two do not cause distress to the wise, they are both subordinated [to the poetic figure]. (Cvc 2.21)
Just as wisdom is like eyes that perceive subtle meanings,
so too does fame reign supreme, leaping over all, like the military expedition of the illustrious King Siṅgha.

In this case, although there is a difference in gender and number between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—as in "wisdom is like these two eyes"—no unease arises for sensitive readers because the power of the composition, through the poetic figure of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the qualifying term "grasper of subtle meanings," overcomes that discrepancy; thus, it is considered a merit (*guṇa*).
Where there is deficiency or excess [of attributes] due to the qualifiers of the standard of comparison...
These two are observed to be known respectively as being comparable to the deficient and the excessive.
The crown of King Siṅgha shines with a deficiency in its comparison:
it resembles the peak of Mount Udaya, which is elevated in pride by the full orb of the moon, yet [the king’s crown] is surpassed by the parasol with its golden finial.
In this case, because even a single attribute comparable to a golden jar has been imitated as a qualifier of the moon, this is a "deficient simile" (*nyūnopamā*).
An example of an "excessive simile" (*adhikopamā*) is:
"King Siṅga shines upon his throne, and within his arms is a necklace of trembling pearls."
With its long clusters radiant with fresh sprouts, it was like a wish-fulfilling tree on the slope of Mount Sumeru.
Here, since the objects of comparison—the rubies—are not mentioned, the object of comparison—fresh coral—is in excess; thus, it is "excessive comparison" (adhikopamā).
Scholars recognize that these two [types of simile] attain the status of a poetic figure (guṇatā) due to convention and inference.
An example of the subordination of the quality of the comparison (*nyūnopama-guṇībhāva*) is as follows:
"King Siṅga shines with his raised, formidable sword trembling in his hand, like the auspicious glory [of a tree] with its branch. (Ckc_2.26)

In this case, although there is a deficiency in the simile because the black serpent, which serves as the object of comparison to a sword-blade, is not mentioned, there is no fault; for its cognition occurs without excessive strain due to the conventional usage of the phrase "black serpents dwell in sandalwood.
An example of an excessive simile is:
"The courtesans of the king, adorned with strings of pearls and shimmering silk garments, captivate the heart."
Clear as the spreading radiance of moonlight, resembling blooming blue lotuses, they shone like a full-moon night with its shimmering stars.

In this case, although the blue lotus is an excessive point of comparison, those whose internal faculties have been refined by the knowledge of the invariable concomitance between the side-glances of a courtesan and the casting [of the lotus] perceive the side-glances—which are the objects of comparison—as being like blue lotuses with little effort through the inference that reveals the comparison; thus, it is considered a merit.
However, they know that which is deficient in meter, pause, action, and so forth, to be defective.
In that regard, an example of a verse deficient in meter is as follows:
"May Maheśvara—who is free from deceit, possesses auspiciousness, and is the left-hand portion [of Śiva]—protect you;
he who is the most excellent among those skilled in the arts and the crest-jewel of King Siṅga. (Ckc 2.28)
In this case, because it lacks the third syllable, this is deficient in meter;
elsewhere, however, even a slight degree of its refinement is counted as a merit.
Just as when the flood of the Gaṅga of glory from the shaking of Sirisaṅghabodhi’s head washes over the three worlds, they become completely purified.

Here, in the third foot, because the second syllable is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), it is heavy; thus, although there is a deficiency in the meter, some maintain that in Prākṛta and other languages, syllables such as *hv*, *ñv*, *ā*, and *lp* are treated as light due to being pronounced with intense articulatory effort (*tīvraprayatna*). Therefore, [the verse] possesses the quality [of being metrically acceptable]. An example of a verse deficient in caesura (*yati*) is as follows: [Example omitted per instructions] In this case, the caesura is not observed at the end of the third foot. Thus, the verse is defective in its metrical pause.
While King Śrī Siṅgha protected the earth— which is eternally girdled by the ocean—
hostile kings clearly fled from the earth, while his allies remained firm upon it.

In this case, since a pause (yati) ought to have been made at the third position, it was not so done in the first quarter; thus, this verse is deficient in its pauses. It is considered to be rendered secondary (guṇībhūta) by the influence of vowel coalescence (svarasandhi).
O Śrī Siṅgha, protector of the earth! Even for those who have fled in fear before your military raid— whether they be forest-dwellers or even those seeking safety in the Phakkaṇa village of Ghorāṅga—
the very line of footprints, marked by the thunderbolt, the parasol, and the hand, reveals to everyone from children to cowherds that these are indeed your own, O king.

In this case, although the rule regarding the caesura at the twelfth position was not observed in the third foot, there is no fault because it serves as the basis for a vowel sandhi (svarasandhi), despite the deficiency in metrical structure.
An example of a deficiency in action is as follows:
"By [the king] who is capable of destroying the host of four-fold enemies..."
O protector of the earth, by your sword, those who are proud of their honor shall meet with misfortune.
In this case, the phrase "ending with the action of reducing [the object] to a mere name" does not exist;
therefore, this is deficient in its action.
In the same way, its deficiency in the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) and so forth is also to be inferred.
This [negation] would either depend on terms such as "is" (asti) and so forth, or it would become subordinate to that which is capable [of action].
Just as Rāma, Śrī Siṅghabhūpa, and [the others] are clearly four portions of Hari,
they are equal therein— both being noble and generous— yet they are unequal in their great haughtiness.

In this context, with regard to the first half [of the verse], when there is an expectation that "they exist" (*bhavanti*), even in the absence of other factors, *as* and *bhū* are employed in the first person according to the grammatical rule: "where there is no other verb, *as* or *bhū* is used in the first person. Thus, they possess the status of a subordinate element (*guṇatva*).

In the second half, although there is an absence of action, because the word ends in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) which indicates a connection with qualities such as being high-pitched (*udātta*), it is self-sufficient; thus, it possesses the status of a subordinate element.
It is merely the cause for the manifestation of wonder that has not yet become manifest.
Just as women on the royal road see the king seated in his palanquin as he approaches, with his retinue before and behind him; Ckc_2.*34 //

In this case, because the causes of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), such as poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, are perceived only indistinctly, it exists merely as a "simple" [type] that resides solely in the genus (*jāti*). That simple type may become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) for Vedic scholars (*chāndasa*) in instances such as the benediction (*āsīr*). (Ckc 2.29)
O illustrious King Siṅga, may all the planets, together with their nodes and lords,
always bestow boons and grant the fruits of their positions in the eleventh house.
And may these sacrificial fires— their hearths arranged around the altar, fed with fuel-sticks, with darbha grass strewn along their edges—
protect you as they dispel misfortune through the fragrances of the oblations.

In such cases, although the charm is not fully manifest due to its being "mere" [i.e., lacking other poetic figures], it is still to be accepted because it is a benedictory statement from the great sage Kaṇva, who is a pure Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*).
Thus ends the investigation into the defects and merits of sentences.

Prosperity! This concludes the second chapter (*vilāsa*) of the *Camatkāracandrikā*, cooled by the essence of the nectar of the fame of the illustrious King Siṅga, composed by the moon among the lords of poets, Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the skill of elegant literature (*sarasasāhitya*).
The Third Vilāsa:
*Camatkāracandrikā* composed by the moon-like poet Viśveśvara. In this third Vilāsa, the expressed (*vācya*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meanings are analyzed.
The meaning understood through the function of direct denotation—such as a genus (jāti) and so forth—is said to be the expressed (vācya).
Just as Karṇa was renowned for his generosity, Dilīpa for his compassion, Kāvya for his statesmanship, and Rāma for his humility—
if the illustrious Siṅghabhuja were not already famous through all these qualities combined, he would surely be so.
In this context, because all words denote universals (jāti) and so forth, the status of being the expressed meaning (vācyatva) is understood to belong to the object;
that which is reached through the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) is called the indicated (lakṣya).
The indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha), however, is of four kinds based on its non-connection with the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) in that very context:
it is said to be inherent (samaveta), conjoined (saṃyukta), related (sambandhin), or similar (sadṛśa).
In this regard, the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is integrated [with the literal meaning] as follows: "On the battlefield against every rival, that line of hair on your cheek reveals Rudra;
for upon this lotus-eyed one who has come for refuge, terrified by the illustrious Siṅgabhūpa, that line of your sidelong glance reveals [the Goddess]. (Ckc 3.2)
In this context, the word *rudra* has its primary meaning faltering;

for it is intended by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to convey the power of destroying enemies, which is inseparably connected with that Rudra. Thus, it possesses the character of having an indicated meaning that is inherent [in the primary]. [This refers to] King Kṣitīṅga, who had conquered various distant lands and whose royal title was manifested upon his entry into his own city.
They scatter handfuls of parched grain and flowers as a traditional offering around the courtyards of the palaces, preceded by shouts of "Victory!"

In this context, since it is impossible for insentient palace courtyards to scatter handfuls of flowers, the women of the city associated with those palaces are indicated by the intention to express the abundance of palaces in the city; thus, there is a "figurative indicated meaning" (saṃyuktalakṣyārthatva). The non-primary relationship—such as that between the contradictory and the non-contradictory—is the "possessor of that" (tadvān), namely, the related entity (sambandhin).
Whatever the illustrious protector of Siṅga strives to accomplish, Destiny, having bound herself by a firm vow, stands ready to fulfill it after a long time.
May she abandon her hostility toward us; may you, having achieved your purpose through your efforts, live long, O friend, as we dwell far away—this is our message to you.

In this case, because there is an absence of the connection between a benediction and its intended object—namely, the wish that she may live long in the forest where the enemy kings have been separated by fate—the meaning perceived is one contrary to that [wish], in the form of a curse.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), relations such as that of part and whole are included; for example:
"Summer is in her sighs, the rainy season in the pair of her eyes, autumn on her cheeks, winter on the faces of her friends, and even the cool season upon the substance of her ointment."
O illustrious King Siṅga, while the kings have arrived to serve you, Caitra dwells in the couches of the wives of those rulers.

Here, because there is an inconsistency consisting of a break in the sequence of the parts (*avayava*)—namely, the seasons—the whole (*avayavin*), spring (*vasanta*), is indicated by the preceding part, "Caitra," in order to avoid that fault.
