Due to similarity, the indicated meaning is as follows: when the beloved, having committed an offense against her lover, was turning away before him, a sudden friendship arose between the lotus and the moon.
As the beautiful-eyed lady was unable to utter even a harsh syllable, the two blue lotuses received a shower of frost.

In this context, because the primary meanings of words such as "lotus" (*saroja*) are incompatible [with the literal sense of the sentence], a secondary meaning characterized by the palm of the hand and so forth—which resembles that [primary] meaning—is indicated through *lakṣaṇā* based on similarity.

Whether indicated by the word or by the meaning, accompanied by *vyañjanā*, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is characterized as a fact (*vastu*), a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), or aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and so forth. (Ckc 3.4)
Regarding this, the first [example] is as follows:
"The herd of deer, greedy to gaze upon his playful movements, shall go into these caves; even the tiger, inflamed with rage and intent on devouring them, will become their protector here.
Therefore, King Śrī Siṅga, having gone quickly to this forest for the pleasure of the hunt,"—thus do the enemy kings proclaim a vow of non-fear toward women.

In this case, the fact that the enemy kings, though hidden within it, were not attacked by the leader of the mountain caves is not due to the thought that this is a "fortress" (durga), but rather is suggested as the underlying reality (vastu) through the intention that they had fled and thus should not be pursued or slain. An example of the second [type] is as follows:
While King Śrī Siṅga bore the earth like the lord of serpents, the two [Nagas] Adika and Puṃsa, desiring with joy to make it their pleasure-couch until the end of the aeon, were restrained;

thus, out of concern for the burden on the ground, they once again fell to the earth under the pretext of being a pleasure-couch, and the title "Bhujaga" (the Serpent), which was previously renowned as appropriate only for the duration of an aeon, is now sung.

Here, the poetic figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is suggested: that because there is no battle among all the kings who are the hero’s servants, the Lord of the Skulls (Śiva), failing to obtain a fresh skull, desires to replace his garland of withered skulls with the serpent Śeṣa, who is now relieved of the burden of the earth. Furthermore, it is perceived through that very same [figure] that the hero, by himself fulfilling the task of protecting the world, seems to desire the sleep of the confident Nārāyaṇa.

An example of the third type, consisting of rasa, is as follows, [concerning] the illustrious Lord of Siṅga: "Terrified by the destruction caused by his raiding parties, his enemies—seeing the quarters of the sky with their palm-leaf huts drying up and their footsteps faltering—ran and somehow reached a cave deeply hidden in darkness; even within it, they searched for other pits by the touch of their hands. (Ckc 3.9)

Here, the *bhayānaka* (fearful) rasa, which takes as its locus that which opposes the hero, is manifested through its own *vibhāvas* and other factors by way of imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*).

As for the fourth type, consisting of a transitory emotion (*bhāva*), it is, for example, the friendship between the hero and the *vīra* (heroic) [rivals], or the friendship characterized by innocence and boldness.
We worship that conjugal union, which possesses the grace of the *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava* dances and the nobility of goodness.

Here, in the passage beginning with "maugdhyena" (by innocence), the speaker’s state of devotion is manifested through the composition of contradictory qualities; in "lāsya" (dance) and so forth, through the composition of contradictory actions; and in "dāmpatyam" (the state of matrimony), through the composition of contradictory natures—thereby expressing the speaker’s devotion to the deity characterized as Ardhanārīśvara, who represents inconceivable sovereignty.

In this manner, other suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*)—such as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and so forth, which are included by the word "etcetera"—are to be observed in their respective examples.
Now, the defects of meaning (*arthadoṣa*): the meaningless (*apārtha*), the useless (*vyartha*), the single-meaning (*ekartha*), the doubtful (*sasaṃśaya*), and the misplaced (*apakrama*).
Harsh, tasteless, disagreeable, excessive, and lacking luster.
The defects pertaining to the subject matter of poetry are: inferiority, superiority, similarity, resemblance, the uncelebrated simile, the indecent, and the contradictory. (Ckc 3.6)

In this context, in the phrase "meaningless" (*apārtha*) and so forth, one should understand the neuter gender as being due to a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant. That which is devoid of collective meaning is called "meaningless. (Cvc 3.7)
And just as when the Persian, whose ten faces were like a shrine of Śambhu, beheld the long tip of [the king’s] hand and, thinking it an inaccessible fortress, cried "Kāmadeva! Huṃ Phaṭ!"—
having thus propitiated him who was eloquent with the *praṇava* while his palms were joined in reverence— the Goddess Lakṣmī, being pleased, bestowed auspicious fortune upon King Siṅga.
In this case, because the parts are mutually inconsistent, the emptiness of the collective meaning is quite evident;
however, in instances such as the speech of the agitated or the insane, that very [inconsistency] may become a subordinate factor and serve as an ornament.
In a state of agitation, [they thought]:
"Who indeed will conquer us, the ornaments of the Lunar dynasty, on the field of battle? Alas, cursed fate has turned us away from the fight; shall we take refuge in a fortress?
This man has slain our ancestral kings for so long—shame on our arms! What is the use of the words of King Anavota Siṅgha? Service alone is the proper course."

In this case, although the meanings of the sentences are mutually disconnected, they possess the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) because they indicate the manifold confusion of feelings among the enemy kings who are agitated by hearing of the hero’s victorious expedition.
An example of this in the state of madness (*unmattabhāva*) is as follows:
"Having painted the likeness of King Siṅghana of Anavota out of longing, she gazed at it and, through the delusion of her passionate obsession, thought, 'This is my beloved.'"
Rising quickly from there, she approached with speed, her face slightly turned aside; she gazed at him with envy, a passionate smile, a playful smile, trepidation, and longing.

In this case, although the collection [of words] is devoid of a unified whole because the meanings—such as the sudden rising up, the retreating, and the changes in the gaze directed at the painting—are disconnected, it possesses excellence (*guṇavat*) because it indicates all the stages of passion that demonstrate the heightening of love.
"They say that what is redundant is useless, and that which is already understood is purposeless. (Kāvyālaṃkāra 3.9)
Just as enemies, seeing King Siṅga with their two eyes, advance in battle with their arrays against those who meet them with pride and arrogance,
they protect their own swords with their arms; yet once they have reached the edge of that sword, they erase the musk from the jar-like breasts of celestial nymphs, and they erase it again.
In this context, by the word "looking" (*avalokya*) itself, the sense of "with the two eyes" is understood;

by the phrase "with the two eyes" itself, the sense of "with both" is understood; and by the phrase "he draws the sword with his arm," the sense of "with his own" is understood through the very force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*). Thus, the explicit mention of "eyes" and so forth is redundant (*gatārthatva*).

Since the fact that the enemies have been reduced to mere mention (i.e., killed) is understood through the very act of applying musk-paste for sport with celestial women, the application of musk-paste to the jar-like breasts of one’s own wife—which is obtained here through the power of the pun on the word *svaḥstrī* ("celestial woman")—is rendered purposeless; thus, it becomes redundant (*vyartham*). This fault is designated as "redundancy" (*guṇapata*) when it is intended to be expressed in its entirety. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 3.10)

Just as a woman gazed upon the Lord of the Śiṅga land with sidelong glances— glances that were steady out of wonder, fragrant with unshaken modesty, overflowing with joy, like the eyes of a startled doe, intense with longing, and revealing the very core of the waves of her love.

In this case, although the phrase "with side-glances" (*apāṅgaiḥ*) is redundant because its meaning is already understood by the fact that "the heroine beheld the hero"—which cannot be established by any other means—there is no fault, as it is employed with the intention of expressing specific qualities such as the absence of movement, modesty, and fragrance.
An example of the "useless" (*aprayojana*) is as follows:
"The slender-waisted woman, whose slimness had been overcome by the arrows of Love—which had taken root and sprouted in King Siṅghana through his mental resolves—became as if sharpened."
"Why are these eyes languid with shame, thinking, 'This body of mine has its root in him'? Let them yawn, for the banner of the Lord of Love has arrived, veiled by the lids of the eyelashes."

In this context, although the description of the fish’s expansion is irrelevant to the actual state [of the hero] and thus lacks a direct purpose, it possesses the status of a poetic excellence (guṇa) because it suggests— by indicating the non-reopening of the eyes— that in the world, for those who have been defeated, an expansion [of power] generally does not occur without first causing calamity to the victor; thus, the ultimate limit of the ninth stage [of love-in-separation] is perceived.
An expression whose meaning is not distinct from what has already been stated is called "redundant" (ekārtha);
for example:
"Having destroyed the enemies, he maintains his army by means of wages and honors."
A virtuous king, having struck down his enemies, protects his forces by providing them with wages and food.
In this case, because the intended meaning of the first and second halves [of the verse] is not distinct, they constitute a single sense;
however, when there is an intensification of rasa (aesthetic flavor), this becomes a merit.

Just as when Prince Śrīsṅga ruled the earth girdled by the ocean, unrighteousness was destroyed along with its boundaries; evil deeds were uprooted, which were the very pledges for falling into hell and maturing there; and the garments of the personified impurity of the Kali age were utterly ruined.

In this regard, although there is no difference in meaning among the second and subsequent quarters, the statement "not even a trace of unrighteousness exists in our land" is considered a merit because it was uttered with an overflowing heart, prompted by an extraordinary partiality for the Master who established the Dharma through three proclamations.
That which conveys a meaning that produces doubt is called "sasaṃśaya" (ambiguous).
Just as enemies with inferior means, during the military expeditions of the illustrious King Siṅghabhuja, take refuge in rows of *sāla* trees and treat their lives as mere grass.

In this context, the meaning is that those with inferior means, being hostile, rely upon the *sāla* grove—the line of ramparts—and treat their lives, their very breaths, as if they were grass; that is, they regard them as mere straw.

Alternatively, relying on the *sāla* grove—a garden—those with inferior means make their livelihood, the maintenance of life, like grass. Furthermore, because the doubt arises as to whether there is an absence of a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*) or the presence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*), this [statement] is "doubtful" (*saṃśaya*).
Even for this [person], there is weightiness of virtue when one intends to express excellence and so forth.
Just as women with conversation rivaling the cuckoo and eyes hostile to deer—
though they be beautiful and dark-complexioned— are unable to bring King Siṅgha under their sway.
In this context, those women whose conversations are as sweet and melodious as the song of the cuckoo, rivaling the cuckoo itself;
those whose eyes are like the eyes of a deer, the enemies of the deer;
those lovely, dark-complexioned young women—by stating that they are "unable" (*neśate*) to subjugate the hero, it is implied that he has no addiction to women.

Furthermore, those women whose conversations are like the chatter of crows competing with cuckoos—crooked, dark-complexioned, and black-limbed—are unable to subjugate him. Whether this is intended to show that he possesses knowledge of the *kāmaśāstra* (the science of love) by implying that he does not take pleasure in inferior women who possess the voices of crows, or whether it is intended as a doubt [regarding his character], in either case, the excellence of the hero is perceived; thus, it functions as a poetic merit (*guṇa*).
Where there is a reversal of the sequence of what precedes and what follows, that is "out of order" (apakrama).
Just as on the field of a fierce battle, rival kings, upon seeing the wealth of King Śrīkiṅka,
have the astrologers and masters of time calculate the purification of the hour for their departure.

In this case, having first departed from the city, the rival kings subsequently perform the clearing of the auspicious time for the march that had already passed; thus, there is a violation of the proper sequence (apakrama).
However, in cases such as "wonderful causes" (citrahetu) and others, they generally consider this to be a merit.
O King Śrī Siṅgha, just as you release your mind toward forbearance only after [an offense],
the eastern kings release their forbearance even before [the offense occurs].
In this case,

although there is a violation of the proper sequence (*apakrama*)— since the cause, namely the hero’s patience and liberation [of the enemy], occurs first, while its effect, the subsequent liberation of his own country from rival kings, occurs later—

the fault does not apply; for the description is intended to reveal how the hero’s patience and liberation serve as the means of intensifying the terror of the rival king characterized by the abandonment of his territory.
That which is harsh, having a meaning that is directly cruel, is called *paruṣa* (harsh speech).
"Just as you cast [us] down upon the surface of the Gaṇa stones, or place us in the midst of pits, or throw us before the tigers while the children cry out;
alas, O crest-jewel of kings, today we are all being consumed by fire because of you, who are searching the forest on every side."

In this context, harshness (*paruṣatva*) consists in the utterance of words with a literal meaning that is abrasive—even if intended merely to stop the crying of children—directed toward noble matrons who are hidden in mountain caves out of fear of the commander’s military raid;
yet, it is a merit when such words are employed in recollecting those who have transgressed beneficial advice, and so forth. (Ckc 3.17)
In the *Hitopadeśa*, it is said:
"Is this pair of breasts on my chest better than two celestial jars? Is the nectar from my lower lip more essential than that [divine nectar]?
Who is this who has given birth to you? O Lord Śrī Vīrasiṃha, the mature women, with words of confidence, drive away the enemy kings in their fury as they taste the thrill of daring.

In this case, although there is harshness due to the intention of indicating death, the conflict with a powerful leader—which would otherwise result in death—is avoided; thus, because it serves as beneficial advice, it is considered a merit (guṇa).
An example of recollection of the past (*atikrāntasmaraṇa*) is as follows:
"This tongueless one has been released from the edge of the blade of your sword by your dear friend, and he was not seen by those wretched Kirātas intent on offering him up to the fortress."
Thus he introduces the majesty of the *Mangalasūtra*: "A certain woman, whose wicked husband had been lost in the confusion of the Lord Siṅga’s raid, was [rescued] by her kinsmen. (Ckc 3.25)
In this case, although there is harshness in the first half-verse, it is considered a merit because it is intended solely as a statement that surpasses what was expected.
A verse becomes "tasteless" (virasa) if its meaning lacks flavor due to the stain of impropriety (anaucitya). Ckc 3.18.
Just as when King Siṅga heard the deep sounds of the commencement of battle, the rival kings— desiccated in their palates and with paralyzed legs— fell down;

they were utterly bewildered as the winds issued forth from the bamboo-like sacrificial fat in the mountainous forest regions, bringing a joy to the ears that surpassed even the pleasure of the Vedas.

In this case, for those fleeing out of fear of an attack, it is inappropriate for the mind to pursue the pleasure of hearing the wind through the hollows of the *kīcaka* bamboos; thus, there is a state of "tastelessness" (*virasatva*).
Scholars should recognize that this constitutes the subordination (*guṇībhāva*) of the non-primary element. (Ckc 3.19)

O Hero Śrī Siṅgabhūpa, when the makara-designs are being fashioned upon the surface of your two cheeks with musk, the bold women of your harem suddenly feel shame under the pretext of their own pride— the rival of the Goddess of Royal Fortune belonging to those wicked kings who are your enemies— as they desire to inscribe praises of you upon their own breasts due to their great familiarity with them, yet do so in silence.

In this context, there is the self-reproach directed toward her own harem, which arises from the cause of scratching the hero’s titles [by the rival heroine], is intensified by the proximity of her own attendants and other factors,
is manifested through dejection, wretchedness, despondency, and so forth— inferred from her bashfulness— and is further augmented by those same states of dejection, wretchedness, and despondency,
and finally manifested through mental loathing and the like, inferred from them. This is the self-loathing regarding her own life.

Love (*rati*), ignited by their boldness and other such qualities, manifested through the creation of the *makarika* and the parasol, and intensified by joy and other emotions inferred therefrom, has been concentrated intensely in one place. Although this may seem tasteless due to its impropriety,

because these two serve as the cause for shattering the hero’s title [of "protector"], and because they have attained the favor of the hero’s compassionate glance, they are regarded as instances of the hero’s altruism characterized by the protection of those who have sought refuge.
It is not defective because of its predominance.
The wise say that "broken" [poetry] occurs when the intended stylistic structure fails to reach its completion.

O King Śrī Siṅgha, the women of Gauḍa sing of your virtues— women languid from the intoxication of drinking spirits from Gauḍa, with jasmine garlands slipping from their loosened braids, whose speech falters under pretexts, who possess the splendor of jewels upon their parting lines in their passion, who are like spray from the ocean of youth, and who perform the rites for the successful sovereignty of the arts of Love.

In this case, because the commencement regarding the intoxicated elephant is not brought to a conclusion through the description of qualities such as "intoxicated" (*madavatī*) and so forth, it constitutes a *guṇa* (excellence).
This also constitutes a *guṇa* when, in some instances, the aesthetic luster (*chāyā*) is not lost. (Cvc 3.21)

Just as in the previously cited examples— "summer" (*grīṣmaḥ*) for the sighs, "the rains" (*varṣāḥ*) for the pair of eyes, and "autumn" (*śarad*) for the cheeks— although there is a discrepancy in that the singular number is introduced in the former seasons while the plural number is employed in the case of "the rains," yet because the plural form *varṣāḥ* is prescribed specifically for the plural sense (the rainy season), the unity of meaning is not abandoned despite the hearing of the plural suffix; thus, the "shadow" of the singular number is not lost, and this constitutes a merit (*guṇatva*).
That which is unbelievable, excessively stated, or beyond measure is called "exaggeration."
O Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla, just as the force of the sighs of your enemies turns the mountains and forests into heaps of scorched thickets with their boulders overturned.

In this case, because of the burden of defeat, it is unbelievable that the breaths of the enemy kings—though exceedingly hot and extremely numerous—could possess such an expansive volume or such power to cause burning and agitation; thus, there is an element of exaggeration (*atimātratva*).
Some maintain that this too is a poetic quality (*guṇa*) when justified as before, while others say it is "fullness" (*sarasatva*) due to its conformity with worldly experience. (Ckc 3.23)
O illustrious King Siṅgha, in the raids of your armies, all the oceans were rendered shallow by the clouds of dust tossed up by the trampling of horses;

yet they were made deep once more by the winds blowing from the edges of your fluttering banners. O blessed one, these very oceans have now been filled even more than before by the ichor flowing from the temples of your elephants.

In this regard, although the drying up and turning into dry land of the oceans by the dust raised by the army's horses is an exaggeration (*atimātra*), it does not contradict the actual state of things because one may again imagine them being filled with water; thus, for clever people who follow the path closely, this constitutes a high degree of poetic quality (*guṇa*).
An example of the second [type] is as follows:

"Is this the ancestral deity of the royal line, or is it the bridegroom’s family deity? Or is it the custom of kings, or perhaps a friend of the bride?"—thus do people perceive her at the wedding festival.
Upon hearing the roar of his army, those kings who were enemies of King Śrī Siṅgha fled; yet he was even more adept at cutting through their vital organs than his own sword-blade.

In this regard, because it is said that words pierce the vital organs of the heart even more than a sword, even though they are excessive, such words of theirs pierce the vital organs of the heart even more than a diamond;

how much more so a sword or similar weapon? By following this worldly convention, the Southerners who follow the Vidarbha style are considered to possess supreme merit. It has been stated that [this style] is not excessively clear in its charm and is not lacking in brilliance.
Like those who hate a virtuous king, they dig pits in the forest, devour the deer and the grass, and sleep in the shade of trees.

In this case, because sleep never approaches the eyes in the cities of the enemies due to their agitation by fear, whereas those who have lost their kingdom sleep trustfully in the wilderness like wild animals— since even the intended aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) is perceived only with great difficulty and the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is therefore not clear, it lacks brilliance (*anujjvalatva*).
Those with refined hearts perceive even that [fault] as a virtue.
As in the previously cited example, "All the planets together with the stars," and so forth;

here, although there is a lack of brilliance due to the absence of figures of speech such as genus (*jāti*) and the like, it possesses the status of a merit because it imitates the benedictions of pure Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*).
This [type], characterized by a lowly object of comparison and so forth, is clearly indicated by its very name. (Ckc 3.26)
In this comparison of the inferior with the superior: O Śrī Siṅgabhūpa, upon beholding the line of your sword, whose edge is as sharp as the tip of a blade of *makura* grass,
the enemy kings have fled into the forest, entering the hollows of the mountain clefts as if they were the cave of Nārāyaṇa’s belly.

In this regard, because the edge of the blade is exceedingly sharp compared to the edge of the *kuśa* grass, there is a "lower comparison" (*atinīcopamāna*) due to its inferiority; and because the belly of Nārāyaṇa is vastly greater in extent compared to the cleft of the forest, there is a "superior comparison" (*adhikopamāna*).
An example of an "unlike comparison" (*asadṛkṣopamāna*) is:
"In battle, King Kalyāṇa, with his bow drawn into a circle..."
With its *kalhāra* lotuses shaken by the wind, it shines like the face of the Fish-marked One (Viṣṇu).
In this case, because the bow (kodaṇḍa) and the fragrant water-lily (saugandhika) lack a common quality of fragrance, there is a state of "dissimilar comparison" (asadṛkṣopamāna);
however, in the first two [cases], the subordinate status [of the common quality] may sometimes arise through the skill of the poet.
Just as King Siṅgha, acting as an obstacle, seized a mere trifle of wealth like a mountain of gold,
yet when a worthy recipient stood before him, he cast away his gold like a blade of grass.

In this case, although the golden mountain and a blade of grass are extremely dissimilar in their degree of loftiness, they do not constitute a fault when used as points of comparison, because the intention is to express the hero's preeminence in the acquisition of wealth and virtue and his lack of negligence.
This occurs when a dissimilar object of comparison is employed in figures such as *vyatireka* (contrast) or *upamā* (simile).
For example:
Neither lacking discernment like a common flower, nor becoming hardened like a wish-fulfilling gem,
the illustrious Siṅgha, the ornament of kings— Śiva, Śiva!— is the auspicious fortune and good luck of the world of mortals.

In this case, although there is a disparity between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object compared (upameya), it is considered a merit because it functions as a comparative distinction (vyatireka-upamā). However, that which possesses an unestablished standard of comparison would be "the unfamiliar simile" (aprathitopama).
Just as the women of Ghūrjara— carrying fragrant flowers in their hands and with feet marked by blooming red lotuses— were shattered by the military expeditions of King Śrīkaṅka.
In this case, because *saugandhika* and *kokanada* are not well-known in the poetic usage of masters as points of comparison for the hands and feet of a beloved woman, there is a defect;
yet, in certain instances, even this may possess the status of a merit due to its undulating aesthetic charm.
O illustrious Siṅgabhūpāla, by the rows of arrows discharged by you that fell all around,
the necks of the enemy heroes were adorned as if with garlands for veiling themselves from celestial nymphs.

In this case, although the relationship of the object compared (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) between the row of kings and the bridegroom-choice garland is not well-known, it possesses the quality [of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*] because of the extraordinary charm arising from the similarity of both being causes for enjoyment by the gods. "The indecent (*aślīla*) is defined as that which produces an indecent perception. (Kāvyaprakāśa 3.30)
O protector of the earth, just as your enemies, incited by your blows,
repeatedly rise up and bow down out of arrogance in order to strike at your vulnerability.

In this case, the intensification of the blow refers to striking at a vulnerable spot; furthermore, bending and rising also occur in the penis. Thus, because of that perception, there is indecorousness (*aślīlatva*).
Nevertheless, its status as a poetic merit (*guṇatā*) should be understood in instances such as those accepted by the lords of poets.

Just as after winning at dice, when the rule for the wager was signaled by the placing of the pieces before her friends— a wager whose very nature was an embrace— the beloved of the illustrious King Siṅga,
her eyes fixed upon his face which reflected waves of luster from her softly smiling cheeks, prepared the parrot-cage with fingers free of perspiration.

In this instance, although there is indecorousness (*aślīlatva*) because the perception of an indecorous play involving the transformation of a female śārikā bird into a male through the act of mating is evoked, it is nonetheless considered a poetic excellence (*guṇatva*), since poets themselves accept such indecorousness.
If one asks, "Where have poets accepted this?"—then we shall demonstrate it thoroughly and clearly.
For example: [Example omitted as per instructions] Thus it is.
Then the lord of the earth, having privately smelled his son's face which was fragrant with the scent of clay, did not reach satiety.
Thus, in the *Raghuvaṃśa*,

that love-making of Pārvatī— with its moon-like faces distressed by the seizing of hair, with nails applied astray, full of passion, and with the single string of her girdle loosened— did not lead to satiety.
Thus, in the *Kumārasambhava*,

Mukunda rejoiced with his beloved through embraces that were primarily focused on the face, preceded by long delays, which pressed her limbs firmly yet yielded as her hands moved with loosened restraint.
Thus, at the onset of passion,

the lord of her heart was embraced by his beloved, who— her sash loosened by her excitement— cast aside her upper garment while clutching her girdle, her broad breasts forming a circle as they pressed against him.
Thus, in the *Bhāravi-kāvya*, she,
whose fingertips had quickly traversed the desired notes, sang beautifully with her eyes half-closed upon her waist-knot,
while the strings of her lower lip were struck by the red-tinged lute-player and the circle of her teeth produced a lovely resonance.
Thus it should be understood in the *Māghakāvya* and elsewhere as well:

"That which contradicts place and time, the arts, worldly experience, logic, or scripture, is declared to be 'contradictory' (*viruddha*) by those who know the essence that is the life-breath of literature. (Ckc 3.32)
In that context, "place" refers to Andhra, Mahārāṣṭra, and so forth; "time" refers to night, day, and the seasons.
Gīti, nīti, and other such arts are times dependent upon the aims of desire and wealth.
The activity of all beings, both moving and non-moving, is called "the world" (loka) in this context;
whereas logic is the science of reasoning (hetuvidyā), and scripture is that which is conjoined with the Dharma.
Examples of what is contrary to place and so forth (*deśādiviruddha*) are as follows:

"O Rādhā! In this month, day and night, the affectionate and proud lords of the earth, anointed with musk and longing for the touch of the breezes from the waves of the Yamunā upon their beds of jasmine, have gathered to serve their nurse and leader;
on the mountain of jewels, they sport with bards whose very presence is like the fragrance of necklaces of gems. (Ckc 3.46)
In this case, "the Yamunā in the Andhra country" is a contradiction regarding place; "the *mālatī* flower as a bed in the month of Rādha" is a contradiction regarding time;
and "the fragrance of necklaces" is a contradiction regarding common worldly experience.
These are contradictions with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"The proud ones have gathered together" is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
"The bards are affectionate" is a contradiction with propriety (*aucityavirodha*).
That he plays day and night with other servants is a contradiction of reason;
these are contradictions of inference.
That he plays with the wives of others who have been taken captive is a contradiction of the *Karmasaṃhitā*.
Devotion to other women while one's own wife is present, and placing trust in women who have done harm, constitute a contradiction with the acquisition of wealth.
Playing day and night during the summer, and [only] for half a month during the rainy season and the heat, constitutes a contradiction with the *Āyurveda*.
Applying musk ointment during the summer constitutes a contradiction with the treatises on enjoyment (*bhoga-śāstra*).

The separate mention here of the arts (*kalā-śāstra*), even though they are included within the traditional scriptures (*āgama*), is for the purpose of making known the preeminence of their knowledge within literary composition (*sāhitya*).
This is a merit when there is an intention to describe great portents, supernatural powers, and so forth. (Ckc 3.35)
In the desire to express a portentous event:

"O Lord whose eyebrows are formidable and terrifying! When a wrathful side-glance, rivaling the hue of a red lotus, arises from Your smiling face, alas, in the kingdoms of Your enemies, the mango trees bear abundant buds in autumn, the lotuses bloom within the fire-pits, the stones laugh at dawn, and the twice-born birds fall asleep at twilight."
In this context, "mango blossoms in autumn" is a contradiction with respect to time;
"a lotus in the interior of a fire-pit" is a contradiction with respect to logic; and "stones laugh" is a contradiction with respect to the world.
Although these are defective, they possess the status of poetic excellences because they are intended as omens indicating the approaching ruin and calamity of the enemy due to the hero's anger.
Regarding the manifestation of majesty (*anubhāva*):

Upon seeing the gardens on Mount Rājācala, which have attained such delightfulness through groves of camphor trees whose bases are frequented by herds of musk deer, people rejoice with wonder in their hearts; having heard the artistic prowess of the illustrious King Siṅgha—a feast for the ears—they are filled with unprecedented joy, like parrots beholding a painting of five colors.

In this context, although the presence of musk deer, camphor trees, and other such things in the Andhra country constitutes a contradiction with the nature of the region, it is treated as a merit because of the intention to describe the power of the king— the leader capable of receiving tributes from the lords of various islands. This poetry, consisting of both word and meaning, is [defined] by those learned in words and meanings.
And it is wondrous in three ways, becoming even more wondrous as follows:
And having analyzed it as being most wondrous, it has been illustrated;
when its primary aim is the beauty of sound, it is called "wondrous" (camatkārī).

Just as the king of mountains, Mount Rājaśaila, dwells upon the shore of a lake filled with a flood of water, where the swans have driven away the cranes, and where there is the sweet warbling of rows of bees gathered for nectar at the edges of the lotus buds; so does he abide.

In this case, since the poet’s effort comes to rest merely in the execution of the alliteration (*anuprāsa*), it is said that this poetry is "charming" due to the beauty of the sound alone. However, when the focus is on the beauty of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), it is considered even more charming. (Cvc 3.38)
O Śrī Siṅgha, protector of the earth, for those terrified by the assault of your army and hidden even by their Śabara appearances in the dreadful courtyard of the outcaste settlement,
it is indeed their own trail of footprints— marked with the thunderbolt, the parasol, and the water-pot— that betrays them from the king down to the cowherd boys, even to the children.

In this context, the inference that "these are kings" based on recognizing the series of words marked by royal characteristics such as the thunderbolt (kuliśa) and so forth—which belong to the antagonists, the Kirātas in disguise—is the poetic figure *anumāna* (inference).

Since the poet’s effort finds its rest in that very [inference], it is said to be "most charming" because its intent lies in the beauty of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), transcending the literal words (*vācaka*). And when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is subordinate, the wise call that very same [figure] *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
Here, the eightfold suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), which has become subordinate, is described.
And so they have said:

"The non-hidden [suggestive], the subordinate to another, the factor for the establishment of the expressed, the unclear, those with equal prominence or doubt, that which is implied by the context, and the unpleasant. (Cāṇakya-kāvya 3.40)
Thus [it is said].
An example of the unhidden (agūḍha) suggested sense is as follows:
"Beholding the gardens on Mount Rājācala, which have attained such delight through groves of camphor trees whose bases are frequented by herds of musk deer,
and hearing the ear-delighting fame of the artistic prowess of the illustrious King Siṅgha, people rejoice in their hearts with unprecedented wonder at the five-colored parrots."

In this case, because the suggested meaning— namely, the power of valor (vikrama)— which is rooted in the power of the literal sense (arthaśaktimūla) and consists of the specific nature of the extraordinary gifts sent by the lords of various islands, exerts its influence precisely over that [literal sense], this is a poem characterized as "unconcealed suggestion" (agūḍhavyaṅgya), which is most highly delightful. An example of "suggestion where the suggested is subordinate to another element" (aparāṅgavyaṅgya) is as follows:

O King Śrī Siṅga Pṛthvīpati, the wives of your enemies suffer in the forest regions: with eyes closed for fear of the sight of mango blossoms, they color their cheeks out of fear of the *bandhūka* flowers; with ears closed because of the fear of the cuckoo's cry, they do not listen to words; and with pale faces, intent on flight for fear of ghosts, they do not perceive the distance of the path.
In this case, the separation from the wife of the enemy serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa*).
An example of that which is a subordinate element for the establishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*) is as follows:
"With six [cows] and sixteen [others], the former, one cow was made into a buffalo."
That very [work] was turned into an arrow by the elephant-like King Śrī Siṅgha.

In this instance, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—namely, the characteristic of being a "female elephant" (*gajakāntā*) indicated by the word *vaśā*—establishes the success of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), which is in doubt between a simile (*upamā*) and a metaphor, in the phrase "by the elephant-like king" (*bhūpālakuñjareṇa*). Thus, this is an instance of the "subservient to the establishment of the expressed" (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*). An example of the "indistinct" (*asphuṭa*) is as follows:
"The illustrious King Siṅgha, having crushed the army of his enemies..."
It scatters nectar, the cause of joy for all who hear it.
In this context, Mandara, having churned the ocean, produced the nectar that is the cause of delight for the tongues of only a few;

the hero, however, having churned his army, fills the quarters with the nectar of fame—the cause of delight for the ears of all the world. Thus, by demonstrating the superiority of the hero over Mandara, the suggested *vyatireka* (poetic contrast) is not entirely explicit.
An example of a doubtful suggestion (*sandigdhavyaṅgya*) is as follows:

Seated upon the jeweled archways of the assembly hall by the commanders of the army of the illustrious King Siṅga, [the women] beheld with smiles blossoming upon their cheeks the rows of kings who had arrived from the various quarters of the world. (Ckc 3.55)

In this case, there is a doubt (*sandeha*)—based on the intention of showing honor, or from the recollection of the state of many of his enemies' cowards in battles—as to whether the smiling glance of the army commanders toward the assembly of kings gathered from various directions is intended as such;
this is an example of a suggestion where the suggested meanings are of equal prominence (*tulyaprādhānya-vyaṅgya*). For instance:
"O King Siṅgha, the rising of the sun of your majesty’s valor..."
It constantly torments those rulers of the earth who possess the royal parasol.

In this instance, the predominance of the expressed meaning—"the one who scorches with his majesty torments the enemies who possess parasols"—and the suggested meaning—"he torments us, who are without parasols," is perceived as exactly equal. An example of what is suggested by intonation (*kāku*) is as follows: "O noble elephant, standing before the mountain rocks that serve as food for you, there is a row of horses, resplendent with a speed that has surpassed the sun’s steeds."

In the case of compounds, the absence of compounds (*asamāsatvam*) itself is the style (*rīti*) that causes no agitation to the hearts of connoisseurs;

“She is slender, youthful, with pointed teeth and lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit. (Cvc 4.29)
And so forth, in the *Meghasandeśa*:
"By the hand of the king, fragrant with nails that fashioned the braid of the fair-limbed woman,
this creeper— though its flowers had been gathered— became one upon which bees clung to the stalk."

Thus, in the *Karṇāmṛta*: "When shall I, taking her hand with my own, enjoy the nectar of conversation in the form of the lotus-eyed one— she whose pair of cheeks are blossoming with a wonderful, gentle smile, whose surging passion embraces the system of love?"
Thus it is said in the *Siṅgabhūpālīya*:
"With his limbs oppressed by neck-holds that were primarily focused on the mouth and preceded by embraces from below,
and by the scratching of nails accompanied by loosened embraces— having obtained these from his beloved, Mukunda rejoiced."
Thus it is in the *Kandarpasambhava*.

In this same way, in other compositions following the Vaidarbha path, one should understand that the form of composition involves the occasional use of short compounds, the absence of compounds, or the incorporation of long compounds in various places.
Furthermore, a compound consisting of fewer than ten words or more than ten words is considered "middling"; a composition possessing such is called *madhyamasamāsā* (middling-compounded).
O illustrious Siṅgabhūpa, through the power of experiencing the sweetness of the stream of nectar that is the play of your words,
the wise become such that drops of tears of bliss flow forth from their pair of eyes with half-closed lids.

Examples of excessively long compounds consisting of more than ten words are as follows: "In the darkness bound to the shoulders of Hari, whose chest was shrouded by a mass of dust raised by the weight of the powerful army of King Śrī Siṅha, which served as a companion to the shadow [of his own body] as it was covered [by that dust]."
In the sky, the Siddhas praise him, their minds delighted by the pacification of the multitude of obstacles to the amorous play of embracing a young woman whose breasts are immeasurable in span.
The *sahakāra* (conjunction) style is the mixture of styles such as those without compounds and so forth;
for example, when there is a mixture of the styles without compounds and with very long compounds.
The three worlds, their impurities removed by the waves of the ocean of fame of King Siṅgha— the crest-jewel of the Avitukṛta dynasty—
vie with the celestial river whose foam is produced by the friction against the matted locks of the many-eyed Śiva.
In this [verse], the first half contains no compound, while the second half contains an excessively long compound;
examples of the absence of compounds and the presence of medium-length compounds are as follows.

O King Siṅga, may the edge of your sword, which clings to your arm upon the battlefield— repelling the service of attendants who apply beautiful *pāṭīra* paste to the wives of rival kings, and possessing the beauty of a series of braided locks for the Goddess of Victory— be ever triumphant!
In this [verse], the first half contains a middle-length compound, while the latter half contains no compound;
examples of very long and middle-length compounds are as follows:
O King Siṅgha, having repeatedly drunk the liquor of fresh fat— its bubbles swelling with the playful luster of the millions of crest-jewels of enemy chariot-warriors in battle—
the Piśācas sport together with their female companions, clapping their hands in rhythm to the *kreṃ-kreṃ* sounds and indulging in the grand clamor of *kahaka-ha* cries.

Here, in the first half there is an excessively long compound, while in the second half there is a medium-length compound; other instances of this kind should be understood in the same way. Thus concludes the analysis of *rīti* (diction).
That which directs the mind toward expansion, distraction, agitation, and likewise toward elaboration— that is a mental activity (vṛtti), and it too is of six kinds.
Kaiśikī, Ārabhaṭī, Bhāratī, and Sātvatī,
as well as Madhyamārabhaṭī and Madhyamakaiśikī.
The erotic and the pathetic are mild; the comic and the marvelous are very slight;
the furious and the loathsome are intense; and the heroic and the fearful are somewhat so.
The Kaiśikī style is desired when both word and meaning are characterized by softness.

Just as the young woman gazed at the Lord of the Mountain with sidelong glances that were steady from wonder, suffused with the fragrance of unabated modesty, overflowing with joy, resembling the startled gaze of a doe, and— due to intense longing— piercing to the very core of the waves of her affection.
They say that the *vṛtti* is *ārabhaṭī* because of the maturity of both its meaning and its words.

O Protector of the Earth, Śrī Siṅgha, may that pride of your enemies— pride which causes even Rambhā and others to tremble with agitation— be utterly shattered in battle by your sword, whose flashing blade is capable of splitting the tusks of the earth-born elephant and is raised aloft as it firmly grasps the necks of the haughty and arrogant Jambha-demons.

Here, the softness of the composition (*sandarbha*) consists primarily in the prevalence of smooth, low-vowel sounds; because the subject matter is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), there is softness in the meaning as well. Here, the density of the composition results from the prevalence of harsh, high-vowel sounds.
Because its subject matter consists in the destruction of adversaries, it possesses depth;
the Bhāratī style is held to have soft subject matter but a mature composition. (Ckc 4.34)

Just as she had previously won from him the embrace and other such favors during the game of dice indicated by the placing of the pieces before her friends, so now, when the rules of the wager were signaled by the setting of the pawns,
that beloved Śārikā— her eyes meeting his face with waves of luster reflecting from her cheeks blooming with laughter— prepared her parrot’s accessories with perspiring fingers, O King Śrī-Śiṅga.
In this case, because the subject matter is erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), there is softness of meaning;
whereas the composition, consisting mostly of harsh-sounding syllables, possesses maturity (*prauḍhatva*).
The *sātvatī* style is desired when there is a mature subject matter combined with a soft arrangement of words. (Cvc 4.35)

Just as the pearls fallen from the crest of the sword and the ploughshare-like weapon of the illustrious King Siṅghabhuja sparkle on all sides upon the battlefields smeared with blood and flesh, like the stainless sprouts of his fame.
Here, because the subject matter consists of the destruction of enemies, there is *prauḍhatva* (maturity/forcefulness);

because the composition primarily consists of syllables with few breath-units (*alpaprāṇavarṇa*), there is *mṛdutva* (softness). When the subject matter is soft and the composition is slightly mature, it is the *madhyamakaiśikī* style. (Ckc 4.36)

O King Siṅga, consider in your mind whose infamy it is when, in the course of conversation, it is said: "She, that girl with the arched brows, has resorted to you, and thus even the opportunity for emaciation does not touch those who have taken refuge in you; yet she herself takes on that thinness. Ckc_4.42*42.
In this case, because the subject matter is one of separation (*vipralambha*), there is softness;

yet, because the composition consists mostly of conjunct consonants and short syllables, it possesses vigor and thus a slight degree of firmness. When the theme is mature, the *ārabhaṭī* style is neither too soft in its progression nor [too harsh]. (Ck 4.37)
Is this the crest of the fire at the end of an aeon, or is it perhaps the tongue of Death, or the fang of Yama at the dissolution of the world?
Thus is the line of the sword brandished by the hand of the illustrious King Siṅga conjectured upon that ground frequented on the battlefield.
Here, because the subject matter consists of the act of combat, there is maturity (*prauḍhatva*);
because the composition is begun with mixed phonemes, there is no excessive softness.
This is the analysis of the poetic styles (*vṛtti*).
They say that the perfection of speech is its ripening, which is rich in aesthetic flavor;
this, in brief, is of two kinds: soft and harsh.
In this regard, an example of "mild ripening" (*mṛdupāka*) is as follows:

"What need is there for Kāma? What need for the moon? Or what need for the fragrant [Malaya breeze] or even for Jayanta? By my good fortune, O King Anavota-siṅgha, I have beheld your form! Blessed indeed are those two beautiful eyes by their very service to you! Thus she speaks before her friend, her hair standing on end, the surface of her cheeks moist with perspiration, and her words faltering.
In this context, the transformation of sound (*śabdapariṇāma*) that yields aesthetic relish without effort, like the ripening of grapes, is called "mild ripening" (*mṛdupāka*).
This is generally observed in the compositions of eminent and impassioned poets, whose works result in the outpouring of bliss through the delineation of the natural lines of poetic art.
For instance, in the case of Kālidāsa:
“Even the Daughter of the Mountain [Pārvatī], revealing her emotion through her limbs... and so forth, in the *Kumārasambhava*.
And likewise, from Śrī Harṣadeva: "The passion of the people has blossomed; shame is heavy; there is no other refuge, dear friend. Love is difficult to bear; death is the final resort. (Ckc 4.46)
And so, casting off the heat of her perspiration with the tips of her nails, Lakṣmī struck me right on the forehead;
yet the Lord, under the pretext of warding off the blow from the wind of the swift ocean, protected himself by bristling his body hair.
Thus it is in the case of the arising of passion (*kandarpa*);
in this same way, it should be understood elsewhere as well.
For example, as in the case of *kharapāka*.

In this mind-pavilion of this fair-bodied woman— where the pillars are established by the neighing of her beautiful eyes, which are lovely with the hue of bashfulness, where the archway is formed by the movement of the corners of her playful glances,
and which is graced by the charm of the blossoming of her emotional fervor— the form of King Siṅga occupies the throne of empire.

In this context, a transformation of sound (*śabdapariṇāma*) that, like the ripening of a coconut, yields its flavor only after being delayed by the labor of reflection, is called "harsh ripening" (*kharapāka*).

This is observed only among the learned who have mastered the stages of poetry, whose inner minds are permeated by the latent impressions of *vakrokti* (poetic deviation), and for whom the fruit is merely the demonstration of their erudition.
For instance, in the case of Murāri:

Whose hearts would not be captivated by these young women, who are charming with a softness blossoming in the present moment; whose breasts, as if out of consideration for their hardness, have been bent down by their youth; and in whom the awakening of passion is made smooth by a momentary lapse of modesty?
Likewise, all the hairs of the poet of the *Naiṣadha* were eager from childhood to behold an excellent woman;
they felt as if they had experienced the stretching out of their necks toward her, whose slender body was thus covered in blossoms.
Just as it was rightly reasoned by you that this very thing is sufficient for yourself— that I shall indeed take refuge in this [forest]—
yet, without him, it would be false speech on your part to strike at your own self and not to do so toward the king.
In this manner, it should be applied elsewhere as well.
Thus ends the analysis of ripening (*pākaviveka*).
Regarding the state of beings (*śayyā*): there is mutual friendliness among them, yet they are incapable of exchanging [their conditions].
That indeed is his ultimate limit; his bed is distinguished by its location.
"This is what is well-known in the world; it is called 'resting' by the wise."
When the drums of King Anavota-siṅga’s army were being struck with forceful beats, resounding with the sound "dhaṇaṃ dhaṇaṃ dhaṇam," his veteran warriors rejoiced,
crying out "raṇaṃ raṇaṃ raṇam," while the opposing kings fell into a state of confusion, thinking "tṛṇaṃ tṛṇaṃ tṛṇam."
Just as the herd of deer, greedy for a playful glance, will go into these caves, so shall the leopard, inflamed with rage and devoted to devouring their flesh,
become here; and the enemy kings, fearing King Śrī Siṅga Bhūpa Udayāditya and others who delight in hunting them, shall observe a vow of not looking at women.
In this context, although synonyms for the words exist, the *śayyā* (bed) consists of mutual friendship because the words cannot withstand being interchanged.
Here, with the intention of providing a detailed exposition in a separate section on *rasa*, the nature of *vṛtti*, *pāka*, and *śayyā* has been defined out of sequence.
Thus ends the analysis of *śayyā*.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Discernment of Qualities," in the *Camatkāracandrikā*, which is cooled by the essence of the nectar of the fame of the illustrious King Siṅgha, composed by the moon-like poet Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the art of elegant literature.
The Fifth Vilāsa. The *Camatkāracandrikā*, composed by the poet-moon Viśveśvara; the Fifth Vilāsa. Manifesting as if visibly present through the artistry of its composition.
And that which is the supramundane taste—this is considered the "flavor" (rasa) here.
Through that lineage, the glory of poetry has attained loveliness;
by means of it, the poet fashions fame that lasts until the end of an eon, indeed for an entire eon.
By the scripture stating "That indeed is the essence," it is declared that the Self is on an equal footing with Brahman;
yet this essence is experienced by only a few through good fortune.
Śiva is declared by the best of those who realize the truth to be Rasa;
otherwise, how could he possess eight forms for the benefit of the world? (Ckc 5.4)
It consists of eight types, including the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the comic (*hāsya*), which are established as the heroic (*vīra*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*);
the furious (*raudra*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*) exist in pairs, as do the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*).
Just as sweetness is universally esteemed among tastes such as the bitter and others,
so too is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) the most worthy of sovereignty among sentiments such as the comic and the rest.
One who desires to relish the poetry of the poet should exert effort toward that [experience],
through the realization of which the wise do not despise themselves.
"For that indeed is poetry wherein the poet's intense resolve resides, or where his mental impression (vāsanā) flashes forth; such was the ancient saying."
May *vakrokti* long endure, and may *svabhāvokti* remain; yet it is my view that only those works containing *rasokti* are worthy of being grasped as poetry. (Cvc 5.9)
Who would approve of word and meaning being devoid of aesthetic flavor even when endowed with qualities and other such excellences, like a husband and wife lacking mutual affection? (Ckc 5.10)
Even a slight expression of aesthetic flavor (rasa) is sufficient to create splendor in poetry;
even a tiny fragment of camphor makes another thing fragrant.
Persistence, manifestation, continuity, completion, nourishment, and commingling;
diminution, appearance, tranquility, and the remainder—these are indeed said to be the expressions of rasa.
The manifestation of rasa within its own locus occurs through the excellence of the qualities of the determinants (vibhāva);
the existence of rasa consists of the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) such as love (rati), and that [love] is itself [the essence]. Ckc 5.13.

The substratum (*āśraya*), the object (*viṣaya*), the incitement (*protsāha*), and the auxiliary factors (*sahakārīṇi*)—through the complete totality of these threefold determinants (*vibhāva*), there occurs in its own substratum a mere manifestation (*unmeṣamātra*) of rasa; this alone is what is meant here by "existence" (*sattā*).
That very existence persists in the form of the mere [emotions] such as love (*rati*) and the rest.

And [the emotions] beginning with *rati*—namely, love (*rati*), laughter (*hāsa*), energy (*utsāha*), wonder (*vismaya*), anger (*krodha*), sorrow (*śoka*), disgust (*jugupsā*), and fear (*bhaya*)—are called "stable" (*sthāyin*) because they persist as a flow of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), serving as the substrata for the successive emergence of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
Among these, the existence in the form of love (*rati*) is as follows:
in the courtyard at the foot of a mango tree, where pairs of bees hum sweetly, where the male cuckoo warbles, and where the ritual of worshiping the sandals of Smara has begun;...
When the king cast his eyes from afar upon the lotus-face of Śyāmā—the deer-eyed one with dark, dangling locks and sweet lips—his gaze was fixed.
In this case, by the mere description of the causal conditions (*vibhāva-sāmagrī*), the hero’s longing is perceived; thus, this is the existence (*sattā*) of rasa.

Whether it be the manifestation of a single ensuant (*anubhāva*) or a natural emotion (*sāttvika*), if there is a throbbing radiance (*sphurattā*) resulting from the sequence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), that is what is designated [as rasa].
Manifestations (*anubhāva*) are briefly said to be of two kinds: physical and vocal.

Although they are manifestations, the *sāttvika* states—characterized by paralysis, fainting, horripilation, perspiration, change of color, trembling, faltering speech, and tears—are mentioned separately in order to highlight their specific distinction.
The radiance of rasa in the form of *rati* (love) is like that which was sought by a king, while fondling a gem on his armlet, in the presence of his own friend.
With the slopes of her dark breasts bristling with horripilation, she gave him her reply with the utmost reverence.

In this context, the manifestation of rasa in the hero consists in the production of the heroine’s *anubhāva*—namely, her fondling of her breasts which reflect the gems of the necklace upon his armlet;
and in the heroine, it is the very throbbing [of emotion] brought about by the single, genuine [sign] characterized by horripilation.
And as follows:
O King, by the festival of touch from the breasts of the young woman, sprouts of horripilation were borne as if they were shoots of passion;
and her sprout-like hand, too, manifests drops of perspiration as if for the purpose of sprinkling them.

Here, the throbbing manifestation of the rasa is indicated by the successive appearance of the involuntary physical expressions (*sāttvika*) of horripilation and perspiration. Through the powerful latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) and other factors, this single consequent emotion (*anubhāva*) may recur again and again. (Ckc 5.15)
Whether occurring simultaneously or as a single transition among these many [elements],
this is called "connection" (anubandha) by those who know the sequence of aesthetic flavors (rasa).
An example characterized by the repeated recurrence of a single sentiment (*bhāva*) is as follows:
at the conclusion of the spring festival perfumed with camphor, as the playful women were departing for their own mansions,
the illustrious King Siṅga was addressed many times with sidelong glances and necks turned back.

In this case, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of sexual passion among amorous women, ignited by the qualities of the hero and the spring season, is continuously bound together by the physical manifestation (*anubhāva*) characterized by the repeated turning of the neck and the casting of sidelong glances;
thus, this [passion] is so described.

An example characterized by its connection with multiple manifestations (*anubhāva*) is as follows: [Her face] drenched with gentle smiles and struck by rising beads of sweat, with horripilation appearing and a constriction in her throat manifesting—
The limbs of the playful women became helpless before the bodiless god of love through the glance of the illustrious Siṅgabhūtalapati.

Here, the love of playful women—whether contemporary or ancient—directed toward the hero is described as such because it is ignited by the hero’s glances and other such acts, and is bound together by many *sāttvika* [emotions] such as gentle smiles, physical exertion, perspiration, and so forth;
and by the *sañcārin* [transitory states], namely: envy, despondency, dejection, languor, fatigue, intoxication, pride, apprehension, fear, agitation, madness, epilepsy, and disease.

Delusion, death, laziness, dullness, shame, dissimulation, forgetfulness, and doubt; as well as reflection, thought, intelligence, fortitude, joy, longing, ferocity, indignation, compassion, envy, fickleness, sleep, slumber, and awakening—these are the thirty-three [transitory states].
Their connection with a single prevailing emotion is as follows: in the dwelling of Vāsantikā, amidst the sweet warbling of bees and the tinkling of Mādhava’s beautiful anklets...
Desiring to be united with the illustrious Lord of Siṅga, she placed the curve of her own cheek upon his lotus-hand.

In this case, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the heroine’s passion, which has the hero as its object, is ignited by springtime and other factors; it is then sustained by the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of anxiety, which is inferred from the heroine’s own physical manifestation characterized by her placing her cheek upon her palm.

This is what is described [in the verse]. Some maintain that when a single transitory emotion is presented alongside a single physical manifestation, this expression of rasa is merely a flash of aesthetic resonance (*sphurattā*).

We, however, maintain that in this liberation [of rasa], there is a connection between the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) and the dominant emotion (*sthāyin*) through the influence of the latter; thus, because a sequential connection is possible, we recognize it as a continuous bond (*anubandha*). Others have declared this very same principle even when there is an abundance of transitory emotions (*sañcāribhāva*).
It is my view that what is being described is indeed a difference [from the effect] due to its production. (Cvc 5.17)
Just as a certain woman with eyes like a deer's, beautiful of gaze, having beheld the Lord who is the ornament of the land of Siṅga,
looks in every direction, reproaches herself, and rests her cheek upon her palm.
Here, anxiety is perceived through looking all around; despondency regarding her own beauty is perceived through self-reproach and censure;
and reflection is perceived through the contact of her cheek with her palm.

In this case, even though there is an absence of the association with actual physical manifestations (*anubhāva*), because the manifestation of *rati* arises— just as in the state of "continuation" (*anubandha*) or during a state of abundance of transitory moods (*saṃcāribhāva*)—

it is easily understood that this is indeed a "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) and not merely "continuation. This is because, like [the rasa] ignited by the perfuming of a dwelling and so forth, it is produced by a specific intensity, and because the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) appears with full perfection.

The fourfold excellence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), arising from the combination of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), the involuntary states (*sāttvika*), and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*), is proclaimed as its "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*).
Just as a certain fawn-eyed woman, upon seeing the Lord of Siṅga— the sole abode of virtues— becomes perspired, smiles sweetly,
and her body breaks into horripilation as her creeper-like brows arch; she trembles, becomes agitated, turns her face aside, presses her cheeks with both hands, and embraces her own friend.

Here, the heroine’s love, which has the hero as its object and is kindled by his proximity and other factors, is refined by bodily-origined *anubhāvas* characterized by a smile and the movement of the creeper-like eyebrows, by *sāttvika* states characterized by perspiration, horripilation, and trembling, and by *saṃcāribhāvas* (transitory emotions) such as fear, shame, dissimulation, and agitation— inferred respectively from her agitated state, the turning of her face aside, the covering of her cheek, and her embracing of her friend.
Thus, this is the production of rasa in the form of love (*rati*).
Its excellence and nourishment are held to result from the object, the basis, the cultivation, the qualities, the natural aptitude, proficiency, and the intensity of the lamp. (Cvc 5.19)
Just as the body of that fair-limbed woman attained a supreme, guileless loveliness before her friends when embraced by the Lord of the Siṅgha realm,
so too does the Flower-Arrowed God, with his mind satisfied by the fulfillment of his own command, wish for her welfare through his own merits for him who closes his eyes at that moment.

Here, the love (*rati*) of the hero— who is of a *dhīralalita* (calm and playful) temperament— directed toward a heroine endowed with qualities such as beauty, youth, and excellent character, is awakened by the intensity of the refinement of mental impressions accumulated through familiarity;

and being further inflamed by the excellence of the excitants (*uddīpana*), which consist of the contemplation of the natural loveliness of her limbs and their arrangement, it [is described] for the sake of his friends...
She dwells in the seventh stage of passion, characterized by the abandonment of shame, which is inferred from the physical manifestation of embracing another in her presence;
furthermore, she is one whose nature is moistened by a steady affection directed toward the hero, arising from the excellence of all her personal virtues.

The heroine’s passion, being awakened by the intensity of her latent impression (*vāsanā*) through familiarity and suitability, and being further inflamed by the excellence of the stimulant (*uddīpana*) of the embrace of her beloved who is dear due to supreme love, occupies the ninth stage—the nourishment of love—which is inferred through the consequent (*anubhāva*) of the closing of her eyes; this, then, is the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasapuṣṭi*).
Indeed, the ten stages of the nourishment of love have been illustrated in the *Siṅgabhūpālīya*. (Ckc 5.20)
Longing, reflection, recollection, praising of virtues, and agitation;
along with playful gestures, intoxication, disease, stupor, and death—these are the ten [stages].
He shows them in succession:
[one might object] that there, this set of ten stages was indeed presented as being produced by the *vipralambha* (separation) known as "love at first sight."
If it is asked how this is determined by means of *saṃbhoga* (union), it is said:
it should be understood that poets have generally cultivated this [sentiment] in *vipralambha* (separation),
and not that it is prohibited in *saṃbhoga*.
When another entity exists as the cause for the simultaneous arising of a power,
that conjunction of one with the other is called "confusion" (saṅkara).
Just as she was seen again and again by King Siṅgha, her former beloved,
she sank into the waves of wonder, anger, and affection, O proud one.

Herein, wonder, anger, and affection—arising respectively from his prior offense, his being witnessed [by her], and his status as a beloved; further inflamed by the discernment of specific qualities in those [characters] dependent on each; and brought to their state of supreme intensification through the power of the verbal expression of the *vācaka* (denotative) words constituting the nature of the narrative—are manifested as appropriate by means of *anubhāvas* (consequents) such as unblinking eyes, quivering lips, and the loosening of the waist-knot, as well as *sāttvikas* (involuntary states) such as paralysis, pallor, and horripilation, and are accompanied by the *vyabhicārins* (transitory states) such as agitation and joy, which are illuminated by the use of the word "wave" (*ūrmi*).
Because they arise simultaneously and with equal force, these waves are intermingled and produce the perception of a mixture of aesthetic flavors (rasa); thus, this is called a "mixture of flavors.
This occurs when [a flavor] has reached the highest pitch for some reason whatsoever.
The wise know that decrease of rasa to be *hrāsa* (decline).
Just as her breathing was inferred from the manner of her speech, the movement of her eyelashes from her glances, and the sandalwood paste from her embrace,
she asked him about his journey to the King’s mountain; and he, in turn, taught her the proper way of service, while she offered her salutation according to custom.

In this context, the decline of the nourishment of love between Pāṇḍya and his consort—characterized by agitation—is brought about by the afflictions of exile from the kingdom and forest-dwelling; this is perceived through the mental effort (cittārambha) manifested as the conceit that sighing and other such acts constitute obstacles to the enjoyment of speech and the like.

This is understood through two types of exertion: in one case, through the verbal effort of addressing her with an invitation to go to the royal mountain for the sake of serving the hero, and in the other, through the exertions of speech and body consisting of the instruction on modes of service and prostration.

Thus, this is the statement regarding the diminution of rasa. Even when it manifests due to the impropriety of the objective basis (*ālambana*), this slight semblance (*ābhāsa*) is said to appear as if it possesses rasa. (Cvc 5.24)
In that regard, the semblance of the erotic (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*) is said to be fourfold:
because of the absence of passion in one case, because of its occurrence through inequality in many cases, because of having animals as its object, and because of having barbarians as its object.
Here, the impossibility of passion is threefold: due to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*),...
This is because of the absence of both prior destruction and absolute non-existence.
In this regard, concerning the prior non-existence of passion (*rāga-prāgabhāva*), there is no fallacious nature (*ābhāsatā*);

for when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for seeing and so forth is present, the arising of passion is possible. However, in the case of the other two [types of non-existence], there is indeed only fallacious nature.

Since passion is utterly absent, the path of her sidelong glances has been rendered useless; her meaningful, slow smile, her suggestive speech, and her prostrations with folded palms have all become false and in vain.
The leader of the Recarla clan truly desires no other wife; O friends, you and I must remember him again and again—he is indeed Satyavrata.

In this context, the passion of a woman belonging to another (parakīyā-nāyikā)— which has reached its highest intensity, characterized by her repeated efforts to abandon her body and inferred through the expressive behavior of her addressing her female companions with prayers for the remembrance of her beloved—

is, on one hand, fragmented because the jewel-like hero (nāyaka-ratna), who is the object of her affection, is entirely devoid of passion for another's wife; nevertheless, it still manifests as if it were the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
This, then, is the expression of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsokti).
In the same way, other examples may also be cited.
When powerful and adverse causes have arisen...
The merging of the abundance of flavors back to their root is said to be tranquility.
Just as when King Siṅgha, enraged at the ruler of Kaliṅga, was about to bestow his daughter— the most excellent of women— as a tribute upon him,
the stream of arrows from his bow turned away; for his eye, beholding the creeper-like brow of that maiden, avoided the outer corner and instead exerted its full power of passion within his heart.

In this case, although the hero’s anger—which had previously been directed toward the King of Kaliṅga—was aroused, it is entirely pacified by a love directed toward the daughter of the Kaliṅga king; for that love is strengthened by the favor generated by the presentation of appropriate gifts by a powerful [ruler]. Thus, this is a statement regarding the subsidence (*śama*) of a rasa.
This occurs either because the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the rasa is stable, or because the character (*prakṛti*) of the person is amenable to being won over.
Even the fragrance that remains when [the body] has dissolved is called the "residue."

Just as King Śrī Siṅghabhūpa— whose mind was profound with the power of his vow of courtesy— did not direct his gaze, rippling with passion, toward the circle of Śyāmā’s breasts, nor toward the two frontal globes of another elephant,
so too did that accomplished lord not perform such an act of the eyes for any other fair-browed woman.

In this case, although the hero— whose nature is that of the *dhīralalita* (the composed and playful)— has been brought to a state of total absorption by a powerful love directed toward his dark-complexioned mistress (*śyāmā*), the particularity of his love for another heroine still manifests through the courtesy of casting side-long glances;
thus, this is an instance of "expression of the remainder of the aesthetic flavor" (*rasaśeṣokti*).

In this same manner, the ten modes of expression such as "vibration" (*sphurattā*) and so forth should also be investigated by oneself regarding the sentiments (*rasa*) of humor (*hāsya*) and the rest. Although we have a particular predilection for the detailed elaboration of poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), we shall nevertheless provide a brief definition of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and the others.

Herein, the aesthetic sentiment known as *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) has for its basis (*ālambana*) a beautiful woman or man; it is stimulated (*uddīpana*) by enchanting objects; it possesses as its manifesting effects (*anubhāva*) the play of graceful creeper-like eyebrows, side-long glances, gentle smiles, and so forth;

it is nourished by the remaining transitory emotions (*sañcāribhāva*), such as all the *sāttvika* states, longing, agitation, lassitude, disgust, and dissimulation; and it has *rati* (love) as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*).

Distinguished by the varieties of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and *saṃbhoga* (love-in-enjoyment), it presides over an expansion of the mind characterized by the disappearance of all other objects of cognition.
Herein, an example of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) is as follows:
With her heart violently shaken by the moonlight, sandalwood paste, and breezes, and with the glory of her longing aroused for a union with King Siṅgha,
the slender lady directed piteous glances toward her affectionate circle of friends— glances that caused her lower lip to wither from sighs and completely suppressed the rising of tears.

Here, the love of a certain heroine directed toward her hero—though its desired embrace and other such acts are unattained—is being intensified; it is inflamed by the moon, sandalwood paste, and breezes (the word "and" implying the inclusion of unmentioned factors such as the warbling of male cuckoos); it is indicated by physical effects such as sighing and the like; it is manifested by the involuntary symptoms (*sāttvika*) such as tears; and it is inferred from signs such as emaciation and a wistful gaze.

Nourished by the various enemies such as lassitude, fatigue, despondency, agitation, and dejection, and because it has dissolved all other objects of cognition, that [joy] manifests in the heart of the lover as a state of expansion; attaining the nature of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), it is thus described.
An example of the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*) is as follows:
The body of the fair-limbed maiden, embraced by the lord Śrī Siṅghabhūti in the presence of her friends, attains a supreme luster that is sincerely desirable;
with his mind satisfied by the fulfillment of his own command, the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma) blesses him with auspiciousness through his own merits for one whose eyes meet hers at that moment.

That which is called "the comic" (*hāsya*) has as its objective support (*ālambana*) those such as the hunchbacked or the dwarf; it is intensified (*uddīpana*) by the contemplation of their true nature and so forth; it possesses as its consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*) the dilation of the eyes, the expansion of the cheeks, the knitting and contraction of the eyebrows, and so on; it possesses as its involuntary concomitants (*sāttvika*) tears, perspiration, and the like; its permanent emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*) is laughter, primarily consisting of joy, dissimulation (*avahittha*), and fortitude;
and it manifests through various distinctions such as the "smile" (*smita*) and the "laugh" (*vihasita*), shining forth precisely as a condition of expansion.
Just as when a king sees a man and a woman presented as gifts by the lords of other islands, he smells their blooming cheeks;
the king’s ministers laugh with wide-open eyes, the lord, pressing his garment, laughs aloud, and the people on both sides, their eyes clouded with tears, laugh.

Here, the humor (hāsya) based on the couple consisting of the hunchback and his partner—which rests upon the hero and other characters—is ignited by the contemplation of the apparent activities of that man and woman; it is indicated by bodily effects such as the expansion of the cheeks and the like; it is nourished by the transitory emotion (sañcāribhāva) of dissimulation (avahitthā), which is inferred from acts such as smelling the toy lotus; and thus, presiding over an expansion of the mind, this is indeed the comic sentiment.

The *vīra* (heroic) rasa is that which has as its locus a protagonist of preeminent nature, whose object is a transcendent matter; it is characterized by the *uddīpana-vibhāvas* (excitants) such as the recounting of the prowess of such ancient figures, innate courage, and so forth; by the *anubhāvas* (consequents) such as a brightened countenance, trembling of the arms, and the gazing of the sword; by the *sāttvika-bhāvas* (volitional states) such as horripilation and trembling; and by the *vyabhicāri-bhāvas* (transitory emotions) such as joy, envy, indignation, fortitude, and resolve; its dominant permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is energy (*utsāha*), which constitutes the glory of the mind.
He presides over vastness;
