just as Rāma felt no joy upon beholding his own two arms when he heard of the method for binding the ocean, so too he feels no joy upon hearing of other islands during his conquest of kings from every quarter of the world.
The foremost of the Recara lineage, the jewel that adorns the lord of the Śrī Siṅga realm, did not prize self-glorification when bestowing gifts, even upon gods who made no requests.

Herein, the enthusiasm—which has the supreme hero as its locus and the attainment of supramundane status as its object—is ignited by such things as hearing the heroic exploits of Rāmabhadra. This enthusiasm is characterized by the name *śobhā* (splendor), which possesses the defining marks of being a genuine human quality (*pauruṣasāttvika*) manifested through the sight of the King’s arm; it is further marked by the hope of conquering other continents, arising from a specific sense of rivalry toward Rāmabhadra indicated by the King’s gaze and by a disregard for the sovereignty over Jambūdvīpa. It is expressed in the words: "Restrain your excessive rivalry! [and so forth].
Manifested by the power of a mental exertion and augmented by envy, lack of fortitude, pride, and the like, it presides over an expansion of the mind;
such is this "heroic warrior" (*yuddhavīra*).

Likewise, in that very same context, the "heroic donor" (*dānavīra*) is also manifested by the power of a mental exertion characterized by the longing and desire of a deity as the agent of a request, [and it presides over] the itch-like urge to bestow specific objects obtainable from that deity.
It attains the highest excellence.

The permanent emotion (*sthāyībhāva*) of wonder (*vismaya*), characterized by extraordinary names, manifested through supermundane sights and the like, with its consequent emotions (*anubhāva*) such as fixed eyes, shaking the head, snapping the fingers, and cries of "well done," its involuntary physical manifestations (*sāttvikabhāva*) such as horripilation, and its transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as joy, agitation, fortitude, and intelligence, presides over the very expansion of the mind.

Having heard in the assembly the account of King Siṅgha’s conduct, the twice-born who had come to the earth to receive the sacrificial offering and had returned related it to Indra and the other gods;
Dilīpa and the others, exclaiming to one another, "Excellent! Excellent!", their eyes wide with wonder at the periphery and their hair standing on end, shook their heads in approval.

Here, even the Kali age—having as its object the meritorious deeds of the Leader (the Buddha) through his establishment of the Dharma and so forth, and having as its support ancient great kings such as Dilīpa—is a source of wonder.

This wonder is intensified by the examples of the high regard shown by Mahendra and others; it is inferred from the physical effect (anubhāva) of the eyes becoming fixed; it is particularly manifested by the involuntary emotion (sāttvika) of horripilation; and it is nourished by joy, agitation, and other states inferred from shouts of "Well done! and the nodding of heads, thereby assuming the secondary characteristic (upādhi) of the expansion of the mind.
Because it is desired [by the audience], this is the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*).
The wrathful sentiment (*raudra*) is that which rests upon cruel persons;

its object is the offender, its primary excitants (*uddīpana*) are the recollection of their injuries and so forth, and its consequents (*anubhāva*) are the knitting of the brows, the clashing of teeth, harsh glances, and the like.

The latent emotion (sthāyibhāva) of anger, manifested through a variety of transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as indignation, envy, restlessness, and ferocity, and accompanied by involuntary physical expressions (sāttvikabhāvas) like perspiration and trembling, assumes the limiting adjunct (upādhi) characterized by mental agitation.
For example:

Your sword, the instrument of retribution, rends the host of enemies of the illustrious King Siṅgha; it flashes with sparks of anger flickering from the movement of its eyes, it is terrifying with the knitting of its brows, it roars harshly while biting its lip with its teeth, and it causes sweat to form and limbs to tremble from the weight of the fever of irresistible and insolent pride.

Herein, the emotion of anger—whose locus is the hero, whose objective is the resorting to an adversary—is ignited by such acts as the invasion of a country, the slaying or binding of kinsmen, and so forth;

it is manifested through physical signs such as the knitting of eyebrows, the gnashing of teeth, and the clenching of lips; it is made manifest by the two involuntary emotions (*sāttvika-bhāva*) of perspiration and trembling;
and it is nourished by the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāri-bhāva*) such as pride, indignation, restlessness, ferocity, and resentment, which are themselves indicated by those very same signs.
That which unseals a wave of bliss characterized by mental agitation in the minds of spectators is called the Furious (*raudra*).

That which is named Compassionate (*karuṇa*) has as its object a deceased friend or similar person; it is excited by the recollection of their virtues and so forth, has lamentation, falling [to the ground], and so forth as its consequents (*anubhāva*), and possesses paleness, paralysis, tears, and facial expressions as its involuntary (*sāttvika*) states; with despondency, exhaustion, despair, wretchedness, agitation, madness, and so forth as its transitory (*sañcārin*) emotions, it has sorrow as its permanent (*sthāyibhāva*).
One perceives only the limiting adjunct characterized by the agitation of the mind;
for instance:
"Is this that face? Is this he with his arms? Is this that breast of yours? Alas, Lord of my life! O friend, I am here—I am not shattered, though the heart of a woman is indeed deeply rent."
Thus, even the elemental beings feel compassion for these laments of the queens of the enemies of the illustrious King Siṅgha, heard in great numbers upon the battlefields.
Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of sorrow— based on the daughter of the enemy clan of the hero and directed toward her deceased beloved— is fragmented;

it is then kindled by the recognition of her various dismembered limbs and so forth, indicated by the non-deviating characteristic of pointing with the hand (*hastārambha*) through the verbal expression "this is that," and its final development follows that [recognition] through inevitable manifestations such as the shedding of tears and changes in complexion.

Manifested by a collection of *sāttvika* emotions, and nourished by transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*)— such as dejection, despair, despondency, and mental distress— inferred from the commencement of speech regarding various appropriate objects like the beloved (*priya*) or the lord of one's life (*prāṇeśa*),
and further embellished by lamentations suggested by the word "etcetera," as well as by others such as exhaustion, fatigue, apprehension, agitation, and madness;
it produces an excess of compassion even for those who are like wooden posts due to their lack of emotion, or even for beings such as *vetālas*.
That which presides over the nourishment of agitation in the mind of the spectator is called *karuṇa* (the pathetic).

That which has loathsome objects as its domain is named *bībhatsa* (the loathsome); it is ignited by the perception of defects in those objects and so forth, possesses external manifestations (*anubhāva*) such as closing the nostrils, contracting the mouth, and narrowing the eyes, has sattvic qualities (*sāttvika*) such as change of color, and has transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as despondency, agitation, fickleness, and shame; its permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is disgust (*jugupsā*).
One whose mind possesses a matured disposition takes hold of the stage of bliss characterized by distraction;
just as one covered all over by swarms of flies might touch a pus-filled ulcer with a piece of cloth, as if it were merely a remnant of darkness.
A poor person suffering from ringworm makes people at the edge of the road quickly move away, with the corners of their eyes narrowed and their noses covered.

In this context, the feeling of disgust (*jugupsā*)—which has as its objects the hero’s enemies, lepers, and those afflicted by disease, and which is supported by people—is stimulated by such things as wounds and hemorrhoids; it is manifested by the contraction of the eyes and so forth;

it is nourished by agitation and restlessness inferred from the act of fleeing far away; and by imparting to the spectator's mind the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) characterized by mental distraction, it is designated as the "Foul" (*bībhatsa*).

The *bhayānaka* (the terrible) has terrifying objects as its domain; its *anubhāvas* (consequent effects) include parched mouth, licking of the palate, and retreating downward; it possesses *sāttvika* [emotions] excluding tears; its *saṃcāribhāvas* (transitory emotions) include despondency, apprehension, terror, agitation, dejection, stupor, exhaustion, fatigue, anxiety, epilepsy, and so forth; and its *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion), fear, takes as its basis precisely that stage characterized by mental distraction, as follows:
The enemies of the illustrious Lord of Siṅga, agitated by the mere sound of his military expedition, look toward the quarters of the sky with parched palm-leaf-like mouths and stumbling feet;
having somehow fled and reached a cave deeply hidden by darkness, they search even within it for other pits by the touch of their hands.

In this case, the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) residing in the enemy who has taken refuge [in the cave]— concerning the vanguard soldiers of the hero Kriyākrūra— is excited by the hearing of the raid,

manifested through consequent states (anubhāvas) such as running, entering the cave, and searching within the chasms, and nourished by transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as agitation, apprehension, and terror, which are inferred from throat-drying, stumbling of the feet, and so forth, [is established] in the mind of the spectator.
Bearing the stage characterized by distraction (*vikṣepa*), it is called "the Terrifying" (*bhayānaka*).

This entire aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and human goal (*puruṣārtha*), though made an object of the mind of sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), appears in some form or another through the assistance of a specific cultivation born from the mature ripening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which are produced by the worship of the pair of lotus feet of the Goddess of Literature, accomplished through thousands of births.

If it is asked, "What indeed is this form (*ākāra*) of rasa by which it is experienced by the minds of the connoisseurs (*bhāvaka*)," we reply: since that form is to be known solely through one's own individual experience (*svasvānubhavaikavedanīya*), how could the verbal activity of those like us ever suffice to fill out its nature? For even Brahmā, though he might drink the entire ocean of milk, is unable to point out that specific excellence of sweetness (*mādhurīviśeṣa*) by defining it as "this. However, the long-lived one should find satisfaction in repeatedly revolving in his mind the traditional formulation—"the state in which all other objects of knowledge have dissolved"—until the perfection of *bhāvanā* is attained. Indeed.

"According to the maxim of the 'space-cake,' this [notion] that 'this is flavor' is clearly [a construction] for those men whose eyes are closed; such is this stage of the imaginative subject. (Ckc 5.28)
The establishment of the object of knowledge depends upon the means of knowledge; this is agreed upon by all philosophical systems.
Beyond this, the talk of "taste" (rasavāda) is merely a false claim; it is nothing but talk of taste.

This [self] is not to be characterized by direct perception, nor is it accepted as being known through inference; it is not easily accessible through scripture, nor is it measured by means of analogy.
It is not established by presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), nor by non-existence (abhāva); it cannot be conceived through tradition (aitihya), nor is it licked [by the senses]. (Cvc 5.31)
To this it is replied: the very manifestation of one's own experience is the proof for the existence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); this is the supreme secret.
This has been demonstrated immediately below.
Furthermore, this other display of verbal bombast is written for the delight of those eminent disputants whose intellects itch with the desire for the amusement of various debates.
For instance: surely, when this [object] is being perceived, does it appear through non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) or through conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*)?
Not the first.

Because non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) has as its own nature the mere manifestation of the essential form of an object, whereas taste (*rasa*) has as its nature a cognition preceded by the recollection of specific qualities such as existence and so forth on the ground;
and because conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is preceded by non-conceptual cognition—if this is argued, then listen:
we say it is by means of conceptual cognition.
The assertion that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) is preceded by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is indeed charming only so long as it remains unexamined;
for a cognition that does not represent a specific object is simply impossible.
Thus, the yogi Hari, while elucidating the intention of the venerable Patañjali—who is a particular incarnation of the Supreme Lord—has declared:
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge is perceived as if it were permeated by speech.

Thus, even inference (*anumāna*), by way of being "seen through generality" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), engenders great confidence within oneself as the revealer of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*): "These members of the audience possess the experience of aesthetic flavor;
for whosoever is characterized by the intended gestures, they all possess the experience of aesthetic flavor."
Just like those who have experienced the direct realization of reality,
so too are these individuals distinguished by their conduct;
therefore, they are indeed possessors of the experience of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Nor should one suspect a deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) regarding the example,
because it is well known that at the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), tears and the like arise from within.
Thus, it is stated in the *Mahimnaḥstava*:

“Fixing their attention upon the inner consciousness, with their vital breaths stilled, the hairs on their bodies bristling with joy, and their eyes bathed in the waters of rapture—beholding which, the self-restrained (yamins) sink as if into a lake of bliss consisting of nectar, and hold within them some ineffable reality; that, indeed, is You.

Thus say the scriptures, and likewise the collections of ornaments by the ancient poets who, having realized the secrets of many philosophical systems, speak according to what they have directly perceived.
And therein, rasa alone is established as being supreme above all;

even the simile—“rasa is like the direct perception of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra), just as a gavaya is like a cow”—serves to confirm the existence of rasa by demonstrating its experience, thereby ensuring that the existence of the self is not in vain.
Furthermore, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) also establishes the existence of rasa as something that cannot otherwise be accounted for.

Just as for Devadatta, who does not eat during the day, nocturnal eating is postulated because his corpulence would otherwise be inexplicable, so too is "rasa" [postulated] because the existence of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), the determinants (*vibhāvas*), the consequents (*anubhāvas*), and so forth, would otherwise be inexplicable.

Now, one might object: even in the absence of the perception of *rasa*, what is inexplicable about the transitory emotions and the rest, which are independent and can themselves be experienced as aesthetic relish in certain instances?
If someone should ever employ an independent designation for the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth merely by way of metaphor— just as one uses the term "king" for the king’s men— they are,
by virtue of their being objects of a countable category of real entities, merely manifesting their own misfortune by failing to perceive the sovereign majesty of the Great King Rasa.
Even traditional lore (*aitihya*) is external when it does not accord with the aforementioned means of valid cognition.
It does not at all encounter any obstruction in the definition of rasa.

Thus, while this nectar-like flow of rasa, established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is being experienced by the wise, even a single instance of the "non-apprehension of the fit" (*yogyānupalabdhi*)— which is the very definition of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*)—
illuminates the lack of discernment in the minds of those illiterate ones who stubbornly persist in their sole obsession with the disparagement of rasa.

And so it has been said by our own teacher, Kāśīśvara Miśra, in the *Rasamīmāṃsā*: “Disregarding the beauty of rasa, to build an archway of mere verbal ostentation is like the experience of dregs [from sugar-cane] out of hatred for the juice of the sugarcane. (Ckc 5.33)
The definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth should be understood from other sources.
For poets employ conventions of meanings established by worldly consensus;
indeed, in this very [tradition], they are the sole witnesses to the direct realization of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
The detailed exposition of the definitions and illustrations of other [figures] not mentioned here is found in the *Rasārṇavasudhākara* composed by King Siṅga Bhūpāla.
The two types of playfulness in the first and second [stages] should be properly cultivated;
however, we have not elaborated upon them here because our gaze is fixed elsewhere.
For it is not possible to demonstrate all the specific details of everything everywhere, because the fault of excessive prolixity would lead to the consequence of the work being cut short.
In the treatises, only a mere indication is taught for the wise;
the specific details manifest of their own accord through thorough cultivation.
Thus ends all that is auspicious.

Thus concludes the fifth chapter, titled "The Discernment of Rasa" (*rasaviveka*), within the *Camatkāracandrikā*, an ornament composed by the moon among poets, Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the art of elegant literature and cooled by the essence of the nectar of the fame of the illustrious King Siṅga.

The Sixth Vilāsa: *Alaṅkāravilāsa*, from the *Camatkāracandrikā* composed by the poet-moon Viśveśvara. [Section on] the Particularity of Location (*Ekadeśagata*): Just as bracelets and other ornaments [adorn only a part], yet [are said to adorn] the entire body.
Those things which adorn poetry are considered to be "ornaments" (alaṅkāra).
Their threefold nature has been explained due to the occurrence [of defects] in the word, the meaning, or both;
herein, eleven [types] residing in the word have been proclaimed by the wise.
Shadow, seal, logical connection, the composition of paronomasia and alliteration, the variegated, the yamaka, dialogue, the hidden, and the question-and-answer—these are the [figures]. (Cvc 6.3)
This is illustrated as *chāyā* (shadow), which is an imitation of *anyoktis* (indirect expressions);
it is threefold, according to whether it follows the style of urban, rustic, or general speech.
In that regard, an example of the style of urban speech (nāgarikokti) is as follows:
"Salutations to that walking pillar who did not sprout, even though he was sprinkled with the nectar-essence of the auspicious words of King Siṅga."

Here, the "shadow" (chāyā) is an imitation of the speech of clever people who utter the word "namas" in a sarcastic manner, as in: "Salutation to the one who is both moving and stationary" (*jaṅgamasthāṇave namaḥ*). An example of the shadow of vulgar speech is:
"Friend, behold the royal splendor of those who have taken refuge at the pair of feet of King Siṅga!"
"O beautiful one, what is this marvel? O Queen, even upon a serpent, why are there bracelets of glass?"
In this fourth quarter, there is a shadow (*chāyā*), which is an imitation of the speech of common folk who claim that a specific excellence arises from a specific basis;
it is a shadow of general statement as follows:
"Who is this that extends the desired object for supplicants? Surely it is the *cintāmaṇi* jewel. But is it truly a stone? No, indeed, it is not a man—what more need be said?"
How is it known that this King Śrī Anavataptasiṅgha is present here? When the hand-palms shine with jewels, what need is there for a mirror?

In this fourth quarter, regarding the matter established by direct perception, the thought "what need is there for anything else? is expressed through an imitation of a statement common to all people—namely, "What is the use of a reflection in a mirror when one can see the bracelet on one's own hand? This is the shadow of a general statement (*sāmānyokti*).
It is the application of a word with a specific intended meaning (*sābhiprāya*) to a sentence.
Those who know the seal of poetry recognize that as the *mudrā* because it bestows great joy (*mud*).
This has been described by the wise as twofold: by way of the word and by way of the sentence.

"O noble elephant of your desires, swallow the petals of our wish-fulfilling vines! May they be transformed by the pedestals of my *cintāmaṇi* jewels; do not run far away!"—thus do the goddesses of the earth cry out at every step from atop their balconies when King Siṅha is intent on bestowing gifts such as wish-fulfilling trees, fragrant cows, and elephants.

In this context, because the *Kalpalatā* and other such works are suitable for deities, the term "earth-deities" (*bhūdevatā*) is more noble than even terms such as "virtuous Brahmins"; thus, this is the *padamudrā*.
As for the *vacanamudrā*, it is as follows:
"O you who have been honored by the streams of milk from the udders of Surabhi in the shade of the *santāna* and *santānaka* trees on the edge of the Cintāmaṇi altar..."
"Do not be proud, thinking 'we are gods,' for we have clearly been seen by the astonished side-glances of the Lord of Siṅga, whose glances are the stage for compassion."

In this context, because of the intention to refer to the plurality of deities who are identical [in nature], the plural form "we" (*vayam*) is employed for the speaker himself; this is the Seal of Speech (*vacanamudrā*). When the wise apply a connection between mutually related words that is appropriate to the subject at hand, that is called "Logical Reasoning" (*yukti*). (Ckc 6.7)
In this regard, an example of the construction of words that were not previously connected is as follows:

"The fame of King Siṅga shines resplendently, situated within the treasure chest of Śambhu’s ornaments, shimmering on all sides like a rival to Śrī, and entering the middle station of Viṣṇu. (Ckc 6.6)

In this instance, regarding the subject matter beginning with "pātāla" (the netherworld), the words such as "Śambhu’s ornament-box" (*śambhubhūṣaṇapeṭikā*) are joined through a sequence of effortless application; thus, this is the figure of speech known as *padayukti* (the conjunction of words).
In this same manner, examples for specific types of sentences, contexts, and compositions should also be observed.
[Furthermore: "The expression of two meanings by means of a sentence of a single form..."
For where there is a double entendre (*śleṣa*) by means of *tantra*, that is considered to be of many kinds.
By means of roots, suffixes, words, case-endings, numbers, and so forth.
In that regard, an example of *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic punning) is as follows:
"O King Śrī Siṅgha, this prostration of yours, which bestows auspiciousness,
is for the learned in this world who know the essence of meaning, and even for those who are hostile."
In this passage, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the verbal roots *dadāti* and *dadati* in the word *kalyāṇada*, and between *vetti* and *vidanti* in the word *sāravidām*.
"O King Siṅga, may your hand bring joy to the learned;
it is clearly the cause of the ruin of enemies and the prosperity of friends. (Cvc 6.8)
In that regard, within the word *kartā*, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the suffixes *tṛc* and *tṛn*. "The agent (*kartā*) of the misfortunes of enemies" employs the suffix *tṛc*;
"the maker (*kartā*) of prosperity" employs the suffix *tṛn*.

Otherwise, since the genitive case governed by a verbal noun (*kṛdanta*) would necessarily occur, two distinct suffixes would have to be intended to connect those two cases; therefore, this has been stated in such a manner.
An example of word-play (*padaśleṣa*) is as follows:

"Hariścandra [shines] in the protection of his subjects, in his delight for truth, in the playful elegance of his speech, in the mastery of words, in great self-restraint, and in the conduct prescribed by the Vedas."
Victorious is the noble King Śrī Siṅgha, the sustainer of the people, who has conquered the son of Gaṅgā and excels in the arts of enchantment and the observances of his vows.

Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the two words "Hariścandra" and "Candra," which both denote a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); between the two words "Vāgīśa" and "Vāgīśa"; between the two words "Gāṅgeya" and "Bhīṣma," which both denote [the same person]; and between the two words "Gāṅgoyaṃ" and [the other term]. This is therefore called *pada-śleṣa* (word-paronomasia).
The pun on case endings (vibhaktiśleṣa) is twofold:
homogeneous (sajātīya) and heterogeneous (vijātīya).
Of these, the first is as follows:
May the Lord, who stands resplendent with the Kaustubha gem and dwells upon the lotus-like breast of Śrī, protect King Siṅga, as he bears that very chest upon his own.

Here, the word *virājī* is in the locative case (*saptamī*) meaning "he shines in the midst of the birds (vīnām)," and it is also in the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) meaning "shining with Lakṣmī and the Kaustubha gem" (*virājī* as "having the nature of shining").
Since these two words *virājī* share the same nominal suffix (*sub-vibhakti*), this is a *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) of identical case endings (*sajātīya-vibhakti-śleṣa*).
Just as King Kīrtiviśāla seized the hearts of his enemies and split open the chests of beautiful-eyed women,
so too did King Śrī Siṅga seize the hearts of his own trusted followers and break through even their formidable fortresses.

In this passage, the hero stripped away the fame of his enemies—that is, he took it away—and by that very act, he caused the breasts of his enemies' wives to be without necklaces (*avidyamānahāram*). Here, within the single word *ati* (in the form *vyatāni*), there is a pun consisting of two distinct grammatical elements: the *luṅ* verbal suffix in the first person and the neuter accusative case ending.
This constitutes a "pun on different case endings" (*vijātīyavibhaktiśleṣaḥ*).
The same should be understood regarding the term "indivisible" (*abhedī*) here as well. An example of a verbal pun (*vacanaśleṣa*) is as follows:
"The auspicious ones who enjoy the sacrificial sessions are the source of hopes and the boundary of glories."
May Śauri and the gods bestow auspiciousness upon King Siṅga.
Here, Śauri Nārāyaṇa, bestowing auspiciousness upon the protagonist, may grant it—*vitaratu*.
This is the third person singular form in the imperative (*loṭ*) of the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) derived from the root *dad*, meaning "to give.
Of what nature is Śauri?
He is the source—the place of origin—of hopes, meaning the fulfiller of the desires of those who bow before him; he is the limit, the ultimate boundary, of fortunes and prosperity.
He is a *sattra* because he protects the virtuous (*sat*);
one whose arm (*bhuja*) is such as that is called *sattrabhuja*.

"Śubhāḥ" means those whose splendors or radiances (*bhāsa*) are beautiful; however, in the context of the gods, it refers to the deities. "Dadatām" means "may they bestow" or "may they grant"—this is the third person plural of the present imperative (*loṭ*) of the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) derived from the root *ḍudāñ* (to give).
Of what nature are the gods? They are the source and lords of the quarters and directions; they are the limit and the boundary of glories and prosperities.
"Those who eat at a sacrificial session (*satra*) are *satrabhujaḥ*.

"Those whose radiance (*bhāḥ*) or luster (*kāntiḥ*) is beautiful (*śobhanā*) are *śubhāḥ*. According to this stated method, when a qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇapada*) in a verbal form (*kriyāpada*) possesses both singular and plural endings simultaneously, this is "punning on number" (*vacanaśleṣa*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), "punning on dialect" (*bhāṣāśleṣa*) is also included, as for example:
O you who are the banner of the people of Pūrva-Rāmā, may sovereignty belong to you for the sake of gathering [the assembly], O hero whose mind is directed toward Gadānasiṅga.
*Gādana*: because he speaks first, addressing [others] beforehand, he is *gādana*.
Its vocative form, *pūrvābhibhāṣin*, means "O you who speak first.
To such a one as you, [is given] the kingdom.
O Sigana, O King Siṅga! You whose banner is the fish— the banner of the city women, the banner of Rāmā, meaning the one who intoxicates women—
[I call you] with my mind for the assembly of heroes.

*Mā* and *ilā*—these two are *lakṣmī* (prosperity) and *bhūmi* (the earth); their *ayana*, or path, is *melāyana*. For that *melāyana*—meaning for the place of residence of prosperity and the earth—let there be for you such a kingdom; let there be the capacity for the duty of protecting the subjects, and may it prevail with supreme excellence. This is how the Sanskrit language is understood. In words such as *melāyana*, where the meaning is expressed through local dialects like "may it become auspicious" (*bhadram abhavat vai*), the Telugu language is also perceived by those who know that regional tongue.
Thus, this is *bhāṣāśleṣa* (punning on different languages).

In this manner, instances of *bhāṣāśleṣa* involving Sanskrit, Prākṛt, and other languages should be investigated for oneself within various highly diverse compositions by great poets. As for *anuprāsa* (alliteration), it is the repetition of phonemes occurring in close proximity.
Briefly stated, this is twofold: the non-pervasive and the pervasive.

O Lord of the Siṅga land, your sword— the affectionate braid of the Goddess of Victory— shatters the non-pervasive [arts]: the melody of the Gauḍī songs, the secret dalliance of the Kosalīs, the musk-deer-mark on the cheeks of the Nepālīs, the drinking games of the Keralīs, the application of sandalwood paste by the Lāṭīs, the arrangement of flowers by the Kuntalīs, and the locks of hair of the women of Kuntala.
In this case, because the alliteration (*anuprāsa*) takes different forms in each sentence, it is an "incomplete" (*avyāpaka*) alliteration;
for example:
"Victorious is the noble one, who is far removed from the conduct of the base, whose nature is to honor the virtuous, and who is favorable to truth that is worthy of praise."
The son of Abhinava-suradhenu, who was nourished by [his] food, was Siṅgabhūpālacandra, dense with virtues praised by the earth.
In this [verse], the alliteration from the beginning to the end of each word (*padādyāntānuprāsa*) possesses a different form in every quarter-verse (*pāda*).

An example of pervasive alliteration (*vyāpakānuprāsa*) occurs in the genealogy of the hero himself: "Where there was the binding of feet, the grazing on grass, and the departure from one's own city..."
Whether it be wandering in the forest or serving those who practice such [ascetic] conduct, it is a refuge for those who are opposed [to worldly life].

In this case, because the pair of the letters *ra* and *ṇa* recurs everywhere, this is all-pervasive *anuprāsa* (alliteration). In this manner, other types such as *vṛttyanuprāsa* and *lāṭānuprāsa* are to be understood.
The proper arrangement (*samyagghaṭanā*) of words in the context at hand is considered *guṃphanā* (composition).
The word *atra* (here) is of two kinds: meaningless and integrated into another composition. Regarding the first, an example is as follows:
"By the sounds of the war-drums of the panegyrists who set forth for victory in battle against the illustrious King Siṅgha, the enemies became newly engaged [in flight]."
Suspecting their own shadows to be rival combatants, they run about, agitated by fear, crying out "Be careful! Be careful! Be careful! at every step.

Here, the stringing together of meaningless words (*nirarthaka-śabda*) in accordance with the context of the subject at hand—beginning with the word *be* and so forth—is what constitutes "the stringing together of meaningless words.
The stringing together of words composed by others is threefold:
the stringing together of a single quarter-verse (*pāda*), the stringing together of two quarters, and the stringing together of three quarters.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"The person is the slave of wealth"— this [statement] is not to be taken as a cause for shame,
for one who observes King Siṅga sees that wealth is indeed the slave of the person.
In this context, because the first [example] mentioned at the outset is composed in accordance with the subject at hand, it is a "joining of feet" (pādaguṃphanā) woven elsewhere.
An example of the second is as follows:
"A youth, with arms long as a yoke, muscular, with a chest like a door-panel and a thick-set neck..."
Thus, while this path of poetic composition finds its true purpose only in King Siṅga, elsewhere it merely plunges into the realm of mere literary artifice.
In this case, the composition of these two quarters [of a verse] is such that it conforms to and completes the first half composed by Kālidāsa.
An example of the third type is as follows:
"Possessing a form that is not surpassed by things of its own kind or of a different kind..."
King Siṅga shines as long as he conducts himself according to the essence [of dharma].

In this case, although the first three quarters were composed by an earlier author of an alaṃkāra treatise, they are arranged here in accordance with the context of the subject matter—existing as something that cannot be bypassed by either proponents or opponents for as long as the aesthetic flavor (rasa) persists; thus, this is a "combination of three quarters. However, figures such as the *cakrabandha* (wheel-arrangement) and others are not approved by all poets.
Because it opposes the flourishing of aesthetic flavor (rasa), it is the sole cause of mental affliction.

Just as the wheel-binding [of the earth] was attained by that sovereign who sported through the quarters with his discus, who possessed a splendor eclipsing the sun, and whose fame shone like light for an eon, filling the sky during his moments of rest—

just as Māndhātṛ attained the beauty of the learned when he entered and made manifest the entirety of the Āgamas— he does not reach even a fraction of the brilliance of one who knows his specific excellence.
In this [work], beginning from the rim, in the third interval the name of the composition is given as *Camatkārajyotsnā*;
in the seventh, the name of its author is *Viśvapati-kavi*;
and in the ninth, the name of the hero is revealed.
By the word "etcetera," the *paṅgabandha* and other such forms are included.
Here, the *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement) is as follows:
"And she [is] that one who has destroyed the demons of worldly existence (*bhāva-rākṣasa*), whose feet are understood through the syllables, and who possesses the essence of the Māra-slayer."
Sārasā is compassionate, Siṅgayā is flavorful, Rasā is flowing, Gajavatī is powerful, and Sā is momentary.
In this world, she by whom the cruel-minded *rākṣasa*s—those of evil disposition—have been destroyed is "Kṣapitabhāvarākṣasā," meaning she has impoverished the cruel folk.

She, whose lotus feet are known through the syllables [of sacred texts] by the learned (*sākṣarāvagatapādasārasā*), that is, whose lotus feet are meditated upon by the wise; may that Lakṣmī, who is the abode of the lotuses of the *sārasa* birds, cause King Siṅga—the one who attains (*yāti*) the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the most excellent object on earth—to resort to her, to worship her. *Sārasādāvāsapadmādayatu* means "may she cause him to take refuge in the lotuses that are the dwelling place of the *sārasa* birds."

Likewise, "Gajavatī" means possessing her own supporting elephants (the *dig-gajas*); she is both patience (*kṣamā*) and the earth (*bhūmi*). Other instances of this kind should be understood in the same way.
The Yamaka (rhyme), however, consists of the repetition of consonants and vowels that are inseparably connected;
it is threefold, occurring at the middle, the end, or both, with the repeated sounds having distinct meanings.
The initial *yāmaka* (repetition of the first two syllables) is as follows:
"O Compassionate One, may my compassionate mind, which has entered [the path], become sweet through you, O Sweet Lord, with your respectful care. (Ckc 6.23)

In this instance, the first three syllables of each of the four quarters, accompanied by the initial syllable, are repeated according to the *āntaratama* (nearest-similar) principle; thus, this is a "yamaka at the beginning of all quarters.

In the same way, other varieties of *dvipādādiyamaka* (yamakas occurring at the beginning of two or more quarters), including their distinctions as separated (*vyavahita*) or unseparated (*avyavahita*), should be understood by oneself.
An example of *madhyayamaka* (yamaka in the middle) is as follows:
O King Siṅha, whose splendor is filled with supreme delight, tell me: what enemy can endure the sword of your majesty, which is eager for battle and adorned with the fame of dense glory? Ckc_6.24
In this case, in all four quarters, excluding the first syllable, the middle syllables are repeated without interruption; thus, this is a "middle-of-all-quarters" *yamaka*.
In this same manner, other varieties of the preceding quarter should also be examined.
An example of the final-quarter *yamaka* is as follows:
May he who has made Vasudeva virtuous, and who has bestowed abundant wealth upon Vasudeva, protect you— who possess fame and fragrance like Mount Meru, O King Siṅha, steadfast as Meru— for all time.

O Merudhīra Siṅga Mahīpāla, may Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who, like Vasudeva, made his own birth purposeful by making Anaka-dundubhi (his father) a performer of virtuous deeds; who, like that deity, bestowed abundant wealth; and who, like Yaśassurabhi, possesses the fragrance of fame—protect you, who are likewise fragrant with glory. This is an example of *dvipādāntayamaka* (rhyme at the end of two lines), as the four syllables ending in *pāyāt* are repeated at the end of both feet, including the final syllable.
In this way, other distinctions should also be inferred by oneself.
There are many intermediate subdivisions of it that are difficult to discern;
they have not been elaborated upon by us because they contradict the path of the dull-witted.
A discourse consisting of a statement and a reply is called *vākovākya*.
"O Rambhā, O friend Menakā, are garlands from the wish-fulfilling trees not easily obtained? Do they not exist in heaven? Where on earth could they be, and for what reason?
When the donor, the illustrious King Anavotasiṅgha, extended his hand and fingers to them, Brahmā himself bowed down; indeed, all the gods of the earth have become wealthy."
In this regard, the dialogues between Rambhā and Menakā are clear.
That which possesses the concealment of the relationship between action and its factors is called "the concealed" (gūḍha). Ckc 6.16.

In this regard, an example of a hidden action (kriyāgūḍha) is as follows: "O illustrious King Siṅgha, protector of the earth, by [your] power, the circle of enemy kings has been severed by the blade of your sword"—
thus [the verse] expresses his great prosperity.

In this instance, because the verbal expression "O All-pervading One, come to fullness" is concealed by the locative case in the word "vibhave," it is a *kriyāgūḍha* (concealed verb), owing to the concealment of the verb.
For example:
[addressing] the illustrious King Siṅgha, who is the very embodiment of the creative imagination of Kandarpa.
On the city streets, the outer corners of the eyes of the women remained motionless.
Here, "they entered" (*āpuḥ*) is the verbal action, which is concealed by the word "women" (*puraṃdhrīṇām*); thus, it is an example of a concealed verb (*kriyāgūḍha*).
An example of a concealed grammatical participant (*kārakagūḍha*) is as follows:
"Out of the agitation and flurry caused by the fear of the plundering raids from the vanguard of King Śrī Siṅgha..."
"Where is the cave? Where is the cave? thus one clearly cries out in the mountain wilderness.

Here, in the act of "shouting" (*raṭati*), the agentive factor (*kartṛkāraka*) consisting of "the enemy's beloveds" (*areḥ kāntāḥ*) is concealed by the locative case in the word "in the forest" (*kāntāre*); thus, among the types of concealed factors (*kārakagūḍha*), this is an example of a concealed agent (*kartṛgūḍha*).
In the same way, examples of concealed objects (*karmagūḍha*) and so forth should be understood.
An example of a concealed relation-word (*saṃbandhapadagūḍha*) is as follows:

O King, the beauty of the side-glances of even those with beautiful eyes does not reach the bow alone; rather, it is your service that captivates them through the graceful movements of their creeper-like eyebrows.

In this instance, the word "of Kāma" (*eḥ kāmasya*) is the term expressing the relationship; however, it is concealed by the instrumental case in the phrase "with graceful sports" (*lalitair vilāsaiḥ*).
Thus, this is an example of "concealed relation" (*sambandhagūḍha*).
Since the genitive case lacks the status of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant), "concealed relation" is mentioned here as a distinct category.

Where there is a distinction between the question and the answer, that is indeed a "question-and-answer" [type]. It is threefold: internal questioning, external questioning, and dual questioning. (Ckc 6.17)
Does the mind-born god, bestowing desire, shine within the palace of a king that possesses a treasure?
Tell me, O King Siṅga, where is the city of Kāmadhurā, for you yourself have described it.
In this context, to the question "What is the mind-born one? [the answer is] "The lotus" (meaning Brahmā);
to the question "What is the palace of the lord of men? [the answer is] "The palace of the lord of Kinnaras," meaning the house of Kubera.

To the question "What is sweet? the answers are "The sweetness of desire" and "The burden of desire. Because these answers lie within the scope of the question, this is called an *antah-praśna* (internal question). "What is the face with cheeks like royal elephants, which is most terrifying and has a fearsome head? If you do not provide an answer to this, O King, then you do not truly know yourself.

In this context, because the term "pratigaṇḍabhairava" is perceived within another interrogative sentence of the latter [verse], this is an internal question (*antaḥpraśna*). An external question (*bahiḥpraśna*) is as follows:
"O Lord of Gods, what is the strength, and what is the address for Śuci, and what is the circle of your enemies?"
O Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla, speak further words, for there is an increase in the fear arising from the previously mentioned colors.

In this context, "Indrabala has been made fruitful," "the pure Sambuddha is holy," and "your circle of virtues is trembling with fear"—or alternatively, "trembling with terror"—these three subsequent [verses] are to be sought entirely outside the question;
this is an external question.
An example of a question pertaining to both is as follows:
O King, he who does not know whom among yogis and enjoyers is desired is mistaken; for by him, Hara, who is clothed in space, has truly not been known.

In this instance, regarding the phrase "living in secret" (*rahovāsa*), the word *rahaḥ* (secret), which constitutes the first part of the answer, is understood internally as being inverted by the word *hara* (seizer);

however, the latter part of the answer, *vāsaḥ* (dwelling), is sought only externally. Thus, because the question and answer exist both externally and internally, this is a "question-answer of both types.
In this manner, the various classes of verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*) have been properly defined.
One should adorn poetry with these [qualities] so that it is not ridiculed by others.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Verbal Figures of Speech," in the *Camatkāracandrikā*, composed by the moon among poets, Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the skill of elegant literature.
The Seventh Chapter: *Camatkāracandrikā*, composed by the poet-moon Viśveśvara. The Seventh Chapter:
Those who are unable to adorn meanings, yet shine by taking refuge in them; [these are the figures of speech].
But those [figures] such as *jāti* and so forth, which are designated by the wise as "ornaments of meaning" (*arthālaṅkāra*), [are not included here].
Birth, elimination, cause, non-cause, the subtle, the superior, contradiction, possibility, mutual [relation], reversal, and illustration. (7.2)
Distinction, synthesis, error, discursive thought, closure, memory,
existence, inference, and presumptive testimony— these are considered the twenty [categories].
In this context, "birth" (jāti) is that which directly brings about those forms of an object that are established across various states;
it is for this reason that it is designated as "birth."
This [compassion] is twofold, distinguished by its natural occurrence and its being produced at that moment.
The first is, for example:
[beholding] those whose tails were repeatedly shaken and whose faces and necks were frequently trembling...
King Siṅga beholds the horses presented as tribute by his enemy kings.
In this matter, there is the following [description] of horses... [omitted] ...

/ As for the instantaneous [mudrā], it is as follows: having placed his graceful forelimb upon a soft lion-throne, he gazes at the straightened arrow with sidelong glances, smiling along with his peers.
Making his speech consist of the essence of nectar for the ears of the discerning, King Anavotasiṅga nourishes a festival for the eyes while seated upon the throne.

In this context, because the king’s state at that particular moment is described, this is a *tātkālikī* (momentary) *jāti*. When, by the exclusion of well-known causes, some other cause or even an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is brought to light, that should be understood as *vibhāvanā* (the description of the extraordinary). (Cvc 7.5)
In this regard, an example of the possibility of another cause is as follows:

O Śrī Siṅgabhūpa, your play of glory shines forth, stretching out [as if] the humility of the king of serpents, bestowing upon the heads of the serpent-king a purity never before cleansed, and binding together the egg of Brahmā as a canopy of sky-cloth. (Ckc 7.3)

In this context, humility, purity, and canopies are well known as the causes for the whiteness, cleanliness, and abundance of the silken garments; yet, having set those aside, other causes for the whiteness, purity, and profusion of fame are conceived.
This is "the poetic figure of the manifestation of another cause" (*kāraṇāntaravibhāvanā*).
An example of "the manifestation of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvavibhāvanā*) is as follows:
O King Śrī Siṅgha, your wisdom has a sharp point that has never been blunted,
and your glories are perpetually imbued with a fragrant scent.

In this context, since sharpness and fragrance are well-known in the world as being produced by sharpening and perfuming respectively, the very nature of wisdom and fame is also made manifest; thus, this "manifestation of nature" (*svabhāvavibhāvanā*) is the causal factor (*hetu*) of the action, and it is twofold: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*).
Among these, the primary cause is twofold, according to the sequence of the producer (*kāraka*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*). (Cvc 7.6)
The first [type] is threefold: through engagement, through withdrawal, and through application.
In this regard, an example of a causal factor characterized by an instigating action is as follows:
"The most wonderful deeds of the illustrious King Siṅgha—expert at shattering the mass of evil actions and perfect at repeatedly enkindling meritorious deeds—constantly bring joy to people. (Ckc 7.5)

In this case, the deeds of the hero are thus engaged in the activity of producing satisfaction for the wise—which was previously non-existent; therefore, this is an "impelling causal factor" (*pravartaka-kāraka-hetu*) that is "engaged in the activity.
That same [deed], when not so engaged, is as follows:
"The three worlds were conquered by the waves of fame from the crest of King Siṅga, who never suffered a defeat."
By those [mountains] which possess most uneven peaks and crests, and which bear the appearance of the celestial Ganges as its foam swirls upon striking them.

In this case, he employs the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) with respect to fame (*kīrti*), which is the cause for the state of being renowned throughout the world, and not with respect to the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, this is an efficient cause (*kārakahetu*) that instigates action without being itself involved in the action.
An example of an efficient cause that is involved in a ceasing action (*nivartakakriyā*) is as follows:
On the forefront of the battlefield of fierce combat, where he excels in destroying the wicked prowess of the enemy hosts,
King Siṅga rides forth, wielding his sword-edge which bears the weighty responsibility of manifesting the expansion of a series of terrible thunderbolts.

In this instance, the hero—who has the sword as his sole companion—is possessed by the impulse to perform the act of destroying the prowess of his adversaries; thus, he is an "effortful cause" (*kārakahetu*) that brings about desistance. That same [impulse], when not yet possessed, is expressed as follows:
"From the bow of the illustrious King Siṅga, whose twanging sound of the string has reached its highest pitch..."
The throats of enemies' wives attain a state devoid of all qualities.

Here, the staff-like bow of the hero (*nāyaka*), not entering into the act of winding the neck-thread of the maiden of the enemy clan, employs the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of a cause; thus, this is a "causal agent" (*kārakahetu*) that does not enter into the action, as opposed to a "prompting cause" (*prayojakahetu*) which enters into the action. For example, in the *Kumārasambhava*, when the glorious Siṃha was ruling the earth girdled by the ocean: "The oceans, whose boundaries were destroyed and who were guarantors for the downfall and expansion [of enemies],..."
Unrighteousness has been uprooted; the vows that ripen in hell have perished; evil deeds—the enclosures of the mass of impurities of the Kali age—have been destroyed.

In this context, regarding actions such as the destruction of boundaries, it has been stated that the hero, entering into these acts by virtue of being the locus (adhikaraṇa) of the occasioned (naimittika) factor expressed by the locative case, becomes the instigator (prayojaka).
That same hero, when not so entered, is as follows:
"O kings who are our adversaries, you have never before known this: service to the illustrious Lord of Siṅga’s realm must be performed by us. Here, the hero is not entered [by the poet].
With palms joined in reverence, the honored elder ministers, having been installed upon the lion throne by him with humility in private, attend upon him with various and wonderful words of praise.

In this context, since it is impossible for the self to be completely absorbed into itself within the activity of practicing service— which consists of such acts as standing in a lowly position, joining the palms in *añjali*, and offering hymns— the term "this one who is not permeated by the ritual action" (*kriyānāviṣṭa*) functions as the causal agent (*kārakahetu*) designated by the word "prayojaka. Furthermore, the second, third, fourth, and seventh [cases] refer to this [agent].
A denotative [word] expresses that which is not entered by an action, and it is also indicative.

Among these, an example of a cause that is indicated by the second case (the dative) is as follows, addressed to King Śrī Siṅga: "Upon the battlefield, various gestures of cowardice are displayed by the enemies who have been mangled by the sword-blade of the moon-like hand [of the king]. (Ckc 7.11)

In this case, the timid gestures that produce fear in those who are hostile are apprehended and qualified by the hero himself, even though he is not explicitly engaged in the action; thus, this is a *lakṣaṇahetu* (a cause characterized by its mark).
Because it produces an accusative case when joined with a *prati* particle, this [cause] is expressed in the accusative.
Similarly, it is expressed in the instrumental, as follows:
In battle, in kinship, and in the royal capital of Acalarāja,
the citizens behold the king with their innate sense of command, as he wears a crown of blossoming *saugandhika* flowers.

In this case, the *saugandhika* flower worn as a crest-jewel makes known the king even without entering into the act of seeing; thus, this is a "signifier-reason" (*jñāpakahetu*) expressed by the third case (*tṛtīyā*) denoting the state of being so characterized (*itthaṃbhāva*).
An example of one expressed by the fourth case (*caturthī*) is:
"averse to service at the feet of the illustrious King Siṅgha."
Untimely intelligence on the part of kings leads to the loss of their kingdoms for their enemies.
Here, by means of a portent consisting in the sudden perception on the part of kings that they have turned their backs on service to their leader, their loss of sovereignty is made known.
Thus, because it is made known by this portent, the "informing cause" (*jñāpaka-hetu*) is expressed by the fourth case;
an example of its expression by the seventh case is as follows:

"Do not face the rival king; abandon your fame now and flee for your lives! Where have you gone, O you of shaken resolve? Behold us!"—while his own army was thus instructing those who had been captured, the illustrious King Siṅgha, with a gentle smile upon his face, stood facing the enemies and bound them with the excellence of his arms.
In this case, through the act of commanding the forces by the generals, the act of manifesting the leader is indicated.
The "causal" (hetu) is said to be secondary because it relies upon secondary function (gauṇavṛtti);
and it is honored as the "variegated cause" (citrahetu) due to its being the cause of manifoldness.
"Simultaneous," "perverted," and "inconsistent with what is logical or illogical"—
thus, in brief, his five varieties have been proclaimed."
In that case, the cause arises simultaneously with the effect itself;
just as the illustrious King Siṅga, whose poetic compositions were his armor, was a preeminent hero on the battlefield, [drawing] from his quiver.
He draws forth sharp iron arrows at the very same moment as the lives of his enemies.

Here, by disregarding the principle that the cause exists in the moment immediately preceding the effect, the simultaneous production of the cause—the drawing of the bow—and its effect—the drawing away of the life-force of the opponent—is described;
thus, this is a "simultaneous" (samakāla) figurative reason (*gauṇahetu*).
A reason that arises after the effect has already occurred is a "reversed" (*viparyasta*) reason.
O illustrious King Siṅghabhu, just as your horn releases its sheath from behind,
so do the eastern kings release their treasuries from the front.

In this case, because the effect— characterized by the abandonment of the eastern quarter, the earthly realm, and the treasury— arises immediately after the occurrence of its cause, namely the release of the hero’s sword, this is the "contrary" (viparyasta) variety of the "wonderful cause" (citrahetu). A cause that produces an appropriate effect is called "appropriate" (yukta).
The opposite of that is an improper reason (*ayukta-hetu*).
For example:
"O King Siṅga, may those two [your sword and serpent] perform the meal of the life-breaths of your enemies."
How could the darkness of grief of your enemies increase, given the power of the heat of your majesty?

In the first half [of this verse], since the serpents performed that very act of breaking their fast on air which was appropriate for them, this is called a "proper" (yukta) figurative cause (gauṇahetu).
In the second half, since they performed that very increase of darkness which was attributed to fire, this is an "excessive" (atyukta) figurative cause.
The causal factor based on the locus (adhikaraṇahetu) is inconsistent (asaṅgata).
O King Siṅga, it is a marvel that while the burden of the earth rests upon the tip of your right arm, the kings bow their heads; while you possess supreme boldness, your enemies are devoid of shame;
while you are full of pride, your rival warriors are overwhelmed; for while the cause occupies one side, the emergence of its effects has pervaded the entire expanse of the sky.

In this case, because the causes residing in the hero, such as the bearing of the earth's burden, and the effects residing in the antagonist, such as humility, are unrelated due to their different loci, this is the so-called "inconsistent" (asaṅgata) figurative cause.
Such is the manner in which the varieties of causes have been shown;
those who are discerning should likewise infer for themselves the causes consisting in non-existence (abhāva).
That which does not produce an effect because it is sublated by another cause or by the very nature of the thing itself is declared to be "non-causal."
The reason [that you lack anger] is subverted by the very nature of things:

O King Siṅga, when your eyebrows have not parted in playfulness, even the corners of your eyes do not turn red; and your smile, though gentle, is not hidden. Even upon seeing kings roaring in defiance, your form—though its actions are filled with intensity—is unaltered even by fierce gestures.

In this case, although [the antagonist] is capable of manifesting actions of extreme agitation, his intended effect—in the form of impurity such as a roar (*huṃkāra*)—does not arise because it is thwarted by the power of the hero’s essential nature and physical form; thus he is described in that way.
An example of the second type is as follows:

O Lord of my life, although you are generally aware that King Siṅga’s sovereignty in battles rests upon the shoulders of kings like yourself who have long served at his feet, and although you hear the bold words of trustworthy men, it is indeed due to some past misdeed that you, being wise, do not wish to serve him.

In this case, although the causes such as the knowledge of the hero’s faults possess the capacity to produce their characteristic effects through the speech of the rival hero, it is stated that their power is frustrated by destiny; therefore, this is a "non-reason" (*ahetu*) whose efficacy is thwarted by another cause.
While the illustrious Siṅga, the crest-jewel of kings, stands before us—a generous patron and an abode of bliss for those with sensitive hearts within the established tradition of literature—...
Whoever on this earth has accomplished their purpose regarding all goals, unless there exists upon their forehead a great and insurmountable inscription of past misdeeds.

Here, although the hero’s magnanimity—which is committed to the cause of knowledge—possesses the capacity to fulfill the aims of all supplicants, the fact that an effect is not produced in some instances is explained by the claim that it has been struck down by the ill-omened marks on the foreheads of those seekers; thus, this reason is refuted by another.
As for what is called the "stream of causes" (hetusantāna), it is merely a designation for a series of causal factors.
Because each [of these] individually lacks causal capacity, that [collection] is also considered by me to be a non-cause.

Just as the wise, through the equipment of their prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), perform service to the assembly of scholars, and thereby gain inspired intuition (*pratibhā*) and a sweet realization of literature; and just as the smiling side-glances of King Siṅgaṇa, who possesses a mature intellect, bring about an abundance of prosperity for those of cultivated mind— so too shall the arising of the three aims of life (*trivarga*) be accomplished.

In this context, although the service of learned men and the other factors serve as successive causes for the arising of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), they function as causes only when combined, since each preceding factor depends upon the subsequent one; thus, because they lack individual efficacy, even the "garland of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*) is not a [separate] figure of speech. Subtle is the intended meaning of the clever [poet], which proceeds through two types of gestures (*iṅgita*). (Cvc 7.14)
Just as the King, while fondling the jewel on his armlet, made a request in the presence of his own female companions,
Śyāmā gave him her reply through the sprouts of horripilation upon the pair of her breasts with the utmost reverence.

In this instance, the gesture (*iṅgita*) consists of the hero’s massaging the breasts— which bear the reflection of the heroine transferred via the gem in the central bead of his armlet— by that [hero].
By means of this, the heroine’s desire is perceived by the clever heroine,
as is her physical manifestation (*ākāra*), namely the bristling of her hair (*romāñca*).
Thus, the heroine’s desire to perform what she herself longs for—manifesting as her acceptance—is known by the clever hero; this is the twofold *sūkṣma* (the subtle).
Following that is the *mahotkarṣa* (great excellence), which consists of meanings that progress higher and higher.
Just as the Andhra region shines preeminently within Jambūdvīpa, so too within it there exists a particularly excellent city named Rājaśaila.
Therein, the assembly hall of King Siṅga—the crest-jewel of monarchs—attains excellence; for even among that king’s [disciples], his composition of speech is the essence of essences.
This is called "the subsequent" (uttara) because it describes the relative excellence [of various regions] in an ascending order, beginning with the Andhra country and so forth.
Contradiction (virodha), however, is the mutual non-coherence of things; it possesses a lack of connection, opposition, disparity, and non-differentiation. (Cvc 7.16)
Thus, this [path] is described by the wise as being twofold, based on the distinction between the appearance of reality and that which is not reality;
and even the appearance of reality is said to be twofold: the pure and the composed.
In this regard, an example of pure, actual contradiction is as follows:
"The bestowing of wealth and the acquisition of riches; imperial sovereignty and the Goddess of Speech on earth;
service to those of increased wisdom and fresh youth—these always flourish in King Śrī Siṅga. (Ckc 7.25)

In this instance, the contradiction between the granting and acquiring of wealth (Dhanada and Arjuna), between Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, and between service to the elderly and youthfulness, is both real (*tāttvika*) and distinct (*vivikta*), as previously described.
An example of a "strung-together" (*grathita*) real contradiction is as follows:

"Is there any killing of demons for one whose speech is free from hatred? Even so, what need is there for sleep for one who is sleepless? And if it be asked whether there is a woman on his chest, how could she possibly exist?"
Having heard such bold assertions by learned men in assemblies during the recitation of that Purāṇa concerning the Enemy of the Daityas, King Siṅga becomes smiling-faced.
In this case, because the contradictions are strung together one after another, it is called "contradiction by way of stringing" (*grathita*), which is a contradiction of reality (*tattva-virodha*).
Where a contradiction appears through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and so forth,
this appearance is said to be of two kinds, possessing beauty merely at the level of cognition.
An example of contradiction with a pure appearance (*śuddhābhāsavirodha*) is as follows:
"We say that King Siṅgha is both kind and learned;
yet the row of heroes says that he is neither kind nor learned. (Cvc 7.27)
In this instance, a contradiction consisting of the union of "kingly" and "goodness" (*saujanya*) is perceived merely through the punning of the words;
however, in reality, the resolution is that the row of heroes speaks of one who is not good but is learned and skilled in battle. That very [contradiction] is composed as follows:

O King, tell me how you possess such gravity; how could there be such depth from the lotus-like feet of your Guru? And how, oh wonder, does that Guru possess such victory? How does the victorious one possess such gentleness?
How is it fitting for the gentle one to be a delight to the earth? O Lord of the Earth, even your status as a son of Śrī Siṅga has been brought forth by the Lord of Lakṣmī.

In this case, because the composition is formed through a progressive accumulation [of meanings] based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*), its status as a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*) is quite evident. [For example:
"Whence comes this sovereignty for the son of King Śrī Siṅgha? This is merely that which has been brought forth by the Lord of Fortune (*lakṣmīśvara*).
Indeed, many varieties of these two [types of *ābhāsa*] are recognized due to the lack of connection with genus (*jāti*) and so forth. (Cvc 7.19)
In this regard, [the following is an example] of a genus [being qualified] by genus, action, quality, and substance:

"Though you are a mountain (*bhūbhṛt*), your mind is like that of Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla; though you are a lotus-pool (*padmākara*), you are devoid of remaining mud (*sphuṭaja-paṅka-śeṣa*); though you are a serpent (*bhogin*), you are affectionate toward people; and though you are a mountain (*suparva*), you are a sovereign of the whole earth (*sārvabhauma*) upon the ground. // Ckc_7.29 //

In this [verse], there are four contradictions of genus (*jātivirodha*): in the first quarter, the contradiction between the genera of cloud and mountain; in the second, between the actions of producing a lotus-pond and drying up mud; in the third, between the genus of being fond of all [beings] and the quality of being lame; and in the fourth, the non-coexistence of the genus of divinity and the substance characterized as a world-ruling sovereign or a directional elephant.

There is a contradiction between the action and its qualities and substances, as follows: "While bringing joy to poets, you obscure the poet in the application of political ethics; your sharp wisdom does not create division among those of cultivated intellect. Though you are the lord of the arts (the moon), you indeed abandon the path of the sky; O illustrious Siṅgha, best of kings, your conduct is truly marvelous. *Note: The term *kriyāguṇadravyavirodhaḥ* refers to a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) where there is a perceived opposition between the action (*kriyā*), its quality (*guṇa*), and its substance (*dravya*). Here, the king's action of "obscuring the poet" contradicts his quality of "sharp wisdom" which "does not create division," while his substance as "lord of the arts" (the moon) is contrasted with his abandonment of the "path of the sky" (which the moon normally occupies).*

In this [verse], there are three contradictions of action (*kriyāvirodha*): in the first quarter, between the two actions of "pleasing the poet" and "disregarding the poet"; in the second, between the two qualities of "sharpness" and "piercing"; and in the third, between the substance characterized as the moon—named "Lord of the Arts"—and the action of "leaving the path of the stars."

Regarding the contradiction between a quality (guṇa) and both qualities and substance (dravya), there are two types of divisions. Among these, the contradiction between two qualities is as follows: "O Śrī Siṅgabhūpa, even though you are the delight of two [ladies], you are the sole tree for both. In this case, there is a contradiction between two qualities within a single locus.
But the state of being the south occurs in relation to the southwest (nirṛti).
Here, there is a contradiction between two qualities, namely "southernness" and "northernness.
As for the contradiction between a quality and a substance, it is as follows:
"O Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla, even by your variegated *arjuna* trees..."
They become endowed with masses of glory, being devoted to gladdening their friends.
Here, there is a contradiction between the substance characterized by Arjuna and the quality of affection for Karṇa.
When there is a contradiction between one substance and another substance, there is only one type of division,
as follows:
In Madhurā, which is always vast and situated within the mountain-king’s domain,
the illustrious King Siṅga rules the earth, just as Māndhātṛ and Kṛtavīrya did.

In this instance, there is a contradiction of substance (*dravyavirodha*), as the first half [of the verse] describes Madhurā as a vast city, while the second half describes Māndhātṛ as being of limited prowess (*kṛtavīryatva*).
Thus, ten varieties of apparent contradiction (*ābhāsavirodha*) have been described.
In this manner, the actual varieties should be inferred by the discerning themselves.
Just as the fortune of the middle world shines upon a certain lion-like king on the King-Mountain (Rājācala), which is unattached to the various types of opposition; there,
the clusters of his enemies— who were once arrogant and powerful— melt away through an excess of intoxication at its very edge.
In this case, the drying up of the rut of elephants that have reached the vicinity of lions is inconsistent; thus, this is the variety of contradiction known as "the inconsistent" (*asaṅgata*).
An example of "the adversary" (*pratyanīka*) is as follows:
[to hear] the composition of Rambhā, which is filled with intense bliss...

O King Siṅga, it is a marvel that in your palaces, as enemies gaze through the lattice windows toward the river on every side, they have been plunged by the edge of your sword into a sleep whose seal is an endless silence.

In this context, for those who desire to hear [your] words and behold [you], taking recourse in boundless sleep is inconsistent as it is contrary [to their aim]; thus, even the "counter-opposite" (*pratyanīka*) is indeed a form of contradiction (*virodha*).
An example of the "unequal" (*viṣama*) is as follows:
O King Siṅga, your laughter is the silken garment of the quarters, your fame is the grace of the Goddess of Victory, and your splendor is her playful ornament.
Though pure by nature, when released, it causes the quarters of space to become rippled with impurity for those who oppose it.

In this case, because of the disparity between what is well-known—that the making of extreme darkness upon the faces of enemies of Dhavala’s fame results in exactly that—and the fact that it occurs [as something different], there is a lack of mutual connection; thus, this is the figure of speech called *viṣama* (the Uneven), which is a form of contradiction (*virodha*). Alternatively, since the act of clarifying the quarters of the sky and the act of blackening the faces of enemies do not constitute a uniform mode of operation, it is *viṣama* due to this disparity.
An example of the excessive (*adhika*) is as follows:

King Śrī Siṅga, possessing sharp intelligence, drew his bow back to his ear and, discharging unerring arrows at every horse, every elephant, and every man, was perceived by all those enemies facing him simultaneously as if he were as many men himself—this is truly a marvel. (Cvc 7.37)

In this case, even though a single hero is seen in many ways by multiple armies, the perception of an excess of number that contradicts the number one does not occur; thus, this is the variety of contradiction called "the Excessive" (*adhika*). Where an injunction or a prohibition is conceived through abundant causes such as light and so forth, it is designated as "Possibility" (*saṃbhava*) by those who know the distinctions. *atraikasyāpi nāyakasyānekairapi sainyair anekadhā dṛśyamānatve naikatvasaṃkhyāviruddhasaṃkhyādhikyaṃ pratīyata ityadhikaṃ nāma virodhabhedaḥ prabhūtakāraṇālokādyatra saṃbhāvyate vidhiḥ / niṣedho vā viśeṣajñaiḥ sa saṃbhava itīritaḥ //* "In this [verse], although a single hero is seen in many ways by multiple armies, the perception of an excess of number that contradicts the number one does not occur; thus, this is the variety of contradiction called 'the Excessive' (*adhika*). Where an injunction or a prohibition is conceived through abundant causes such as light and so forth, it is designated as 'Possibility' (*saṃbhava*) by those who know the distinctions."
In this regard, the possibility of such a prescription is as follows:
O Lord of the earth, when the expanse of the quarters is shrouded by the dust of the ground trampled by the millions of horses in the vanguard of your formidable army,
it would be conceivable that the ruby-gems on the crests of the sovereigns rising at the borders serve as the likeness of lamps behind a thin curtain.

In this very situation, since such a state of affairs for the crest-jewels of neighboring vassals is possible given the nature of destiny, this is an instance of the "possibility of a positive injunction" (*vidhi-sambhava*).
An example of the "possibility of a prohibition" (*niṣedha-sambhava*) is as follows:

while the King of Pāraśīka, who delights in the moon, was contemplating an alliance and the Lord of Elephants (Gajapati) had merely touched upon the scent of a matrimonial bond by offering his jewel-like daughter;
It was not fitting to display such rashness in battle against the king of the Raichar family, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, while among the host of petty kings dwelling on the banks of the Gautamī.
"Such reckless audacity in enduring the fury of a leader as this is not to be expected among base kṣatriyas"—this constitutes the "possibility of prohibition" arising from a prohibition.
As for mutual retaliation, that is what I consider to be *anyonya* (mutuality). (Cvc 7.22)

O crest-jewel of the Siṅga kings, O treasure-house of greatness! Just as the ocean, with its cool and pure currents of water—the very essence of your gifts—purified by contact with the hands of the gods (the trees) standing firm in the windless state, daily fills its treasuries with priceless gems; thus you and the ocean possess wealth that flows forth through mutual assistance.

In this case, because the hero and the river-heroine mutually assist one another through the flow of the water of their gift and the collection of excellent jewels respectively, there is this "mutuality" (anyonya). Furthermore, oneness, the crest-ornament, delusion, and mutual ground are its stages. (Cvc 7.23)
In this regard, their mutual identity is as follows:
Your fame possesses the clear radiance of a cluster of upraised white lotuses, and your majesty has the beautiful form of a shimmering *campaka* flower;
upon the grounds of the palaces of your rival kings, O illustrious Siṅgha, these two appear as if their colors have become blended through the merging of their mutual splendors.

Here, because fame (*kīrti*) and majesty (*pratāpa*) stand in a relationship of the modified and the modifier toward one another, the perception of their mutual counteraction results in their mutual identity;
this is "mutual crowning" (*anyonyacūlikā*). For example:
"By learning and fortune he shines; by learning, fortune; and by fortune, King Śrī Siṅgha, through his speech."
The means is also [established] by means of the being, and the being by means of the means; as it is, so is that very thing.

In this case, while learning (*vidyā*) and prosperity (*śrī*) exist in a state of mutual assistance as they shine forth, the fact that both act as impediments to the preeminent activity of the hero constitutes what is called "the crest upon a crest" (*cūlikopari vardhate*);
this is *anyonyacūlikā*, which is indeed a form of mutual contradiction (*anyonyabheda*).
An example of mutual delusion (*anyonyabhrānti*) is as follows:

O illustrious King Siṅga, your enemies who travel as wayfarers hide slowly within the thickets, fearing you might be mistaken for mendicants; yet upon seeing them, your soldiers, perceiving them to be thieves, look out from both sides and move quickly forward, fully prepared for combat.

In this case, because there is no relationship between the travelers moving through the forest—who are antagonistic to the hero—and their respective roles as the object of reference and the subject who refers, the perception of a remedy results in a mutual delusion, which is in fact a mutual deception.
"Exchange," however, is the transposition of one thing for another, or a mutual barter;
it is called *parivṛtti* (exchange), and it is said to be of two kinds: primary (*mukhyā*) and secondary (*gauṇī*). (Kāvyālaṅkāra 7.24)
When King Siṅga,

the best of monarchs— who serves the wise who have taken refuge in Acyuta’s incarnation, the Sun-like Lord whose womb is the jewel— was ruling, prosperity was preeminent and possessed of reversals: it favored the virtuous, abandoned the wicked, unrighteousness went to its destruction, and the path of Dharma flourished.

In this kingdom of the hero, the reversal of fortune between the good man and the wicked man, as well as the reversal of dissolution between righteousness and unrighteousness, is perceived primarily; thus, this is the primary *parivṛtti* (reversal) called "possessing transposition.
An example of the secondary (*gauṇī*) [reversal] possessing transposition is as follows:
Indeed, that very darkness which was brought upon the moon by the fame of the illustrious Siṅghabhūpa becomes manifest upon the lotus-faces of his rival kings.

In this case, the fact that the moon's spot—which has been removed by the fame of the hero—is perceived upon the faces of rival kings is impossible [in reality]; therefore, since it is not primary, this is a figurative "exchange with reversal" (*vyatyayavatī parivṛtti*). An example of exchange as primary is as follows:
Resonating with the sound of the victory drums of the illustrious King Siṅga, the rival monarchs flee in haste to conceal their true forms;
having bestowed their ornaments—bracelets, necklaces, and the like—upon the tribe of hunters, they meekly purchase even inferior guñjā seeds as their own decorations.

In this case, since the exchange between the jewel and the *guñjā* ornament occurs primarily as a direct substitution, this is "Exchange" (*parivṛtti*) with substitution as its primary characteristic.
