The same [figure], when secondary (*gauṇī*), is as follows: "O King Siṅga, your sword-blade is skilled in the practice of distinguishing between the crooked and the straight."
Causing trembling among the enemy kings, they seize the glory of the seven-limbed kingdom.

In this case, since the bestowing of trembling upon the enemy kings by the hero’s sword and the taking away of their sevenfold royal splendor from them cannot occur in a primary sense, there is a figure called *parivṛtti* (exchange) characterized by figurative transference.
For the purpose of establishing the established [meaning], that which serves as an illustration for the sake of proof is called *nidarśanā* (illustration).
This is considered by the wise to be threefold, according to whether it occurs through similarity between what precedes and what follows. (Cvc 7.25)
In this regard, the first illustration is as follows: Just as wicked people who are favorites of the king inflict harshness upon others,
so too does this sword of King Śrī Siṅgha cut through the very vitals of his enemies.
In this case, because the example of the cruel person favored by the king was stated previously, it is called *pūrvā* (prior) *nidarśanā*. An example of *uttarā* (subsequent) is as follows:
"The bow of King Siṅga performs the slaughter of the lives of its enemies."
Even for those who bow down and are otherwise crooked, attachment to the king's ear leads to the torment of others.

In this instance, because the account of the crooked person dwelling near the king is mentioned after [the description of the river], this is an *uttara* (consequent) form of *nidarśanā* (illustration).

For example: "Just as the Mandākinī, having descended from the courtyard of the sky onto the surface of the earth, rises up from the stream of the Veṇī with a fragrance equal to that produced by lotuses."
The creeper of King Śrī Siṅgha’s fame proclaims the wondrous deeds of the men who took refuge in him, which arise in an ever-increasing succession of continuous success.

Here, because the praise of both the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*)— which possesses a progressive arising through the patronage of the hero— and the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), characterized by the progressive elevation of the people dependent on that hero, is expressed using the present-tense suffix (*śatṛ*) as occurring at the very same time, this is the figure of speech called *samā* (simultaneity).
[It occurs] when the similarity between two things has been either explicitly stated or understood.
The mention of difference would be a [real] distinction, and that is traditionally understood as exclusion (vyatireka).

Herein is stated the figure of speech known as *svajātīyavyatireka* (contrast with its own kind), characterized by similarity: "Other kings, even those who perform the sacrifice of liberality, do not equal His Majesty Śrī Siṅgabhūpati;
for while they rejoice in the poetic plays of the learned, he himself rejoices in them to the full. (Ckc 7.51)

In this instance, having stated the similarity between the hero and other kings of his own class regarding the act of bestowing gifts, the specific excellence of his poetic playfulness—which serves as the cause for their mutual gratification—is described; thus, this is the aforementioned type [of *pratīpasama*].
As for that same [type] when the similarity is already well-known (*pratītasādṛśye*), it is as follows:
"O Śrī Siṅgabhūpa, because of your acceptance [of me], this poet is afraid of [the god of] Dharma, who is powerful."
And she gives two shares to those who have stolen her kinsmen, such as those bought from others; the first kings do not equal you in this regard.

Here, when a similarity is perceived through the commonality of the *rakta* (red/attached) nature between the Lord of the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Mahā-yugas and the hero, the statement of the specific excellence of his protection— which serves as the means for returning the dharma stolen from that kingdom— constitutes this "vyatireka based on perceived similarity" (*pratītasādṛśya-sajātīya-vyatireka*).
An example of "vyatireka of one's own manifestation" (*svavyakti-vyatireka*) within stated similarity (*kathitasādṛśya*) is as follows:
O illustrious Siṅgabhūpāla, you are like Bhava (Śiva) in being free from defects;
yet, by your daily increasing prosperity, you are distinct from Bhava, who possesses Śrī (Lakṣmī).

Here, having stated the equality with himself regarding the absence of faults in the hero, the statement of his own superiority over himself day by day through an increasing abundance of horses and other wealth constitutes this *svavyaktivyatireka* (distinction from one's own manifestation) within the context of "stated similarity" (*kathitasādṛśye*).
If an example of *svavyaktivyatireka* is possible within "implied similarity" (*pratīyamānasādṛśye*) and if it nourishes aesthetic charm (*cārutā*), that too should be examined.
An example of a single negative concomitance (*ekavyatireka*) in the context of stated similarity (*kathitasādṛśye*) is as follows:
"O Śrī Siṅgha, protector of the earth and abode of the ocean of compassion!
How could Jīmūtavāhana be equal to you? (Ckc 7.54)

In this case, because the distinguishing characteristics of the hero and the Vidyādhara hero—who have been described as similar by virtue of being repositories of compassion—are stated only later on, this is an example of the aforementioned [type].

An example of the "exclusion of both" (*ubhayavyatireka*) in that same context, within the genealogy of the hero himself, is as follows: "Whose elder brother is Balabhadra in form, whose beloved queen is Rukmiṇī, whose son is Pradyumna, and whose multitude of grandsons includes Aniruddha and others."
This very Lord of Lakṣmī, the king known as Annavota, bears a beautiful splendor like that of the Sudarśana discus upon his lotus-face; yet he bears it in the lotus-hand of the Universal Soul.

In this case, regarding the hero and the heroine Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, whose similarity has been stated through such qualities as being the brother of Balabhadra and so forth, the fact that [the hero] possesses the Sudarśana [discus] on his face and [the heroine] possesses the Sudarśana [discus] in her hand constitutes a statement of distinguishing attributes belonging to both; therefore, this is a *kathitasādṛśya* (stated-similarity) *ubhayavyatireka* (mutual vyatireka).
An example of a *ekavyatireka* (single vyatireka) where the similarity is already understood is as follows:
How can Rāhu— who turns a friend into an enemy and is currently preoccupied with devouring the moon— serve as a comparison for the edge of King Śrī Siṅgha’s sword?

In this case, since the similarity between Rāhu (the son of Siṃhikā) and the sword (kaukṣeyaka)— both perceived through their shared quality of being dark— is stated in the very first [verse] by means of the mention of a distinguishing attribute, it is as described above.
An example of the "exclusion of both" (*ubhayavyatireka*) in that same context is as follows:
Siṅghabhūpati presides over enjoyments without remainder and is free from sloth;
Nīrajāvara presides over enjoyments with remainder and is prone to sleep.

Here, because the similarity between the two—Nārāyaṇa and the hero (nāyaka)—is perceived through their being consecrated for the protection of the world, this is an *ubhayavyatireka* (double contrast) where the similarity is perceived;
it is a "contrast based on similarity" (*sadṛśavyatireka*) by means of a stated similarity, as in:
"The King and the Mountain of the Lord of Gods (Mount Meru) are both auspicious and always providing refuge."
This [city] shines under the rule of the illustrious Siṅghabhūpa, and not under the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).

In this case, since the distinction between the two mountains—which have been described as equal—is stated by means of the implied similarity [of each] to a hero and the Lord of the Three Worlds respectively, it is called such [i.e., *pratīyamāna-sādharmya-vyatireka*].
An example of *visadṛśa-vyatireka* (dissimilar contrast) in that same context is as follows:
"The birth of the Lord of the Earth from the temples of the world-elephants and for the welfare of the world..."
Though you have attained the state of a Mātaṅga, you are blinded by pride; yet though your lineage is exalted, this [other] one is free from arrogance.

Here, having stated the similarity between the world-elephants (the guardians of the quarters) and the leader-elephant (the Buddha) by virtue of their being beneficial to the world, the distinction is expressed through qualities that are similar— namely, being born of the lineage of *mātaṅga* and high birth— but which are dissimilar in terms of being blinded by rut and being free from pride; thus,
this is a "dissimilitude based on stated similarity" (*kathitasādṛśyavisadṛśavyatireka*).
The *sadṛśavyatireka* (contrast with the similar) based on well-known similarity is as follows: "The Lord of waters shines with waters that are naturally pure;
this King Śrī Siṅgha shines with virtues mingled with purity."

Here, because the hero and the river—the two subjects perceived as similar through qualities such as profundity—are distinguished by the very same jewels and virtues used to express their similarity, this is called "Distinction by Similarity" (*tulyayogitā-vyatireka*).
In that same context, an example of "Distinction by Dissimilarity" (*visadṛśa-vyatireka*) is as follows:
"While Śeṣa sleeps, devoid of learning, with a mouth full of poison, and bearing the Earth [on his head], she—her heart fearing calamity—is surely agitated to remain [with him]."

While the illustrious King Siṅga protects the earth—free from sloth, possessed of clear learning, fair-faced, and walking upon a path that is not crooked—the land attains its highest state of stability.

Here, because the similarity between the secondary hero (śeṣanāyaka) and the particular [primary] hero is not perceived through such factors as the mastery of knowledge and the bearing of the earth's burden, the statement of distinguishing attributes— such as being overcome by sleep versus being free from languor—
constitutes this *visadṛśavyatireka* (dissimilar contrast), wherein the similarity is implied. Thus, some varieties of *vyatireka* (contrast) have been illustrated.
By this very path, others too should be inferred for themselves by the wise.
It is asserted that when a task is being undertaken by someone,
it is accomplished through the attainment of an accidental auxiliary cause.
Just as those who had entered mountain caves in the forests out of fear of King Śrī Siṅga’s soldiers desired to sweep away the tracks of their own footprints,
so too was our assistance accomplished by the power of fate through clouds that suddenly began to fill the vicinity of the valleys with the water of their streams.

In this context, the divine (daivika) resolution is illustrated by the fact that for the enemies of the hero—who desired to wipe away the tracks of their own footsteps on the paths of retreat—a sudden rain made that perfectly accomplished. The non-divine (a-daivika) is as follows: at the time of the first awakening from sleep following the rains, the lotus-dweller [Lakṣmī] abandons her sleep under the pretext of the crocodiles, snakes, frogs, and insects [in the water].

Through the agency of his benefactor, the enemy of the Daityas, the sound of the war drum for the expedition to conquer the ends of the quarters of the omnipresent Lord Śrī Siṃha remains ever awake with an awakened mind.
In this context, by the Blessed One— who, under the pretext of sleep, desired to loosen the firm embrace of Lakṣmī—
the sound of the hero’s armor-clashing, which had been obtained as a human auxiliary cause for causing alarm to the Lotus-Dweller (Brahmā), was brought about as a non-divine factor.
[This is an instance of] *bhrānti* (error), which is a cognition of misapprehension arising either from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) or from similarity.
It is twofold: that which has an object and that which is without an object, and so forth. (Ckc 7.29)
Possessing an objective support, it is as follows:
having painted the likeness of King Anavatapta out of longing, she gazes at it, thinking, "This is my beloved," due to the delusion of her intense application of love.
Then, having approached him swiftly, she turns her face slightly away; surely she looks at him with a charming smile, with trepidation, and with longing.

In this case, when a certain woman who is enamored with her lover perceives him as being actually present in a portrait of the lover, this arises by taking on the form of the lover depicted in the painting through the power of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of her constant contemplation of the lover; thus, this is an error (*bhrānti*) called "arising from mental impressions" (*saṃskārajā*) and "having an objective support" (*sālambā*).
An example of that which is "without an objective support" (*nirālambā*) is as follows:
Beholding the extreme ferocity of the formidable Bhairava in the field of battle, the opposing kings flee toward the vicinity of mountain caves;
agitated, they look in every direction and at every tree, searching for him nearby with their hands busily raised by the terrible sword-blades brandished from their arms.
In this context, when enemies who have directly perceived— or even merely heard of— the hero as possessing such fierce prowess at the front of the battle,

experience a cognition of the hero upon mountains and other objects, even in the absence of an actual object resembling the hero, this is what is called "unsupported" (*nirālambanā*) error arising from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
And the second [type of ignorance] is to be fully understood by the wise as being of two kinds:
that which takes the form of reality regarding what is not reality, and that which takes the form of unreality regarding reality.
Just as Śiva desires to dance, the serpents stand at the edges; the proud Gaṅgā rises up and cannot endure his insistence on pride;
Pārvatī looks on with jealousy; and the Lotus-born Brahmā strives to embrace him—this is when the preeminent and wondrous rise of the glory of the fame of King Siṅga occurs.

In this case, because of the similarity in whiteness, the manifestation of the hero’s fame—in the form of the snowy mountains and so forth—as having those very forms is an error (*bhrānti*) that takes the nature of reality (*tattvarūpā*) despite being non-real (*atattve*).
An example of the second [type of error] is as follows:
"Overcome by thirst, with the thought 'this is water,' they run again and again toward the intensely white patches of light from the sun's rays upon the parched plains."
The enemy kings, utterly emaciated by the raids of King Siṅga, did not trust even wells that possessed the appearance of water.

In this context, the cognition of those who have been repeatedly deceived by a mirage—that there is no water even in what is ultimately water—among those who oppose the leader, is an error consisting of the non-real within the real;
this is an error produced by similarity.
Both of these are termed "a succession of errors" (*bhrānteḥ paramparā*) and "a chain of errors" (*bhrānteḥ śṛṅkhalā*).
It is my view that knowledge which is distinct from error is indeed itself an error.
In this regard, there is a succession of delusions:

with the hope of finding sprouts on the branches of trees, with the hope of pieces of camphor in the bellies of boxes, and at the end of their enchanting rites, with the hope of attaining silk garments;
O Sovereign Lord of the Earth, Siṅga, the Siddha-women grasp your fame—which endures until the end of the aeon—as they emerge from the caves of Lokāloka.

In this context, the successive series of errors (*bhrāntiparaṃparā*) refers precisely to the illusion of flowers and the like that arises repeatedly in the fame of the hero through the sequence of garlands worn by the perfected women (*siddhāṅganā*).
An example of a "chain of errors" (*bhrāntiśṛṅkhalā*) is as follows:

Brahmā is enamored [of the sky] thinking it to be a swan; those birds [the stars] are taken for the celestial Gaṅgā; she [the night] is taken for the Ocean of Milk; and the ocean is taken for moonlight.

O Śrī Siṅgakṣitinātha, you who are the wish-fulfilling tree for the aspirations of virtuous people, that splendor [of the moon] is perceived as the unimpeded fame of you, by means of the notion that it is the orb of the autumnal moon.
In this context, because errors are combined according to the principle of a successive chain, this error is called "the chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*); it is indeed a specific variety of error.
Reasoning (*ūha*) is conjecture (*vitarka*); it is of two kinds, being delimited by either certainty or uncertainty. (Cvc 7.32)
In this regard, an example ending with a definitive conclusion (*nirṇayānta*) is as follows:
"Is he Kandarpa? Is he the son of the Lord of the Immortals? Is he Śrī Rāma? Or is he the son of the Lord of Alakā?
"Friend, it is known: victorious indeed is King Siṅga, the storehouse of good fortune that bears fruit for the eyes of young women!"
In this case, because a definitive conclusion is stated—namely, "This is that very hero"—following the initial doubts regarding Kandarpa and others, it is described as such.
An example ending in non-conclusion is as follows:
"Is this the crest of the fire of universal destruction? Or is it the tongue of Death? Or perhaps the fang of Yama at the end of the age?"
Thus was the line of the sword, brandished by the hand of the illustrious King Siṅga, inferred by the enemy armies upon the battlefield.

In this case, while the opposing army reflects, "What is this? What is this?", they fail to state a definitive conclusion, [merely thinking] "This is the edge of the leader's sword"; thus it is so described.
The concealment of one thing by another thing is considered *mīlita* (the hidden). Ckc 7.33.

Just as the pride of shame is concealed by the naturally downward-turning face of the celestial cow, and the mass of teardrops from the coral tree is hidden by falling droplets of honey-pollen— so too is the Goddess of Fortune ever concealed within King Anavataptasiṅha, who delights in giving and for whom the leaders of the gods compose verses of praise for his tireless generosity.

In this case, because the cow of plenty (*kāmadhenu*) and the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*)—who were surpassed by the generosity and praise bestowed upon the hero—are overcome by shame, their natural downward-turning of the face and the flow of tears are concealed respectively by the nectar of flowers and [the hero's] humility; thus, this is *mīlita* (concealment). Its varieties include that which is obscured by similarity, as well as that which consists of the possession of its qualities and the non-possession of its qualities. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 7.34)
In this regard, the general [comparison] is as follows:
O King, crest-jewel of Raichalīya’s lineage, treasury of praise, you who discern the true substance from the counterfeit—O Kīla, the swans abandon their pride in their own proficiency;
for they have long been unable to distinguish even slightly between the mouthfuls of lotus-stalk fibers falling from the mouths of Brahmin women and the non-dual discourse attained from you.

In this context, even the commonality consisting of the identity between fame and the lotus has already been expressed by the principle that "the similar is concealed by the similar. An example of such concealment is as follows:

when King Śrī Siṅga Bhūmibhuja cast his gaze, rippling with passion, upon the orb of a certain woman’s breasts—which were like the two frontal globes of a young elephant intoxicated by youth—[his own] fame was thereby eclipsed.
With a mind fearful of breaking his vow of courtesy, the King, acting with skill, offered her in that very same manner to the eyes of the other fair-browed women as well.

Some explain this as *pihitam* (the concealed): when a hero, seeing his beloved manifesting affection toward him, conceals his own internal state by casting similar sidelong glances even toward other women. This concealment of emotion is what is designated as *pihitam*.

That too is merely *mīlita* (the concealment of one thing by another), because it is the suppression of a simultaneous operation of passion and sight by an operation of passion and sight that has already been established.
An example of its excellence (*tadguṇa*) is as follows:
"By the bowers formed by the spreading of creepers consisting mostly of leaves... [and so on].

On the clear crystal grounds, the soldiers of King Siṅga’s vanguard— who had smeared themselves with white dust from the earth— were instantly perceived as enemies by their counterparts on the red stones who were anointed with red chalk, for they appeared as such at that very moment.

In this case, because those who hate the hero have their [perception] obscured by resorting to qualities such as the thickets and groves, it is indeed *tadguṇamīlita* (concealment by the adoption of another's qualities).

When the three worlds were whitened by the glories of King Siṅga, the Gaṇas rejoiced; their own lord’s throat, which had been worn out by the concoction of the Kālakūṭa poison, was now [seen to be] free of it.

Even regarding color, Pārvatī, the beloved of her husband, abandoned her hostility; yet the well-established reputation for a dark spot remained attached even to the full moon, as it was obscured by the people.

Regarding this, some explain that *atadguṇa* (the "non-possession of its qualities") occurs when there is a manifestation of transformations belonging to something else—such as the case of Kālakaṇṭha and others.
However, even under this view, since the causes of the action lack efficacy, it remains nothing other than the figure of speech *ahetu* (the "absence of cause").
The cognition of an experienced object through a similar thing is considered *smaraṇa* (remembrance). (Cvc 7.35)

Just as the enemy kings, terrified by him, fled into the caves of the Upavindhya forest, there they beheld the temple boundary-stones from which streams of honey were oozing and which reached a height of a fathom; seized by their formidable opponents with upraised trunks, those elephants— whose temples were marked by the tightening of knots from thirst— now remember their own kin, the fragrant ichor.

In this context, the recollection of his own lordly elephants, which were carried off by the enemy leader and are similar to these boulders seen here due to the sight of the *gaṇḍaśailas*, constitutes the poetic figure of *smṛti* (recollection).
"Bhāva" (internal state) is said to be an activity that proceeds in accordance with one's underlying intention.
Just as the wise Śrī Siṅghakṣitināyaka, desiring to join the limbs of the world to the arts of graceful movement through various artistic methods,
performed whatever secret actions were ordained, each of which produced a contrary effect.
There was a certain fawn-eyed woman, possessed of wisdom and virtue, and skilled in discernment.
In this passage, the hero’s engagement in teaching elegance— which serves as a metaphor for the pleasure of the mutual touch of those two garments— is the figure of speech known as *bhāva*;
and it is just as if she were desirous of sprinkling her breast with the water from the auspicious horn during the time of sporting in the fresh spring.
King Siṅha, with his head bowed very low, desires [to see her], but that proud woman does not look upon him; she sheds tears.

In this context, the fact that the hero intended to sprinkle water on his chest but the heroine released not the water from her love-play (*śṛṅgāra-salila*) but tears suggests the underlying meaning (*bhāva*) that another woman,
his heart’s beloved, dwells within the hero's heart. Others, however, have shown that this is merely a suggestion of emotion (*bhāva-vyañjanā*).
Because its nature is that of a cognition of something otherwise, it is indeed an error; such is my opinion.
As in this very example, such is the intention of the hero:
"Why do you wish to sprinkle me, who am already present within your own heart?
O beloved, if you wish to sprinkle me, then sprinkle my head."
Then, because of the apprehension that another [man] might be present, the thought "he must not be sprinkled" awakens the heroine's burgeoning longing; this is *arthāpatti* (presumption).
In this manner, *arthāpatti* based on the impossibility of a fact established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) should be inferred by oneself.

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Analysis of Figures of Speech" (*alaṅkāraviveka*) in the *Camatkāracandrikā*, cooled by the essence of the nectar of the fame of the illustrious King Siṅga, composed by the moon among poets, Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the skill of elegant literature.
The Seventh Chapter on Amorous Sport.
The Eighth Vilāsa:
*Camatkāracandrikā*, composed by the poet-moon Viśveśvara; the Eighth Vilāsa:
the definition of both types of figures of speech (*ubhayālaṅkāra*).
Those specific meanings perceived from words such as "iva" and others, which constitute similes and the like among poets, are considered to be both types of poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra).
Simile, metaphor, comparison, poetic doubt, denial, the statement of resolution, the concise expression, poetic fancy, and praise by means of the irrelevant; Ckc_8.2 //

The figure *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), *lāṭa* (the Lāṭīya style), *sasahokti* (simile with "together"), *samuccaya* (accumulation), *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis), *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), and *viśeṣā* (distinction) constitute *pariṣkṛti* (embellishment). Ckc 8.3.
The varieties of illumination (dīpana), sequence (krama), excellence (atiśaya), and double entendre (śleṣa) compositions—
these twenty-four types of blending (saṃsṛṣṭi) have been pointed out by the wise.
When a similarity based on common attributes is well-known through worldly convention,
whether it be already established or explicitly described, that constitutes a simile (upamā) between two objects.
This [simile] is threefold according to its divisions known as *pada*, *vākya*, and *prapañca*.
Among these, the *padopamā* is twofold: by means of a compound (*samāsa*) and also by means of a suffix (*pratyaya*).
In that regard, the first [type of simile] is to be known as fourfold and applicable to all [types of similes]:
it has the sense of being included within [the subject], the sense of illuminating [it], and it contains the sense of shared attributes.
And that which contains both meanings within it—thus the objective referents (lakṣya) of these [categories] are demonstrated.

This earth rests upon the arm of that moon of the Raghu dynasty— whose fame spreads through the expanse of the sky and space, who is a mass of fortune and grace, and whose splendor is as lovely as the moonlight—

as long as it remains upon his hand, which is like a lotus and as vast as the serpent Śeṣa, while he bears the line of his sword, fierce-faced with its mouth like the fangs of an enraged black serpent.

In this instance, in the phrase beginning with *krudhyad-*, since the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)— the snake’s fanged mouth— the common attribute (*tulyadharma*)— its hideousness (*vikaṭatva*)— and the object of comparison (*upameya*)— the sword-blade mouth— are each expressed by their own respective words, the meaning of the indicator (*dyotaka*) is manifested; thus, because all [elements]— the standard of comparison, the object of comparison, the common attribute,
and the indicator— are possible within a compound, this is a "compound simile" (*samāsopamā*) consisting of all [these elements].

In the expression *śeṣāhidīrgha* ("long as the serpent Śeṣa"), the meaning of the indicator (*dyotaka*) is expressed by the compound according to the rule "comparisons [are compounded] with words denoting the common property" (*upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*). Thus, this is the compound-word simile called "one in which the meaning of the indicator is internal. In the expression *jalajakaratala* ("whose palm is copper-red like a lotus"), the compound itself—being a *bahuvrīhi* whose referent is another word (*anyapadārtha*)—contains within it both the indicator (*tulya*) and the common property (*dharmavat*). Therefore, this is the compound-word simile called "one in which both meanings are internal."
There is also another fourfold distinction regarding the meaning of the suffix:
the suffix likewise shares in the qualities of expressing the standard of comparison, the object compared, and their similarity.
In that regard, an example for the cognition of meaning through comparison is as follows:
"The earth was protected by the graceful King Śrī Siṅghabhaṭa, whose arms were like many Rāhus and who was like the wish-fulfilling tree."

In this context, although— by way of excluding metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*)— the words *rāhu* and *kalpapādapa*, which function as standards of comparison (*upamāna*), are applied to the arms (the objects of comparison, *upameya*) in the forms *rāhuriva rāhuḥ* and *kalpapādapa iva kalpapādapaḥ*,

and although the suffixes *-vat* and *-kalpa* in those two terms denote their own respective meanings, nevertheless, just as the suffixes such as *-tara* arising from words like *śūra* convey only the excellence of valor and not the excellence of the person possessing that valor, so too do these two suffixes here.

Since they state that which has become a subordinate quality for the sake of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), this is called *pratyayopamā*, specifically the cognition of the standard of comparison.
An example of the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*) is as follows:
"O Śrī Siṅga, jewel-ornament of the earth’s lord, whose prowess is irresistible, you who are like a beautiful mountain-bow, a treasury of the expansion of the exertion of battle!"
When the victory-drums resound across the near and far shores, the families of their enemies become like crows shrieking and deer fleeing.

In this context, regarding the verse "pārāvāravirāviṇyaḥ," where [the women] are crying like the near and far shores (*pārāvāra*), although the suffix should have been applied in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sense of the agent—since the rule states "the standard of comparison [is used] when the agent is meant"—the fact that the suffix expresses the meaning of the object of comparison constitutes a *padopamā* (word-simile).
This same principle should be understood to apply to the expression "kākakrośikuraṅgadhāvī" as well.
An example of a suffix expressing the meaning of the indicator (*dyotaka*) is as follows:
While the illustrious Siṅghabhūpatilaka, who is like Mount Kalyāṇa with the Pārijāta tree clinging to it and who is the lamp of the Kaṭaka region,
reigns, the earth attains stability through meritorious deeds performed day by day, like the lineage of the Recarlas.

In the phrase "here Kalyāṇaśaila is like Meru," the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "that [is] like that" (*tadvat*), according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*. However, in the phrase "like the continuity of a stream of water," the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the indicator itself—according to the rule *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ*—and not in the sense of "equal action. Thus, these are called word-similes (*padopamā*) where the suffix has the sense of an indicator. An example of a simile where the suffix has the sense of a common property (*tulyadharmārtha*) is as follows:
O Lord, terrifying with your upraised arms and shoulders, as your glances flash with wrathful passion, the mountain caves of your enemies become like homes; the grassy meadows serve as their couches;

and as they wander through the forest, the monkey hosts on its slopes act as if they were palaces, while they behold you, the formidable lord, appearing like fierce hunters, and even the female deer seem like young wives.

In this context, regarding the example *gehīyanti* ("they act as if they were houses"), the suffix *kyac* occurs according to the rule "after a word denoting a standard of comparison, [the suffix *kyac* is added] in the sense of behaving [like it]. Since this suffix arises specifically to characterize a particular action for the purpose of expressing a common property (*tulyadharma*), this is what is called a "compound simile" (*padopamā*) based on a suffix whose meaning is a common property. That same type [of simile] occurs with the locative *kyac*, as in *saudhīyati* ("he acts as if he were in a palace"); here too, the locative *kyac* suffix occurs precisely for the purpose of expressing a common property, and thus it is of that same kind.

Just as it is through action, so too, O Śrī Siṅghakṣitipāla, whose virtues are protected [by you], the expansions of your fame—through their deeds—act like fierce clubs and mallets, act like Bhairavas, act like arrows in battle, act like *vetālas*, act like *halāhala* poison, act like flames of fire, and act like Time (Death) itself; they act like frost, they captivate, they act like the food of the best of gods, and they act like necklaces.

In this context, in examples such as *bhetālam* ("fearing excessively") and so forth, the suffix *kvip* is added in the sense of "acting like that," which characterizes a similarity of attributes (*ācāra-lakṣaṇa-tulyadharma*). Thus, this too is a "simile of words" (*padopamā*) consisting of a suffix denoting a similarity of attributes.
Furthermore, because there is a correspondence between two word-meanings (*padārtha*), there is likewise a correspondence between two sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*).
Therefore, the "simile of sentences" (*vākyopamā*) should be known as twofold; of these, the first type is considered to be of two kinds. (Kāvyālaṃkāra 8.10)
Regarding "the full is lost," here the full is that which is well-endowed with four factors.
O King Siṅga, just as the goddess Śrī possesses supreme splendor upon the full moon that brings joy to the entire world, upon the white lotus, upon the cow that perfumes the ten directions,
or upon the chest of the enemy of the demons (Viṣṇu) which shines with great jewels, so too does she shine exceedingly upon you.

Here, due to the connection of the four components—the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), the indicator (*dyotaka*) of that relationship, and the common property (*tulyadharma*)—this is a complete (*pūrṇā*) sentence simile (*vākyopamā*) possessing identity between the word-meanings (*padārtha*). However, the elided (*luptā*) simile is of three kinds, resulting from the omission of the indicator, both [the indicator and the common property], or all [four]. (Cvc 8.12)
In this regard, an example of the omission of a common attribute (*tulyadharmalopavatī*) is as follows:
"O King Siṅghadharaṇīpāla, your succession of fame vies with the floods of moonlight, being arrogant due to its powerful support."

In this case, although the common property such as whiteness is not explicitly mentioned, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is understood through the force of conventional usage; thus, this is a sentence simile (*vākyopamā*) possessing a common property.
That same [simile] lacking the indicator (*dyotaka*) is as follows: "O King Śrī Siṅghadharaṇīpāla, you too are a mountain of jewels."
Their arms shone with radiant bracelets and were beautiful with their auspicious forms.

In this case, even without an indicator such as *iva*, the similarity between the two— the mountain peak of jewels (*ratnasānu*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the jewel as the object of comparison (*upameya*)— is perceived through the single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the two members joined together, as well as through the collective of their respective qualifiers; thus, this is a sentence simile (*vākyopamā*) characterized by the elision of the indicator (*dyotakalopavatī*) and possessing the equality of word-meanings (*padārthasāmyavatī*).
There is no suspicion of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) here.
*Śleṣa* is the simultaneous expression (*tantrēṇābhidhāna*) of both an established fact and a similarity;
whereas similarity (*sādṛśya*), on the other hand, is the intended relation between a standard of comparison and its object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*).
Therefore, it is clearly evident that *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and the simile (*upamā*) involving the elision of the indicator (*dyotaka*) have distinct domains of application.
An example of the latter, where both [the common property and the indicator] are elided, is as follows:
"Neither camphor, nor frost, nor the autumnal moonlight..."
But the glories of the illustrious Siṅgha, the protector of the earth, shine forth.

In this case, even without words indicating common attributes (*tulyadharma*), the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood through the very rejection of the mistaken notion that the hero's fame is camphor and so forth; thus, this is a sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*) possessing identity of meaning (*padārthasāmyavatī*) characterized by the elision of both [the attribute and the particle]. Some authorities consider this to be a simile characterized by the elision of all three [elements].

If only one of the two—the object of comparison (upamāna) or the subject of comparison (upameya)—is mentioned, it is our view that it is untenable [to call it simile], as it remains uncertain with which [the other] there is similarity.

Simile residing in the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthagāminī*) is of four kinds according to some: that which contains the word *iva*, that which has multiple indicators such as *iva* and so forth, that which is devoid of indicators like *iva*, and that which possesses dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). (Cvc 8.13)
He alone is the illuminator, as King Siṅha shines upon his throne with a pearl necklace swaying against his chest,
like the wish-fulfilling tree on the slope of Mount Sumeru, beautiful with its long, supporting pillars.

Here, when there is an intention to express a mutual relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the two lion-thrones on the slopes of Mount Meru and the two clusters of blossoms that are the lords of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), since both sentence-meanings are conceived through the construction of the relationship between qualifiers and the qualified, their mutual relationship as standard and object of comparison is expressed by a single indicative word; thus, this is called "single-indicator" (*ekadyotakā*).
Sentence simile (*vākyopamā*) consists in the equality of the meanings of two sentences; it employs multiple indicators (*dyotaka*), as for example:
"The illustrious King Siṅgha, like the sun, possesses great prosperity."
In battle, he destroys the host of enemies as darkness is destroyed by the sun in the sky.

Here, with the desire to achieve the unification of two sentences, a distinct expressive word (*dyotaka-śabda*) has been employed for each—namely, for the agent, the object, and the locus as the standard of comparison. Thus, this is the "sentence simile" (*vākyopamā*) characterized by multiple expressives and possessing equality of sentence-meaning. An example of one devoid of expressives is as follows:
In heaven, Maghavat remains awake with his thunderbolt to protect the gods; on earth, this King Siṅga protects the virtuous with his sharp-edged sword.

While the former rejoices in the splendor of jewels and the like with Rambhā and other celestial nymphs, this king, though having surpassed him in power, delights in the company of the beautiful women of his own harem, having planted his fame even there.

In this instance, because the two leaders of the gods— the one of the heavenly world and the one of the earthly world— possess an identical singular splendor, as do the gods and the earthly deities, and the wielder of the thunderbolt and the wielder of the sword,
the relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison) among the sentence-meanings is understood even without an explicit indicator (*dyotaka*). Thus,
this is called "sentence-simile devoid of an indicator" (*dyotakaśūnyā vākyopamā*), characterized by the equality of the sentence-meanings.
An example of the dissimilar [type of comparison] (*vaidharmyavatī*) is as follows:
Unlike one who lacks discernment, he is not fragrant; unlike a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), he does not become hard.
O Śiva, Śiva! The crest-jewel of King Siṅga is the good fortune of the world of mortals.

In this case, among the indicators of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), that property known as "non-discrimination" is restricted by the poet to the standard of comparison alone; thus, this is the sentence simile (*vākyopamā*) called "possessing dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyavatī*).
Where similarity is understood through the manner of expression within the meaning of the sentence, that is the "elaborated simile" (*prapañcopamā*) of two sentence-meanings, as follows: [Ckc 8.14]
This [simile] is indeed twofold, according to its form: natural (*prakṛta*) and unnatural (*aprakṛta*).
Of these two, that which has a natural form is the complete simile (*sakalopamā*), which is fourfold.
Others [mention] *ekadeśopamā*, as well as *mālikā* and *mekhalā*.
In that regard, an example of a complete simile (*sakalopamā*) is as follows:

"With mountains led by Maināka as its elephants, with waves as its horses, with excellent warriors as its crocodile-like elephants, and with its own lord—the moon of the Raichuri dynasty—as clearly as Viṣṇu himself, this army proceeds like the ocean, utterly difficult for anyone to cross. (Ckc 8.15)
In this case, since the ocean and the army are described as being difficult to cross, when there is an intention to express a relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between them,

just as in the case of the mountains such as Maināka and the elephants such as Mātaṅga— which possess the attributes of the ocean and the army respectively and whose similarity is well-known— there occurs,

through the employment of distinct expressive words for each, a comparison between the two whole sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*), including both the wholes and their parts, either in full detail or as appropriate.
This is the style known as *sākalyavatī* (comprehensive), which is an elaboration consisting of the essential nature [of the subject].
An example of *ekadeśavatī* (partial) is as follows:
"King Siṅga shines with his fingers like the buds of young sprouts."
With the luster of her nails like flowers, and with her pair of arms like a pair of branches; // Ckc_8.*16 //

Here, while the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) ought to be stated between the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and the leader (*nāyaka*), the standard of comparison characterized as the wish-fulfilling tree is abandoned; instead, a portion of that [standard] is compared with a portion of the object of comparison through the limbs of the pair of arms—specifically the fingers and the luster of the nails—as well as with the sprouts and flowers representing the parts of the desire for the pair of arms. Thus, because these are compared in detail through the employment of distinct expressive words, this is the *prapañcopamā* (prolix simile) known as *ekadeśavatī* (possessing a single part), which is its natural form.

The three worlds are seen to be pervaded by the glorious majesty of the fame of King Siṅga, as if by garlands of camphor, clusters of moonlight, groves of *kāśa* grass, waves of the celestial river, and blossoms of the *ketaka*; as if by flocks of *kādamba* geese, autumnal sandalwood pastes, throngs of stars, and the orbs of the cool-rayed moon.

In this instance, the fame of the hero is compared to camphor and other substances in the manner of a garland (*mālikā*) for the sake of perceiving each individual excellence; thus, this is the *prapañcopamā* (elaborated simile) known as *mālikā*, which consists of the primary subject itself:
"O King Siṅga, your stainless fame is like a girdle (*mekhalā*), and your wisdom, too, shines forth as exceedingly sharp as a sword."
The sword, like his majesty, burns the hearts of his enemies; and his majesty, like his fame, spreads to the ends of the quarters.

Because the qualities such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and others, whose similarity is being expressed here, are described in detail by synthesizing them according to the analogy of a girdle (*raśanā*), this is the simile of expansion (*prapañcopamā*) known as the "girdle" (*mekhalā*), which takes the form of the subject (*prakṛtarūpā*).

It has been stated that there is another [type of simile] which takes a modified form (*vikṛtarūpā*); that too is fourfold, characterized by the names "inversion" (*viparyāsa*), "produced from both" (*ubhayotpādyā*), and "non-connection" (*ananvaya*).

Among those [examples], the simile of the reversal is as follows: "Let certain ancient ones, such as Kṛṣṇadāsa and others, remain in some corner; we do not speak of their faults because of our reliance on them.
Only the serpent Śeṣa is worthy of equality with the armlet of the God of Love, the bed of Viṣṇu, and the teacher of words—[namely] Śrī Siṅga, the lord of the earth. (Ckc 8.19)

Here, since the status of being the bearer of the earth is what is intended to be understood, the fact that Śeṣa and others are the standards of comparison (*upamāna*) while the hero is the object of comparison (*upameya*) is a case where some speaker,

desiring to express the excellence of the subject under description, has conceived the relationship of standard and object of comparison in reverse; thus, this is the variety of *prapañcopamā* known as *viparyāsopamā*, which is a distorted form.
An example of the double simile (*ubhayopamā*) is as follows:
O illustrious King Siṅga, while you extend both the protection of the virtuous and the instruction of the wicked,
your army possesses the unassailability of the ocean, and the ocean possesses the unassailability of your army.

Here, when there is an intended relationship of mutual comparison between the commander of the army and the army itself, a deviation from established convention occurs regarding one of the two sides; thus, this is the "mutual simile" (*ubhayopamā*), a variety of the "elaborated simile" (*prapañcopamā*) in which the object of comparison is produced [by the poet], as follows: "The arm of King Siṅga, resplendent with its sword, which rests upon the great branch of the wish-fulfilling tree that is the Kālāpa dynasty—this [arm] is equal to this [tree]."
If the moon were situated above Mount Hemādri, the blinding darkness in the west would be like a parasol made of golden pitchers, providing a fitting comparison for the Jātī flower.

Here, having produced the mental conception of a black serpent from the branch of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*), the hand of the hero is compared to this [serpent] which possesses a sword; thus, this is the variety of *prapañcopamā* (prolix simile) known as *utpādyopamā* (simile with a produced object), which takes a distorted form.
The same should be applied to the second half of the verse as well.
An example of *ananvayopamā* (simile without a correlate) is as follows:
The illustrious Siṅgabhūpati shines like [the ancient] Śrī Siṅgabhūpati in warding off the rutting elephants that are his formidable enemies.

In this case, since the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) belongs to one and the same thing, this is the figure known as *ananvaya* (non-connection), a variant of *prapañcopamā*.

When the standard of comparison is applied through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) as the object of comparison itself, such that the two become contradictory, that is defined as *rūpaka* (metaphor). 8.18.
Due to its predominance, this [ornament] is threefold, arising from word, meaning, or both;
that which has the word as predominant is twofold: the original (prakṛta) and the modified (vikṛta).
That [ornament] is composed of words modified at the beginning or the end, and it is of four kinds:
combined, separate, both, and also with qualifiers.
Among these, the metaphor in the form of a compound (samāsavat-rūpaka) is as follows:
"The rain-clouds that are the swords of King Siṅha extinguish the forest fire of the prowess of his enemies."

Here, when similarity and so forth are intended, through the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of non-difference, the object of comparison (*upameya*), the sword (*karavāla*), is designated as "milk-drinker" (*payomuk*)—just like [the moon]—and thus becomes "payomukpayodanirūpaṇīya. Since the common attribute (*sāmānya*) is employed at the beginning, the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*) is obscured and a compound is formed;
therefore, this is a "compound" (*samasta*) metaphor (*rūpaka*) in which the primary form is the word that constitutes the base (*prakṛti*).
It is not at all surprising that the intense luster of the moon, which was dispersed by the fame of the illustrious Lord of Siṅga, reached the sun and spread its heat throughout the world;
yet it is truly marvelous that when these two [the moon and the sun] are embraced so closely by him, the enemy kings become guests at his door.

Here, because the two objects of comparison—*yaśasaḥ* (of fame) and *candreṇa* (with the moon)—are placed in grammatical apposition with the words for the objects of comparison (*pratāpam* [valor] and *tapanam* [the sun]), the literal meaning of the standards of comparison is obscured; furthermore, since a compound has been formed, this is a "compound" metaphor (*samasta-rūpaka*) in which the primary element is the word under discussion. An example of both the compounded and uncompounded forms is as follows:
O Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla, your sword— the fang of the serpent that is your staff-like arm—
renders the orb of the moon, which is the assembly of hostile kings, devoid of its lunar light, namely their fame.

In this instance, "the serpent of the arm" (*bhujābhujaṅgamasya*) is a compound (*samasta*), while "fang" (*daṃṣṭrā*) is not a compound (*asamasta*); thus, both of these are examples of what is called *rūpaka* (metaphor) where the base word (*prakṛti-śabda*) is predominant.
An example with an adjective (*saviśeṣaṇam*) is as follows:
"The Mandara mountain that is King Siṅga, whose movement within the interior [of his enemies] has its splendor obstructed..."
It becomes a sea of nectar for enemies and a mine of poverty for [his] kinsmen.

Here, just as the leader [of the army] is characterized by the attribute "agitated by Mandara," the armies of the enemies of the lords of the [hostile] forces are likewise characterized by specific attributes; thus, this is a "qualified" (saviśeṣaṇa) type of metaphor where the primary status belongs to the words denoting the substrata (prakṛtiśabdapradhāna-rūpaka).
An example of a "chain" (paramparā) is as follows:
"The silken banner-cloth of the banner of virtue is the lime-plaster for the mansion of the three worlds."
O King Siṅgha, your fame is the eastern moon for the ocean of virtuous people.
Here, first there is the metaphorical representation of the virtues as banners;
second, the silk cloth-strip as being related to them;
and third, its fame as being related to that [cloth].
Thus, this so-called *paraṃparā* consists primarily of metaphorical expressions using modified words (*vikṛta-śabda*).
This same figure can also occur by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*),
as for example:

O King Siṅga, the line of your sidelong glance shines forth like a fresh torrent from the clouds that burns away the impurities of the Kali age— a divine streak like a wish-fulfilling tree, a mountain-cleaving thunderbolt.
Some say that this very [figure] is called "metaphor-cause metaphor" (*rūpaka-hetu-rūpaka*) because it serves as the cause for the metaphor; however,
that too is indeed a mere distortion,
just like a girdle (*mekhalā*).
This royal capital on the king of mountains is adorned with elephants by the princes, rocks by boulders,
and palaces by graceful mansions.

Here, because the metaphors of the prince, the elephant, and so forth are linked in a successive chain according to the principle of the *raśanā* (girdle), this is called *mekhalā* (a girdle), a type of metaphor in which the modified word (*vikṛta-śabda*) is predominant.
Some call this *śṛṅkhalā* (a chain);
however, that is merely a difference in name.
Like a crest-jewel to kings, like a *pārijāta* tree to supplicants, like a playful garden to those of good conduct, and like a treasure-store of fortune— to you,
O fair-bodied one, [I am] a stage for sport.
This lord of the earth, Siṅha, shines upon the royal mountain, having brought an end to misconduct.

In this case, because the metaphors are presented in the manner of a garland (*mālikā*) with respect to a single hero, this is the metaphor named *mālikā*, which is a transformation (*vikṛta*) primarily consisting of words.
An example of a metaphor upon a metaphor (*rūpakarūpaka*) is as follows:
"The sword is a serpent for the arm of King Śrī Siṅgha."
The entire mandala of the enemy kings, like a jewel-moon, remains [subdued] without exception.

Here, because the sword—which has been superimposed as a creeper—is further described as having the form of a serpent, this is called *rūpakarūpaka* (metaphor-on-metaphor), a type of metaphor primarily characterized by its distorted linguistic expression.

These four types [of metaphors] are termed "distorted" (*vikṛta*) because they are composed through distortions such as the *paraṃparita* (successive) and others. That which is primarily concerned with meaning is twofold, according to whether it pertains to the principal element (*aṅgin*) or the subordinate element (*aṅga*).
The primary fourfold division [of poetry] has been defined by means of metaphors and other such figures.
[This occurs] through the distinctions of being complete or incomplete, and appropriate or inappropriate.

Therein, O illustrious Siṅgabhūpa, the goddess Kamalā dwells with supreme reverence within your lotus-face, which possesses the essence of the nectar of flowing, sweet speech and is exceptionally beautiful with the petals of its wide eyes— thus it is complete in every respect.

Here, the hero and the lotus-face, as the whole (the composite objects), are metaphorically represented in their entirety according to the speaker's intention, along with their own parts— the expressed similarities, the nectar-like eloquence, and the eyes like petals— by means of descriptions that establish them as the substrata for appropriate entities; thus, because this very [metaphor] holds primacy, it is called *sakalarūpaka* (complete metaphor), which is primarily concerned with the subject and primarily concerned with the meaning.
Just as one who has not experienced the full moon does not perceive it when it is incomplete,
so too one who has not tasted the nectar of the Blessed One’s face— charming with the moonlight of his smile—
does not truly comprehend it even when his own lotus-eyes are blossoming.

In this case, because the two parts— the moonlight of the smile and the [moon’s] rays— are described, yet the standard of comparison (upamāna), namely the full moon, is not explicitly mentioned by means of that part, this is the figure of speech called *vikala-rūpaka* (deficient metaphor), which is dominated by the principal object (*aṅgin*).
"O King Siṅga, you exist as a lotus-pond (*padmākara*) served by royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*), possessing the beauty of the lotus-stalks of royal fame."

Since there is a mutual compatibility between the two things being superimposed here, this is appropriately termed a *rūpaka* (metaphor) in which the subordinate is primary (*aṅgipradhāna*). Although in this case the word "padmākara" relies upon figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*) and thus the word itself is adorned by the qualifiers, nevertheless, through the power of the pun (*śleṣa*)— namely, that it is the "source (*ākara*) of Padmā"— the primacy of the primary meaning of the word is understood as if it were its literal sense.
Thus, this [verse] has meaning as its primary focus.
It is inappropriate [to take it literally], for example: "While bearing immortal nectar that is pure, the stream produces fear by means of poison."
O Śrī Siṅgabhūpa, the Yamunā of your sword shines forth.

In this case, because the two things being superimposed—ambrosia and poison—are opposed by their very nature, their mutual connection is impossible; thus, this is the type of *rūpaka* (metaphor) called "the improper" (*ayukta*), in which the subordinate element is primary.

The wise know that there are four clever varieties of the *aṅgapradhāna* (subordinate-primary metaphor), distinguished by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of: being innate (*sahaja*), being acquired (*āhārya*), the combination of those two (*tadyoga*), and the disparity between them (*tadvaiṣamya*). (Kāvyālaṃkāra 8.23)
In this regard, an example of the primary [type of] natural limb is as follows:

"Adorned with clusters of blossoming breasts, strewn with the flowers of smiles, possessing creeper-like arms that are exceedingly tender and reaching out with passion, and having copper-red lips for their outer petals—
these vine-like maidens, presented as offerings by neighboring kings eager to serve, bestow their affection upon King Śrī Siṅha."

In this case, regarding the maiden, the primary elements are the breasts, the gentle smile, and the slight curve of the arms; and regarding the creeper, they are the clusters of blossoms, the flowers, the bees, and the excellent leaves. Since these constituent parts are the principal factors in making the hero long for her, this is an example of *sahajāṅgapradhānarūpaka* (inherent metaphor where the subordinate parts are the principal).
An example of *āhāryapradhāna* (metaphor where the subordinate parts are artificially constructed) is as follows:
Ripening at the very edge of hope, rising in favor of the universal joy of the white lotuses of his kinsmen swelling under the spreading heat of his mature majesty,
and bringing an end to the pride of the departure of the arrogant rival Gaṇḍabhairava, this [sun] prepares itself to destroy the ketakī-stalks of the fame of the enemy kings.

In this case, regarding the perspective of the hero’s victorious expedition, the [qualities] characterized as majesty, kinsmen, and enemies, as well as the heat, white lotuses, and *ketaka* flowers in the context of autumn, are conceived as constituent parts (*avayava*). Because these superimposed elements (*āhārya*) hold primacy in the act of donning armor, it is called "Metaphor with Superimposed Parts as Primary" (*āhāryāṅgapradhāna-rūpaka*). Thus, this constitutes the primacy of both [the whole and its parts]. An example of their conjunction is as follows:

O Lord Bhairava, whose arms and shoulders are raised high, you are seen like a mass of smoke from the fire of the prowess of your sword— a dense cloud of smoke from the great blade fanned by the heat of your valor— intense with sparks of wrath;

and as the flames from the tips of your arrows blaze forth clearly, filling the hollows of the quarters of the sky, they appear like a forest fire consuming the thicket of the armies of your rival kings.

In this instance, regarding the side of the hero’s majesty, the artificial parts—characterized by the sword, wrath, and arrows—and regarding the side of fire, the natural parts—smoke, sparks, and flames—are all metaphors (*rūpaka*s) that hold primary importance in causing agitation among the enemy kings; thus, this is a metaphor in which both natural and artificial limbs are predominant.
An example of "discordance" (*vaiṣamya*) is as follows:

With the serpent-like arms of the illustrious Lord of the Earth [Śrī Siṅgha], whose fingers are like copper-colored sprouts, upon which the beautiful and sweet [sword] is firmly set, and which shine with the lines of auspicious marks;
and with the proud [king] consecrated as minister over the cities of the far-reaching wicked teachers—the Earth expands, possessing a stable state of happiness in her royal camp.
Here, since the arm as a whole has been metaphorically identified with a serpent (*bhuja-gata*), its parts—the fingers—are metaphorically identified with lotus petals;

furthermore, the spaces between the feet and the beautiful lines on the shoulders are also metaphorically identified [with other parts]. Thus, because of this total disparity (*vaiṣamya*) and because the copper-colored fingers and so forth are predominant in their capacity to bear the burden of the earth through the medium of fortune (*bhāgya*), this is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) in which the dissimilar limbs are predominant.
The primary [meaning] of a word and its referent is twofold: the simple and the exclusive.
May the moon-like King Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla shine forth, who, like the moon itself, is intent upon delighting the night-lilies and bringing joy to the dark lotuses.

Here, by the metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of the whole subject—the *kuvalaya*—as the moon, the predominance of the word is established; however, because of the specific epithets that are *śleṣa* (punning), the predominance belongs to the meaning. Thus, this is a "pure" (*kevalā*) metaphor where both [word and meaning] are predominant.
An example of the *vyatireka* (contrast) type is as follows:

By the good fortune of the people, King Siṅga protects the earth— he who is an unbreakable ocean, a moon free from stain, a discerning mountain of gold, a Lord of Love who has assumed his own form, an irreproachable Indra, and a king of serpents devoid of crooked gait.

Here, because the ocean and so forth—whose distinctions such as "unbroken" and so on have been brought forth through contrast (vyatireka)—are described as being in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the hero, their predominance is determined both by implication and by the words themselves; thus, this is a Metaphor (rūpaka) named "Possessing Contrast," wherein both [elements] are predominant.
In this way, the eighteenfold form of Metaphor has been defined.
Because it is of a mixed nature, the "mixed" is not distinct from "intermixture."
For one who claims that there is no aesthetic charm (*acamatkriyā*) in the individual forms of the *vidyādhara* and so forth,
the primary cause is a lack of skill in composing illustrative examples (*lakṣyanirmāṇakātarya*).
Where a comparison is understood through the cleverness of expression in both [the subject and the object],
yet it differs from simile (upamā) and metaphor (rūpaka), that indeed is the figure of speech called *sāmyam-ahaṅkriyā*.

This non-controversial statement regarding phenomenal proliferation (prapañca) is threefold— by way of example, illustration, and counter-illustration— and it possesses the qualities of equality, superiority, and non-inferiority.
In this regard, an example of an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*) characterized by similarity (*sāmyavatī*) is as follows:

"King Siṅga, who filled the quarters with his military expeditions, [attained] the ripening of speech through fruits produced by his discernment; he naturally [achieved] the graceful [melody] of the lute-sounds of beautiful women, while those seeking victory [prepared for battle]. (Ckc 8.42)

Here, the equality— held in a balance— between the standards of comparison (*upamāna*), such as the ripening notes of the *vipaṃcī* lute and the grapes on the family mountain (*kulagiri*), and the objects of comparison (*upameya*), such as the voices of female singers accompanied by intoxicated elephants,
is perceived through the artful turn of speech even without an explicit indicator [of similarity].
Thus, this is the variety of the figure of speech *sāmya* (simile) called "the description of the present expansion" (*prakṛtaprapañcokti*).
This [speech] may also be distorted, as for example:
"He measures with intoxicated elephants the family of the great mountains with their lofty peaks; he measures the grapes with the ripened words of those whose intellects are perfected."
King Siṅha, desiring to conquer the sound of the lute heard by the ears of beautiful women during his expedition that filled all directions, [was defeated].

In this instance, the primary mountains and so forth are treated as the objects of comparison (*upameya*), while the intoxicated elephants are treated as the standards of comparison (*upamāna*); since this is conceived through a reversal of conventional usage, it is the variety of similarity known as "the description of a distorted manifestation" (*vikṛtaprapañcokti*).
An example of excellence through the subject itself (*prakṛta*) is as follows:
"O Earth, do not be proud; the illustrious Siṅga, the foremost of the Cālukya dynasty, steals away thirst with his gifts."

There exist such practitioners of action who surpass the celestial cow, the wish-fulfilling tree, the series of wish-granting gems, and the elixir of immortality, and who are joined with the trunk of abundant compassion.
In this regard, O you gods who support the universe, why do you take pride in this very hero who is distinguished by his generosity?

For the givers to the inhabitants of heaven are the many lineage-born Kalpa-trees and the like. Because this elaborate statement (prapañcokti) excels through such an excellence of the comparison, it is called "the figure of speech consisting of similarity characterized by superiority" (utkarṣavatī sāmyabhakti). That same [figure], through inferiority, is as follows:
Wiping the sky as if it were a cloth, washing yourself in the ocean, and rubbing your body against the rocks of Mount Meru, you wander day and night with the speed of the moon.
Having done what, O King, have you become a king whose fame rests in your heart? What can we say? Truly, it cannot be removed; no, no, this natural darkness is innate.

Here, because the excellence of the hero’s fame—the object of comparison—is superior to that of the moon—the standard of comparison—it is called *apakarṣavatī* (inferiority), a type of elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*). In this same manner, *vikṛti* (transformation) is also to be characterized. When there is the presence of something possessing true splendor, it is called a statement of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntokti*).
Through these [factors] such as ritual action, whether combined or uncombined, this [result] may arise in many ways.
Here, through the blending of actions,
as she turns back and turns away, having extended herself and fashioned her expansion,
the Goddess Lakṣmī constantly shines like a shadow following the line of the glance of the illustrious King Siṅga.

In this context, there is either a similarity produced by the application of the action of mere exclusion (*nivartana*) and so forth, or it is preceded by an illustration; thus, this is an illustrative statement possessing mere yoga of action.

That same [illustration] possesses mixed yoga of action, as for example, in the very place of the second quarter, where the reading is *kṛtaprasādām* (one who has performed grace) instead of *racitaprasādā* (one who has fashioned grace); here, the action of exclusion possesses a similarity caused by the quality of grace, and this is an illustrative statement possessing mixed yoga of action.
In this way, the statements of examples (dṛṣṭāntokti) should be understood as being based on the causes of mixed and unmixed classes, qualities, substances, and conjunctions.
Now, what is the distinction between a statement of an example and the figure of speech known as "example" (dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra)?
Listen.

The meaning is that there is no difference whatsoever regarding the object for which there is a consensus among worldly investigators; however, with respect to the stylistic formulation of the expression, many variations exist. For instance, an example (dṛṣṭānta) is that which serves the purpose of establishing the probandum (sādhya).
The statement of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is for the purpose of establishing similarity (*sādharmya*).
In an [ordinary] example, even the scent of an indicator (*dyotaka*) is not pursued;
however, here there is an occasion for the employment of an indicator, and for this very reason, this is an ornament of both.
Having introduced some object and then placing another possessing its same characteristics alongside it,
such that a similarity is understood— this is called *prativastūkti* (the expression by way of a parallel object).
It is considered to be twofold by way of the expression of examples and the expression of elaborations.
An example of *chāyā-prativastūkti* (the shadow-like correspondence) is as follows:

On the tiger-skin garment of Śiva, which is radiant with the brilliance of a rutting elephant and upon which his matted locks quiver, one might fear the sound of a drum signaling the humiliation of a deer from any quarter;

yet, if other kings were to behold at the front of battle the face of the illustrious Siṅga, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose fame consists of faultless poetry, that face would be terrifying with its knitted brows.

Here, the object in the form of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is presented first, and the corresponding object (*prativastu*) that serves as the illustrated case is presented afterwards; thus, this figure of speech called *prativastūkti* possesses the shadow of an illustration and constitutes a division of similarity (*sāmyabhakti*). An example possessing the shadow of an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*) is as follows:
If the story that rests upon the illustrious King Siṅha does not delight me, then the sight of Mount Meru is useless; if the beholding of the moon is in vain, then let it be so.
If the assembly of Mādhavī’s sweetness does not enter behind one's back, then the service of her is the very attainment of genuine excellence for the wise.

Here, in three cases there is an inferiority of the standard of comparison, while in the fourth there is equality; thus, this *prativastūkti* possesses the shadow of an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*).

In this way, the ornament of general similarity (*sāmānya-sāmya*) has been defined. As for its specific varieties, let them be identified by those who possess specialized knowledge within the detailed treatment of the illustrative examples.
When the mind wavers between two objects due to their extreme similarity, that expression of doubt is considered to have both a single and multiple objects. (Ckc 8.33)
That [cognition] which is manifold yet apprehends a single object is one whose object is singular; whereas that which is single yet apprehends many objects is known as having a manifold object.
Sharing the same domain [of asceticism]:
"Your diet consists of vegetables; you find delight in solitary reflection within mountain caves; your bed is the bare ground; your body is white with ashes; your head is matted with locks;
your limbs are composed of bone. Alas! Are you a great ascetic, or perhaps a king at enmity with the powerful Pratigaṇḍabhairava? // Ckc_8.49 //

In this case, regarding a single object characterized by the person Tapasvin, which possesses the two attributes of being a hero and being an adversary, there arises a state of hesitation (*vimarśa*) due to the perception of a commonality expressed in reality, the non-perception of specific distinctions, and the recollection of the specific qualities belonging to both [possibilities]. This should be understood as a statement of doubt (*saṃśayokti*) having a single object. An example of one with multiple objects is as follows:

There are two who are the roots of joy for the eyes in this world, ever vigilant in delighting the blue lotuses; their own minds are inclined solely toward the path of the virtuous, and they are being filled with artistic perfections.
Who then is that Siṅga, the ornament of the earth? Who is the full moon? What is the moonlight? And what is fame? Though I reflect upon it for a long time, I simply do not know the truth.
In this case, since both [possibilities] are suspected for each of the two—the hero and the non-hero—who are being described as possessing similarity, this is that [type].

This also occurs when the similarity is based on what is already well-known (*pratīta*); for example, in the very same context, "What is moonlight? And what is fame?"—since both possibilities are suspected for each of the two, namely moonlight and fame, which possess well-known similarities such as whiteness, this is that [type]:
the variety of *anekaviṣaya* (multiple-subject) based on the similarity of description (*varṇana-sāmya*).
In this same way, even those [figures] that share a single object are to be characterized.
Now, what is the distinction between the figures of *vitarka* (conjecture) and *saṃśaya* (doubt)?
Listen.
Doubt is a reflective awareness that clings to two alternatives;
deliberation (*vitarka*), however, is that which has rejected one alternative.
Deliberation is a state of mind that is on the verge of some degree of certainty.

Doubt is proximate to discursive thought (*vitarka*); for one who is doubting ascends to the pinnacle of discursive thought and, having abandoned the stage of mere reasoning, becomes intent upon the reality itself—
whether by denying some object or [by focusing] on what is similar or dissimilar.
Where there is the attribution of another object, that is considered *apahnuti* (concealment).
An example of *apahnuti* (concealment) involving the placement of a similar object is as follows:
"O friend, this is not the autumnal moonlight; it is the glory of the fame of King Śrī Siṅga. This is not a swarm of flickering bees; it is the ill-fame of those who hate him.
This is not the warbling of cuckoos; it is the concert of the fame of those deer-eyed women. Thus, O friend, does the fair-eyed woman whose beloved is far away string together her words.

Here, although moonlight is real, it is denied by means of speech; instead, other objects—namely, the characteristics of the voices of female singers who sing the ill-fame of the hero's rival, which possess perceived similarity—are introduced.
Thus, this is *apahnuti* (concealment) characterized by similarity (*sādṛśyavatī apahnuti*).
"Alas! My eye, so unlike [anything else], weeps because it is touched by the pollen of the flower-cluster in your ear-ornament; my body, touched by this gentle breeze, experiences horripilation.

Having thus declared that there was no other cause for these symptoms when her heart’s desire had been attained upon the arrival of the illustrious King Siṅga, a certain woman felt bashful with soft smiles toward her own friend.

In this case, a certain woman of modest character, concealing her passion directed toward the hero— which would otherwise cause tears of joy and horripilation— fabricates the presentation of a dissimilar cause characterized by the wind of detachment; thus, this is the figure of speech called *apahnuti* (concealment) characterized by dissimilarity (*asādṛśyavatī*),
which is considered a "statement of resolution" (*samādhyukti*) because it is the attribution of the properties of one thing to another.

Based on the etymological derivation as "the superimposition of one thing upon another," there are three types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*): the superimposition of two subjects (*dharmin*), the superimposition of an attribute (*dharma*), and the superimposition of both attribute and subject.
Among these, regarding the superimposition of two subjects alone, it is said:
"At that very moment, he becomes a jewel protecting his own wings; for one whose mind is fearless, taking refuge in Durgā is not even conceivable."
O illustrious King Siṅga, as you were thus intent upon the conquest of the earth, the stubbornness of the neighboring mountain-kings attained its full growth.

In this case, having set aside the superimposition of attributes (*dharmāropa*), there is the superimposition of the very ruler Parvata—who possesses those attributes—upon the hero; this is *dharmisamādhi*.
An example of *dharmasamādhi* is as follows:
"O Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla, when your blazing majesty has conquered the majesty of the sun..."
On the horizon, her inner being blossoming with joy, she has embraced fame most intensely.

In this instance, having set aside the qualities of being a warrior, an adversary, and possessing those respective characteristics— which belong respectively to the hero, the hero’s majesty, and the hero’s fame— upon the insentient horizons of the quarters, only those qualities consisting of victory, defeat, joy, embracing, and the surging of waves are superimposed;
thus, this is *dharmasamādhi* (the superimposition of attributes).

Regarding the superimposition of those attributes upon those subjects: just as previously, out of fear of what had occurred, she was placed upon the back of a snake whose girth was overcome by terror; who, trembling at the tip of its fangs, was seized by hundreds and led away by its foot;
and who, smeared with blood and mud, was abandoned according to her father’s words—was it not because of the thought, "Is this not Kṛṣṇā"?
By you, born of the Rāicarlīya clan, this [earth] is considered stable.

In this case, regarding the hero [Nala], there is this *ubhayasamādhi* (double superimposition) consisting of the superimposition of the ocean’s agitation and so forth upon the attributes of Nārāyaṇa—namely, his incarnations from the Fish-form down to Balabhadra—which are themselves superimposed [upon the hero].
The wise call that *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression) where the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood from the well-known object of comparison (*upamāna*). (Cvc 8.37)
This [reproach] may be of three kinds: praise, censure, or reproach.
Just as a boastful woman who is parched with thirst finds fulfillment in her life upon meeting a traveler— her friend in times of wretchedness and despair— who has now become a bowman and a river.

Here, by means of the simile of the desert (*marudeśa*) which protects the lives of travelers, and through the implied [meaning], the common attribute characterized by the protection of travelers is established as the speech of King Siṅga— who is the sole refuge for the world of kings and the world of mortals defiled by the faults of the Kali age— and it is by the very shadow of that [simile] that his praise is perceived;
thus, this is "Samāsokti with Praise" (*ślāghāvatī*).
That very [eye] is indeed censurable, as it were:
one for the preceptor of the Daityas, two for the slayer of Mura, three for the Lord of creatures, eight for the two whose abode is the lotus-womb, twelve for the Lord of Laṅkā, and twenty for us;

yet we have a thousand eyes—O Vāstoṣpati, do not be proud! Do not be angry! For this has been said by one who remembers the state beyond passion: "Is it not rather shame that comes upon you...? (Ckc 8.57)
