Here, the simile is established through the expression of a certain base king as the object of comparison (*upameya*), by means of the comparison (*upamāna*) with Duścyavana himself— who, on account of the fault of pursuing Ahalyā, possessed a thousand eyes that surpassed [all others] precisely because of that defect, and who thus despised eminent persons such as Bhārgava— [the base king being one] whose wealth was acquired through injustice and who was surpassed by the sovereign class beginning with Siṅga-bhūpāla, who were inclined toward the path of justice. Thus, the commonality (*sāmānya*) is implied.

Since the censure of the object of comparison (the *upameya*) is intended to be expressed through the door of the comparison itself, this is a "Samāsokti with Censure" (*garhāvatī*). An example of "Samāsokti with Rebuke" (*upālambhavatī*) is as follows:
"Even having experienced bitterness from tender sprouts, even from shoots, and even from flowers..."
O friend, you dwell among the *palāśa* trees; why then have you become bitter yourself, like the *nimba* tree?

Here, bitterness is established through the description of a certain person who, though devoid of merit and unworthy of praise, possesses a resemblance that is implied by his very own consecrated (mūrdhābhiṣikta) self as a point of comparison; since the statement "even when matured, he remains bitter" functions as a reproach, this is a *samāsokti* (condensed expression) characterized by reproach (*upālambhavatī*), wherein the subject of comparison depends upon the object of comparison arising from the point of comparison.
Praised for its expressed resemblance to fortitude,
which is the support of constancy, and made resonant by the pure Sarasvatī who constantly displays her noble flow—
only the Golden Mountain (Meru) is fit to bear the weight of the earth, as it is the sole abode of the wise gods in the Sudharmā assembly hall, and not any other mountain.

Here, since the similarity expressed through qualities such as being the support of fortitude is established by the mention of King Siṅga—the object of comparison—by means of the simile of the Golden Mountain (Meru), the praise of the object of comparison is understood through the medium of the standard of comparison; thus, this is the aforementioned [type of simile].
That same [simile], when accompanied by censure, is as follows:
Abstention from the objects of the senses has been indicated by subsisting on air alone; the removal of evil karma has been manifested by immersing one’s entire body in the sand.

Having thus worshipped the one pierced by those heretics, I join my palms in salutation from afar to you, O Śiṃśumāra, whose nature is exalted and who is robust with illusory power, lest I be swallowed by them.

Here, because the censure of a certain hypocrite dwelling at the gate— who is the subject of comparison (upameya)— is understood through the mouth of the crocodile, which is the standard of comparison (upamāna), by means of the similarity expressed [between them],
this is a *samāsokti* (condensed expression) characterized by the censure of the expressed similarity. That same figure is "characterized by reproach" (*upālambhavatī*), as for example:

Who else here could possibly equal the ocean— the source for fulfilling the desires of the wise, which delights in its own boundaries, which supports many living beings, which possesses innate splendor, and whose beauty is kindled by the shimmering of the moon— if it were not for its dullness?

Here, because the ocean itself—the standard of comparison—is censured, a censure of something possessing some quality—the object of comparison—characterized by a stated similarity, which acts as a cause of delay, is perceived; thus, this is *samāsokti* (suggestion by ellipsis) characterized by a censure of the stated similarity. By this, cases involving a mixture with praise (*ślāghā*) and so forth are also explained.
In this regard, an example of the mixture of praise and censure is as follows:

"Ocean, how many small shells do you not produce from your streams of water—shells that serve as a cause for a mass of ill-repute because they are smeared with the fat and filled with the remains of internal creatures?
Yet, it is from you, the ocean, that this very conch shell of auspicious clockwise-turning was born, the source of good fortune for those whose lot is supreme."
Here, in the first half [of the verse], because the comparison is not explicitly stated for the reservoirs of water that are the birthplaces of small conchs,

the disparagement of the objects of comparison— the lineages of other kings who are the birthplaces of very petty Kṣatriyas— is understood through the medium of the comparison itself, as their similarity is merely implied.

Furthermore, in the latter half [of the verse], the praise of the subject (the upameya)— the descendant of Recara, whose fortune has not yet fully matured— is established through the very expression of the comparison with the object of comparison (the upamāna), namely the ocean of milk that produced the right-spiraling conch. Thus, this is a *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor) characterized by a mixture of censure and praise.
In this way, other varieties should also be characterized;
their distorted forms are also possible,
as follows:
Protecting the worlds with a hand that guards the virtuous and holds hundreds of millions [of coins], King Siṅga shines resplendent.

Here, while the hero who is the subject of description is appropriately the object of comparison (*upameya*), he is instead treated as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) according to the logic of "inverse simile" (*viparyāsopamā*). Consequently, the praise directed toward him is expressed with particular force, whereas the praise for Śatakratu (Indra), the common point of reference, is merely implied.
Thus, this is a "transformed" (*vikṛtā*) *samāsokti* in which the commonality has been explicitly stated.
In this manner, other varieties [of figures] that are not to be consumed (? should also be understood by oneself.
Now, one might ask: what is the distinction between simile (*upamā*) and the compound-based figure *samāsokti*?
Listen:

the superimposition of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) upon the object of comparison (*upameya*) is *samādhi*, whereas the attribution of the attributes of the object of comparison onto the standard of comparison is *samāsokti*; thus, the distinction between these two is manifest.
[It is *samāsokti*] where the qualities and actions of the object to be seen are perceived as having attained the state of another.
The wise conceive of it otherwise; they call that "utprekṣā" (poetic fancy).
Because they have the same form, fruit, and cause, and because they follow from existence to existence,
this [classification] of substances and so forth may occur in many ways through conceptual differentiation.
Among these, an example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the essential nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"Thinking in his heart, 'It is not fitting for me to remain forever in the abode of the gods,' Viṣṇu abandoned the Lord of Waters;
having thus descended into the Recara lineage, this King Śrī Siṅgha protects this entire world. (Ckc 8.64)

Here, the hero is imagined as the lover of Lakṣmī, who has descended from the Recara lineage; thus, this is an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpotprekṣā*).
An example of an *utprekṣā* regarding the fruit of a substance (*dravyaphalotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"I believe [the mountain] exists for the sake of protecting the lineage of the second serpent, and for the sake of kissing the breasts of the mountain-mountain-damsels of the quarters..."
At the very threshold of the abode of the gods, the fame of the illustrious King Siṅga enters the three worlds for the sake of the Himācala mountain.

In this instance, because the entry of fame into the three worlds is presented as the purpose, there is a mention of the second lord of serpents and other substances; thus, this is called such [an *utprekṣā*].
An *utprekṣā* based on a substance that serves as the cause is as follows:

"Having calmed the elephants of the quarters, having made the mountain ranges of the world-system free from agitation, having uprooted the foremost of serpents, and having caused the primordial tortoise to shine forth..."
The earth, consecrated by the installation performed by the illustrious Lord of Siṅga, brings delight as if by another Sumeru.

In this instance, there is a *dravyahetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause consisting of a substance), because the substance characterized by the hero—who is the cause for the establishment of the earth—is imagined as being another Mount Sumeru.
An example of *guṇasvarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the nature of a quality) is as follows:
"O King Siṅga, the movements of the internal states of those fawn-eyed women with bodies full of youth are directed toward you."
Her playful glances are like gently rippling waves, and her soft smiles are like blossoming flowers under various pretexts.
In this case, the affections of young women toward the hero are imagined in the form of waves and so forth; thus, it is described as such.
And as it has been said:
"O illustrious King Siṅghadharaṇīpāla, your mastery of literature..."
It causes poets to sprout forth within, like bliss incarnate.
Here, the poetic artistry (sāhityacāturya) is imagined as being the personified embodiment of bliss; thus, this is called such [an *utprekṣā*].
An example of *guṇahetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a quality as the cause) is as follows:
"In the moon, which has taken refuge at the crest of the king's head, your dancing fame seems to compete [with it]."
O King Siṅga, the city of Rājamaulivapura shines resplendent in the world, adorned with the rays of its golden palaces.
Here, because there is both the quality and the cause of rivalry, this is called such [a figure].
An example of *guṇaphalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a quality as a fruit) is as follows:
"Having made all the remaining serpents his own snakes, all the oceans his oceans, and all the elephants his celestial elephant Airāvata..."
The brilliant fame of the illustrious King Siṅga travels as if to entreat the Creator to fashion a third world for his assembly.
In this case, both the quality and the fruit of the *anunaya* (conciliation) are present; thus it is described as such.
An example of *kriyāsvarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the nature of an action) is as follows:
"The illustrious Lord of the Earth, Siṅga, who is marked by the name 'Pārijāta' [the patron of those who seek refuge], is surrounded by his great fame."
Because of the fruitlessness of its own kin due to lack of discernment, the wish-fulfilling tree seems to sink once again into the ocean of milk.

In this instance, the obscuring of the Kalpavṛkṣa by the fame of the hero is conceived as being submerged in the ocean; thus, this is called "Poetic Fancy" (*utprekṣā*) regarding the result of an action. An example of Poetic Fancy regarding the result of an action is as follows:

[The earth], possessing a compassion that is unshakable due to the impact of the mass of flames from the Vāḍava fire—which is crackling with the sound of *dhagadhaga* as it swallows the waters of the Ocean of Milk—[is described].
As if to soothe the torment of inner anguish, the moonlight of King Siṅga’s fame—entirely cooling—enters the caverns of the Mandara mountains.
In this instance, "as if to pacify" indicates the result of the action.
An example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the cause of the action is as follows:
"as if enraged by the offense of rivalry with the extreme generosity of the illustrious Siṅgaśārṅga-dhanus."
Under the pretext of encircling creepers coiled from their very roots, the Lord has bound the wish-fulfilling trees of his subjects.
In this context, it is stated that the commission of an offense is both an action and a cause;
this should be understood as an illustration, and the same should be seen to apply to its genus as well.
Thus, a few varieties of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) have been described; the four remaining types among those mentioned should be identified by the discerning.
Aprastutapraśaṃsā (indirect praise) is the praise of that which is not intended to be praised.
Victorious are those blessed mountains where this King Śrī Siṅga resides; for even though they are kings, they are not fit to be his targets of conquest, nor is he merely their friend, the moon.

There, the multitudes of trees, though laden with the weight of beauty, are surpassed by the lake which, through its superior fortune, alone has fulfilled its purpose by manifesting the greatness of the lofty Puṇḍarīka.

Here too, while the censure of the consecrated king—who is a leader desiring victory and situated on the side of the enemy—is the subject at hand, the praise of irrelevant objects such as the mountain, the moon, and the lake is performed; thus, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description).

When, for the sake of praising or censuring one thing, there is a statement that equates it with others through qualities superior to those [of the subject], that is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). (Cvc 8.44)
An example of *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is as follows: "By the Grandfather of the World,
in creating Rādheya, Rajanīkara, Ratipati, Ratnākara, Rāghava, Vaidharaṇīdhara, Rasānidhi, Ranti, Rasāla, Ravi,
and Raicharlīyakulodvaha for the sake of performing acts that benefit the world, the very essence of compassion has been manifested."

In this instance, because the praise of the hero is established through the conjunction of Karṇa and the others—who have themselves received praise for being devoted to the welfare of the world—this is *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) intended for the purpose of praise. An example intended for the purpose of censure is as follows:

[The sun is] "inferior" (*mandādi*) because it causes the melting of minerals; "seizing" (*grahaṇāt*) because it takes up the waters; "causing distress to others" (*anyopatāpakaraṇāt*) because it scorches the earth; and "devoted to women" (*pramadādhikārāt*) because it is the domain of the goddess Pramadā.
Alas, these fickle men desire life even by taking refuge with the enemy of the illustrious King Siṅgha!

In this context, by placing alchemy and similar practices—which have incurred censure due to their nature as mere destruction and transformation of a young bride—on an equal footing with the taking of refuge in a king other than the [right] leader, a similarity is perceived for the purpose of censure;
thus, this is what was stated.
"The subordination of a fault to the status of a merit, and the transformation of a merit into a fault..."
Therefore, that which contains a slight [element of truth] is not different from this; it is remembered as "feigned praise" (vyājastuti).

In this regard, an example where a defect becomes subordinate (guṇībhāva) is as follows: "O King Siṅga, treasure-house of the wealth of fame, when you honor those kings who wish to serve you in person—kings who, having crushed the crowns of rival monarchs with deceptive stratagems, have drawn from them excellent articles of tribute sent by the hands of their own friends, consider them to be the most honorable of men. In this context, the praise of the forest kings' skill in employing crooked means— which was offered by those wandering along the banks of the Upagautamī— is intended to appear as a fault in the mind of the hero, who is devoted to the royal highway [of straightforward conduct]. With this intention, the ministers, possessing clever intellects and desiring to avoid manifest harshness, have characterized even the fault of employing deceitful stratagems as a virtue consisting in the acquisition of wealth through the means of the hero’s army.
Thus, this is called *leśa* (the slight), wherein a defect becomes subordinate [to a quality] and is described very subtly and slowly so as not to be noticed by others.
An example of a quality becoming a defect is as follows:
"O dear friend, even for such an offense, what request can there be regarding my life? What use is that cruel-hearted, deceitful moon of the Recarla dynasty?"

For him, the foremost of the accomplished ones, the constant vow of cleansing away the offenses of others is clearly like an innate training in the essence, resonance, and sweetness of conciliatory words.

In this context, a certain heroine who is not overly steadfast, having made a promise before her friends and the hero that was consistent with her resolve to maintain her pride, now fears she may fail to fulfill it.

Desiring to avoid the ridicule of her circle of friends, she presents the host of the hero’s virtues—which are characterized by flattery and the like, and which serve as obstacles to her pride—as if they were defects. This is the figure known as *leśa* (the slight), wherein a quality is treated as a defect.
O Śrī Siṅghabhūpāla, just as you do not rejoice when the lotuses have their shade removed,
why is it that by removing the shade [of your own work], you also remove the verses of the Primordial King? Ckc_8.79*79

In this case, because the quality of the hero, characterized by the seizure of royal fame, is described as a defect for the sake of producing aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) through the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), it is also *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
When there is a conjunction of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) with other actions and so forth, that is *sahokti* (joint description);
it is of two kinds: based on dissimilarity and based on similarity. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 8.46)
O Lord of the Earth, Śrī Siṅgha, the rows of subordinate kings run to the ends of the quarters together with the expanses of your fame, as if they were its unequalled counterparts.

In this instance, the referent of the term "enemy" (*śatru*)—which signifies the expansion of the hero’s fame—is joined with the action of fleeing to another land along with things that are dissimilar yet possess perceived similarity; thus, it is called "possessing similarity," as in: "The glory of his fame, skilled in besieging the mountain ranges (or the enemy's camp) and possessing the auspicious rise of its activities, attains a splendor that is the cause for fulfilling the quarters of the world."
O jewel that adorns King Śrī Siṅga, foremost of the Recarla lineage, you bring joy to the learned through your wealth as if through your own poetic compositions.

Here, by the power of the words, the similarity between Lakṣmī and Kīrti—whose common attributes are expressed—and the similarity between the substance (the king) and the poem—which possess perceived common attributes such as desirability—is illuminated by the word *iva*.
Furthermore, the sense of "together" (*saha*) is obtained through the force of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*).
Nor should any suspicion of a simile (*upamā*) be raised here.
In a [conventional] simile (*upamā*), the action is attributed solely to the object of comparison (*upameya*);
in the case of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it is attributed directly through the medium of the object of comparison.

Here, however, because both possess equal prominence, when there is an intention to express their relationship as object, instrument, and so forth, there is an attribution of actions such as "attaining bliss" and "contemplating. Thus, this [figure] possesses similarity, characterized by the shadow of a simile brought forth by *śleṣa* (punning).
This is *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
In this way, the various distinctions among the agents and other factors—which serve as the primary points of comparison—such as "secluded" (*vivikta*) and so forth, are to be understood by oneself.
It consists in the placement of many things, such as substances (*dravya*) and the like, within a single substance or similar category.
There may also be other meanings [of the word "and"] as a conjunction; these are merely its various modes of application.
That [question] is first of four kinds:
based on two words, based on many words, based on both categories, and based on neither.
Among these, that based on two words is twofold: that which elucidates the preceding word and that which elucidates the subsequent word.
Among these, the first is as follows:
O illustrious King Siṅgha, your form and your fame, possessing supramundane qualities of purity and radiating a splendor greater than that of a king, spread joy upon this earth.
Here, the two entities "form" (*mūrti*) and "fame" (*kīrti*) are placed together in a single action—"he extends"—by means of the particle *ca*, which serves as an indicator for each word.

Consequently, there is a dual ending in the verb *tanute* (it extends), and a copulative compound (*dvandva*) occurs in the sense of "and. This is what is called "the conjunction of substances within an action," where the indicator relies on both words.
The same [principle] applies when the indicator relies on the subsequent word, as follows:

O King Siṅga, your desire for victory, accompanied by the intense exertion of those who are perpetually blinded by the activities of intoxication, manifests a surrounding retinue that is ever-blinded; yet the excellence of the clear resonance of the drums creates a mingled effect that both agitates and excites your enemies.

In this instance, two entities characterized by "trembling" and "longing" are placed simultaneously through conjunction (*samuccaya*) within a single substance consisting of the property "the Fortune of the Enemy," which is expressed by the suffix located in the final member of the compound; thus, this is the variety of conjunction based on two words known as the "suffix residing in the final member."
Even that which relies on many words is divided into two types based on the preceding word.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"the method of reasoning and the prowess of his staff-like arms, as well as knowledge of the proper time, compassion, and gratitude."
O Siṅgabhūpa, your knowledge of poetry, your own poetic skill, and your generosity together adorn you.

In this instance, *nyāya*, *parākrama*, and the others are introduced by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*) into a single act of embellishment (*pariṣkaraṇa*), as indicated by the word "each" (*pratipada*). Consequently, there is no use of the plural number (*bahuvacana*) nor a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*). Thus, this is what is called the variety of conjunction based on multiple words (*bahupadāśraya-samuccaya-bheda*) that functions as an indicator for each individual word.
Furthermore, in our opinion, because it invokes the appearance of antiquity through a multiplicity of causes, it does not produce much aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
Nevertheless, this which has been set forth out of faith in following the path of the ancients should be endured by those who know the essential principles of elegant literature.
As for the second [type], it is as follows:
having infinite enjoyments as its support, omnipresence, being beloved of the Discus (Viṣṇu), and possessing dense goodness.
When King Śrī Siṅga, who was like a celestial *pārijāta* tree, manifested his state as the visibly present Nārāyaṇa.

Here, by means of the particle *ca* occurring in the final member [of the compound], the objects such as "the basis for infinite enjoyments" are manifested; thus they are conjoined (*samuccīyante*) within a single action, rather than being manifested (*vyañjayanti*). Consequently, there is neither a plural number nor a compound. This, then, is the variety of conjunction based on multiple words, known as the "indicator residing in the final member" (*uttarapadagatadyotaka*).
Furthermore, that which relies on both categories is merely an indicator occurring within the latter member [of a compound],
just as this [work] has appeared through the extraordinary merit of the illustrious King Siṅga, the lord of poets.
Your poetry is praiseworthy, as is your narration of [your] deeds; it brings glory to the virtuous and delights the noble.
In this context, there are two actions: composing poetry (*kāvyam*) and proclaiming it (*kīrtanam*);
and two qualities: the excellence of the work (*śrīsadbhāvaḥ*) and the delighting of virtuous people (*sajjanānurañjanam*).
Thus, even many entities are presented as pairs—by means of the particle following the final member of the compound—as being subsumed under a single action, namely "has appeared" (*avirāsīt*).
Because of that, there would be neither the plural number nor the *dvandva* compound; thus, this is a collective (*samuccaya*) based on both categories.

Furthermore, that which is based on neither [category] is not illustrated here, as its scope is brought forth by the *dīpaka* just like that of *anvācaya*, since it merely indicates what is already present. *Itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) is also fourfold, distinguished by its basis on two words and so forth.
In this context, *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), which relies on two words and illuminates what resides in the latter member [of the compound], is as follows:

"Behold the constant, great glory of the rise of both the jewel-like King Siṅga and the sun, who are ever intent on bestowing auspiciousness upon those who have come for refuge, and who are exceedingly devoted to serving the station of Viṣṇu. (Ckc 8.87)

In this context, when two substances— the hero and the anti-hero— are presented through the conjunction of mutual association (*itaretarayoga*) within a single word expressing a quality (*guṇapada*), such as "see the two," then because there is an expectation for the dual number (*dvivacana*) regarding those two and their respective qualifiers, a compound (*samāsa*) also occurs; thus,
this aforementioned *itaretarayoga* is indeed a variety of *samacaya*.
In this way, examples of the connection of indicators (*dyotaka*) in mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) should also be cited.
That very same [conjunction] which does not depend on either [of the two] is as follows:
"Her gaze was lovely and motionless; her gestures were devoid of shame; and the beauty of her smile blossomed upon the surface of her cheeks."
In the city of Śrī Siṅgabhūmi, the female companions reveal the state of passion within young women to their friends.

Here, the things—glances, gestures, and smiles—are presented through mutual conjunction (*itarētara-yoga*) as being employed in the action of communicating the passion of young women; thus, this is indeed a "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) based on neither [of the two] through mutual conjunction. Furthermore, "aggregation" (*samāhāra*) is also fourfold, as previously described.
Among these, that which rests upon neither [of the two] is as follows:

beauty in Madana, happiness in the Lord of the Gods, fortune in the sovereign of treasures, compassion in the Leader of the Raghus, cleverness in the enemy of the wrestler Cāṇūra, righteousness in the Son of Dharma, and generosity in the Lord of the Vidyādharas— all that splendorous excellence shines forth in Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in him.

Here, by the phrase "all that" (*sarvaṃ tat*), the collection of beauty and the other qualities alone is intended. Since its constituent parts have become obscured, it is a collective whole (*samāhāra*).
And this is expressed here by the neuter singular pronoun "that" (*tat*).

And here, the particle *ca* or others do not exist anywhere [as constituent members]. Since it is a "clarifier" (*dyotaka*), this collection (*samāhāra*) based on both is precisely a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Other collections that possess clarifiers should be inferred by oneself.
Conjunction (*anvācaya*), however, pertains exclusively to the domain of action;
in that case, the indicator (*dyotaka*) depends solely upon the subsequent member (*uttarapada*),
as for example:

O Lord Bhairava, whose arms and cheeks are raised high, you who are a wish-fulfilling tree for those with resolve, the crest-jewel of the illustrious Siṅga kings, and the deliverer from the spreading darkness of infamy—

having conquered the earth for the protection of the virtuous, may you enjoy prosperity and the company of those who follow in your footsteps, as they are each established again in their own respective positions.

Here, by introducing the action "you should worship" (*bhajethāḥ*) with the Lord as the agent and Śrī as the object, the actions of "guarding" and "establishing" are likewise introduced as being performed by that same agent through *anvācaya*.
Thus, this *anvācaya* is also a specific variety of *samuccaya* (conjunction).
"A *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) is the statement of a prohibition, or else it is the statement of an injunction from which a prohibition is implied. (Cakravartin 8.48)

An example of prohibition by injunction (*vidhinākṣepa*) is as follows: "O beloved, if you, whose mind is weary from dwelling in the wilderness, intend to go to the city of Andhra—the capital of the illustrious Lord of Siṅga—to visit him, then let it be so;
may your paths be most auspicious, and may Sītā [be yours]."
In whatever land a gracious king bestows [favor] upon you, may my birth occur right there, O you of virtuous mind.

In this case, by means of a benediction for another birth—which is itself favorable to the injunctive statement "Go here"—the prohibition of the indication of death is effected; thus, this is an *ākṣepa* (implication) of an injunction (*vidhyākṣepa*).
An example of an *ākṣepa* of a prohibition (*niṣedhākṣepa*) is as follows:
"Indeed, we are not poets; those who describe even non-existent qualities of the city are the true poets."
Indeed, we are not able to describe even a fraction of the lineage of virtues belonging to the Lord who enjoys the earth of Siṅgha.

Here, by the negation "we do not desire," there is a negation of the definition of poetry as the description of superimposed qualities; since this is done through the nature of things (*dharmataḥ*), this is *vidhyākṣepa* (prohibitive suggestion). That [suggestion] should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), which occurs when, having introduced a certain subject matter, one presents another matter capable of establishing it. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 8.49)
Just as you,
O Lord of the Earth, having made pride your measuring rod, bestow whatever wealth upon others through daily acquisition,

and then repeatedly deposit it in the hands of worthy recipients until it is as if forgotten in your mind— who indeed could harbor any longing at the conclusion of his task toward those who are masters?

In this case, having introduced the primary subject (*vastu*) characterized by the hero’s lack of regret regarding the religious gifts bestowed upon him, another subject (*vastvantara*)—characterized by his sovereign nature capable of accomplishing that goal—is presented;
thus, it is called *sāhasa* (the bold).

Here, having introduced fame as crossing the seven oceans, another subject capable of accomplishing that—namely, the sixfold policy (*ṣaḍguṇa*) consisting of three thousand [elements]—is presented; for this reason, it is so designated.
Where there is a description of the deficiency of substance and so forth regarding the object being praised,
for the sake of manifesting its excellence, that is intended as *viśeṣokti* (the figure of particularity).
Just as his chariot is not swift, nor his weapon fragrant with perfume, nor his bowstring talkative, nor his bow effortless and exceedingly sweet;
nevertheless, this illustrious King Siṅgha utterly bewilders the minds of fickle-eyed women, like the God of Love himself.

In this case, even though objects such as flower-carts are unavailable, the fact that the hero has made this intoxicated woman delude his mind allows one to infer a specific cause for her beauty and other qualities; thus, this is an "implied cause" (pratīyamānahetu) variety of *viśeṣokti*.
The "expressed cause" (*abhidhīyamānahetu*) should be understood in the same way.
*Upaskāra* (ornamentation) is *parikara*, which consists of [the use of] qualifiers for verbs and so forth. (Cvc 8.51)

The circle of the earth, its turtles having found rest and its great mountains rising up, was brought under control by the arm-staff of the illustrious Lord of Siṅga, while Ananta looked on with longing.

Here, through the qualifiers beginning with "exhausted" (*aśvasta*), there is an embellishment (*upaskāra*) consisting of a unique characteristic of the earth’s act of bearing [the world]; thus, this is *kriyāparikara* (the embellishment of action).
In the same way, *kārakaparikara* (the embellishment of the case-factor) and others should also be inferred by oneself.
It is my opinion that *ekāvalī* (the single-string necklace) is not distinct from *parikara*.
Just as the earth was brought to well-being by King Siṃha through his protection, his freedom from obstruction, his power, his prowess,
and his accumulation of merit— by Hari, by Hari, by Hari, by Hari, by Hari.

In this instance, by the single-stringed ornament (*ekāvalī*) of words such as "by Hari" (*hariṇā hariṇā*), which possess distinct meanings, the agentive factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*) characterized as the hero is embellished; thus, this is a variety of the *kāraka-parikara*.
In the same way, the *artha-ekāvalī* and the *ubhaya-ekāvalī* are to be understood.
[This occurs] when there is a single substratum for terms denoting action, genus, quality, and substance.
If it serves to assist other sentences, that is cited as *dīpaka*.
The varieties of that [repetition] consist of repetition of meaning, repetition of words, and so forth, including the combination of both.
In this regard, an example of *kriyādīpaka* (the illuminator of action) is as follows:
O King Siṅga, lord of the earth, your glories have ascended to the three worlds; the multitudes of kings of feeble splendor have become great caves within the mountain-rocks of your lineage;
the graceful charms of their fortune have resorted to the homes of learned men whose speech is tender; and the ears of the virtuous have become the verses of praise for those words of yours.

Here, because all the sentences are illuminated by the word *gūḍham* (hidden), which expresses an action and occurs at the beginning of the first quarter-verse, this is called *ādidīpaka* (illumination at the beginning).

In the same way, the varieties such as *madhyadīpaka* (illumination in the middle), *antyadīpaka* (illumination at the end), *jātidīpaka* (illumination by genus), and so forth, should also be understood.
Regarding the varieties of *dīpaka*, there is also repetition of meaning (*arthāvṛtti*), as for example:

O glorious Siṅgabhūpa, the moons of your fame’s play sport with the night-lotuses that are the beauty of the serpent-king, they frolic with the stars that are the pearls from the temples of the elephants of the quarters, and they dally with the moonlight of the smiles of celestial damsels.

In this case, the action of the feet and so forth, occurring solely for the sake of play, illuminates all the sentences; thus, even though this is a repetition of meaning (*arthāvṛtti*), it is indeed *dīpaka*.
An example of the repetition of words (*padāvṛtti*) is as follows:
"This king of the Recara lineage makes the night-lotus bloom exceedingly."
The king, too, like a white water-lily born of the Indus, rises up.

In this context, the word *kumuda*, which recurs for the two meanings "satisfaction of the subjects" (*prajā-saṃtoṣa*) and "white water-lily" (*kairava*), illuminates both; thus, even the repetition of a word (*padāvṛtti*) is indeed *dīpaka*.
By these same [examples], the repetition of both [word and meaning] is also explained.
Just as here, the word *rāja* (king/water-lily), recurring in the two sentences, energizes them; therefore, this repetition of both is also indeed *dīpaka*.
The *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) form, consisting of three or four repetitions of the feet, is as follows: "O Siṅgabhūpa, the glory of the Lord of Talapa sports effortlessly like a sprout of jewels;

it has ascended to the palaces of the hoods of the foremost serpents in the netherworld (*pātāla*), and to the cheeks of the divine damsels in heaven with their playful smiles amidst the waves of the ocean—the very birthplace of Lakṣmī. (Ckc 8.100)

In this context, since the words expressing the action, the agent, and their relationship recur in each sentence and illuminate them through the structure of a "box" (saṃpuṭa), this repetition of the "box" is also nothing other than *dīpaka* (illumination).
Other varieties [of *dīpaka*] should be understood accordingly as they occur.
Sequential expression (*paripāṭhyā bhaṇanam*), however, refers to the sequence of either word or meaning.
In this regard, the sequence of words is threefold: that of compound words, that of non-compound words, and that of both.
Among these, the sequence of compound words is exemplified by the majesty, beauty, and purity of King Śrī Siṅga.
The sun, the moon, and fire all stand equal to one another.
In this case, there is a sequential application of the qualities contained within the compounds one by one; thus, this is an example of the sequence of compounded words (*samasta-śabda-krama*).
An example of the sequence of uncompounded words (*asamasta-śabda-krama*) is as follows:
"He performs salutation, honoring, and disparagement."
The illustrious Siṅgha, protector of the earth, [was the adversary] of the learned men of former times.

In this case, the intended lack of correspondence (*ananvaya*) is according to the sequence of "east" and so forth, "salutation" and so forth, and "without compound" and so forth; thus, this is the sequence of non-compounded words.
The sequence of both [compounded and non-compounded] words, which consists of the sequence of compounded and non-compounded words, is as previously cited: *hariścandro rakṣākaraṇarucisatyeṣu*.

In this instance, because the qualities such as *rakṣā* (protection) and others are combined in the first and third quarters, while the qualities of those [qualities] are not combined, the sequential correspondence between *hariścandra* and *hariścandran*, and between *gāṅgeya* and *gāṅgeyan*— which are expressed through the power of word-pun (*padaśleṣa*) in both cases— is not intended; thus, this is "sequential correspondence of both" (*ubhayakrama*).
The sequence of sentences, however, must be inferred by oneself.
The sequence of meaning is of two kinds:
spatial and temporal.
Regarding that, the first [example] is as follows:

O illustrious King Siṅgha, when the women of your enemies—whose silken garments have been snatched away by the Śabaras during the forest-like raids of your army—the manifestations of your fame serve as lower garments upon their hindquarters, as upper wraps upon their chests, and generally as veils upon their heads; or rather, we praise the condition of their lips! *Cakrapāṇi-kṛta-kāvyacandrikā 8.103*
In this case, there is this attainment of a comparison through the gradual transition of Vardhamānā’s girdle across the various parts of the body of the rival heroine’s wife;
thus is the sequence of meaning by way of space (*deśataḥ*).
As for [the sequence] by way of time (*kālataḥ*), it is as follows:

Having brought about calamity for the multitude of lotuses by drying up their waters, lifting them from their depths, swallowing the swans out of fear of their falling, causing them pain with frost, and turning them into beds for those separated from their lovers; and having abandoned her former state, the Goddess of Fortune (Ramā) now dwells with King Siddha when you have met with misfortune.

In this case, because the causes of danger to aquatic creatures—such as the drying up of water—are described in the sequence of time from summer down to spring, this is "sequence of meaning" (*arthakrama*) based on time.
That which is the progression of speech under some pretext is called "circumlocution" (*paryāya*).

When the circle of dear friends had departed with these words—"Ah, the śārikā bird cries incessantly! The pet deer kicks about! The lute outside is weary from its harsh tuning!"—the newlywed beloved was left by the king, her longing for her circle of friends expanded only by his touch.

In this instance, a circle of clever friends, fearing the discovery of their secret, proposed a means for an easy exit under the pretext of listening to insults and the like; thus, this is *paryāya* (circumlocution).
In this way, its various subdivisions—such as the statement of a cause under the guise of an effect, or the non-intention of what was intended—should be inferred by oneself.
That intention toward a specific detail which does not cause excessive agitation [is *paryāyokta*].
This is hyperbole (atiśayokti), the life-force of all poetic ornaments.
This [cognition] has as its object qualities and actions, not genus or substance;
for there is never any direct excellence (atiśaya) belonging either to a substance or to a genus.
Among the various distinctions of excellence in his qualities, his preeminent fortitude is as follows:

O graceful one, though he has reached a state of distinction, no harshness of ego exists; even the corner of his eye does not turn red when his brows have changed their expression, nor does his smile fade away even when it is slow.
Even upon seeing kings roaring back at him with a splendor filled with fury and with bodies of violent action, the form of the illustrious King Siṅga remains unaltered.

In this instance, by describing the absence of physical transformations such as the knitting of eyebrows in the hero during the great onset of battle, a particular kind of fortitude is intended; thus, this is an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) of quality (*guṇa*). An example of hyperbole of action (*kriyā*) is as follows:
"O King Śrī Siṅga, because of your acceptance [of this work], this poet is afraid of the powerful Dharma."
But those first kings do not equal you, who possess two portions that have stolen away the very bond of the Tretā age and the others.
In this case, what is intended to be expressed is a specific act of protecting the qualities pertaining to the hero; thus, this is *kriyātiśayokti* (hyperbole of action).
*Śleṣa* (paronomasia) is considered to be the expression of multiple meanings by means of a single word. (Cvc 8.59)

Just as those of noble intent, who have protected their lineage and do not tread upon the borders of unrighteous lands, do not transgress even formidable commanders of armies— though they possess established strength and are renowned for their greatness— so too do the virtues of the illustrious King Siṅga remain inviolable.

Here, by the word *vāhinīśa*, two meanings—namely, "the ocean" and "a neighboring king"—are suggested; furthermore, in its qualifying attribute, two corresponding meanings are likewise suggested through paronomasia (*śliṣṭa*). Thus, this is the figure of speech known as *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Where there is the suppression of an emotion (*bhāva*), that is declared to be *udbheda* (suppression). (Cvc 8.60)

Just as a slender maiden, with her curls and breasts half-revealed by the bracelets on her arms, placed a seal upon a bud of jasmine— intended to be offered by her own friend’s hand to the illustrious King Siṅghabhuṣaṇatilaka— using a leaf inscribed with the words of the Conqueror of Smara.

Here, a certain clever woman suspects that the flowers suitable for her beloved are being touched by the wind, which carries the scent of the flower-bees (the arrows of the Flower-Arrowed One). This is the *bhāva*; it is manifested—that is, indicated—by the words "curling locks," "hooded serpent," and "conqueror of Smara," which serve as protective measures by acting as adversaries to the bees and other such creatures.
This is what constitutes *bhāvanā*.
The wise declare that the mutual conjunction of the manifold ornaments residing in both word and meaning is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture).
In this context, the commingling of purely verbal figures of speech is a verbal figure; the commingling of purely semantic figures of speech is a semantic figure;
and the commingling of both types of figures of speech is a figure of both kinds.

Regarding the commingling (*saṅkara*) of verbal and semantic ornaments, of both verbal and semantic ornaments, and of both semantic and verbal ornaments, it is indeed a "both" ornament (*ubhayālaṅkāra*), because the commingling is established as being dependent on both by virtue of its own respective ornaments;
for such a possibility exists.
An example of the commingling of purely verbal ornaments is as follows:
Having performed the ritual service of *siṅka* which destroys fear and delusion,
the *būpas* residing in their own homes [performed] that which destroys fear and delusion.

In this context, *sādhvasaṃmatividhvaṃsi* means that which destroys (*vidhvaṃsayati*) or causes the disappearance (*nāśayati*) of the disapproval and lack of confidence (*asaṃbhāvanā*) felt by the virtuous (*sādhūnām*) when it is not being obtained; thus, it signifies the "threatening of the wicked. Having performed such service to King Siṅga, the construction is: "the destruction of the minds of the kings staying in their own homes (*nijagṛhe*)," resulting in fear (*sādhvasam*). Here, the verb *nigṛhītam* ("was seized") is hidden within the locative case *nijagṛhe*; thus, the figure of speech is a combination of *kriyāgūḍha* (hidden action), characterized by the repetition of the subject word, and *viṣayapadāvṛtti-yamaka* (repetition of the subject-word alliteration).

This is an instance of the commingling of purely verbal figures of speech (*kevala-śabdālaṅkāra-saṅkara*). An instance of the commingling of purely semantic figures of speech (*kevalārthālaṅkāra-saṅkara*) is as follows:
"O King Siṅga, your broad chest, which is a rainless thunderbolt, [acts as such]."
He [slew] the enemies dwelling in the city within the forest, and the deer dwelling in the forest within that city.

Here, in the first half [of the verse], there is the figure of speech *vibhāvanā*, and in the second half, there is *parivṛtti*; thus, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of these two figures of sense. An example of the commingling of both types of figures of speech is as follows:
King Siṅga is served by goddesses as if they were his fortunes, by wise men as if they were his modesties, and by great ministers as if they were his statesmanlike policies.

Here, by the word *iva*, not only the sense of "as if" (*sahārtha*) is indicated, but also the sense of "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanārtha*); thus, through the simultaneous entry into a single expressive unit (*ekavācakānupraveśa*), there is a commixture (*saṅkara*) of *sahokti* and *utprekṣā*.
An example of the commixture of verbal and semantic ornaments (*śabdārthālaṅkāra-saṅkara*) is as follows:
"O King, by you, who were yourself wretched (*dīna*), I have been made wretched (*dīna*)."
O you who possess complete conduct, tread upon this earth which was previously incomplete.

Here, in the first half-verse, the word *dīnārī* is formed from *dīnāriṇā*, while in the second half of the middle *yamaka*, it is formed by *samagrāmavat*; thus, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of two apparent contradictions (*virodhābhāsa*).
An example of the commingling of both verbal and semantic figures (*śabdobhayālaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"This King Śrī Siṅgha is attended by the women of Andhra, just as the moon is attended by the stars."
How wonderful are the bracelets on those women with long, white eyes—bracelets that appear as if doubled upon their waists and their wrists!
Here, it is remarkable that there are rows of lines in the form of bracelets upon this belly.

As one observes them—moving the bracelet on the hand—the singular and plural forms of the agent and the verb are intertwined in such a way that "bracelet" (*valaya*), "ring" (*kaṭaka*), and "bracelet-less" (*avalaya*) are joined; thus, the distinction between the pun on number (*vacanaśleṣa*) and the simile (*upamā*) "like the moon with its stars" is perceived, making this a combination of both verbal and semantic figures of speech (*śabdārthobhayālaṃkārasaṃkara*).
And just as King Siṅga rejoices through courtesans as if they were rubies, through sandalwood trees as if they were chariots, and through noblemen as if they were virtues of goodness; Ckc_8.*115 //
Here, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of alliteration, simile, and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
An example of the commingling of both verbal and objective ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra* and *śabdālaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"The fame of Your Majesty is being established in every direction, causing terror to Your enemies... [and] "In every step, the wives of Your foes run about and sing of Your fame."
Exhaustion finds rest upon the earth amidst the many locks of hair of your enemies; O jewel among kings, Siṅga, your arm finds rest upon the ground while the wives of your foes sleep.
Here, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of the figure of speech *citrahetu* (the "wondrous cause") and the figure of speech *upamā* (simile).
An example of the commingling of word, meaning, and both types of figures of speech is as follows:

"To the illustrious Lord of the Earth, who causes the joy of the minds of the virtuous to bloom in every direction; Indra bestows dense prosperity, the King of Justice (*Dharmarāja*) an exceedingly pure purity, and..."

May the Lord of the Rākṣasas grant protection; may Pracetas, whose mind is intent on destroying the crooked; may Vāyu; and may Dhanada grant full life and wealth; and may Śaṅkara bestow auspiciousness.

In this passage, through the repetition of "diśi diśi" (in every direction), "sumomānaseti," "śaṃkaraḥ śaṃ kotu," and "rakṣāṃ rakṣo," there is a *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration of consonants). Furthermore, in "sāndrābhidra" and so forth, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) of "sumanas. This is further enhanced by the figure of speech known as *anyonyārtha* (mutual relation), characterized by the mutual protection between the world-protectors (Lokapālas) evoked by each respective word—specifically, the sequence of the directions beginning with the East.
The arrangement [of these] appears together with the ornament of *krama* (succession) and the ornament of *ubhaya* (both); thus, this threefold ornament...
[should be understood as] a commingling (*saṅkara*) of ornaments.
Although these qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are accomplished through separate efforts, [they may still coexist].
They would be accomplished with a single effort for the meritorious poet in his poetic work.

Even the commingling (*saṅkara*) of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth has been declared by Bhoja and others to be an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), because they maintain that [these elements] can serve as such. (Cvc 8.63)
In that regard, an instance of the commingling of poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:

"May the wondrous creation fashioned by the Lord of the Universe and the fame of Siṅga shine forth together—lasting as long as the moon, the sun, the earth, the king of mountains, the mother, the sky, and the daughter of the mountain. (Ckc 8.118)
In the first half [of the verse], there is *sahokti* (joint description);
in the second half, there is *śeṣa* (paraleipsis)—the commingling (*saṅkara*) of these [figures] brings forth the stainless aesthetic charm (*kāvyacamatkāra*) of the poem.
In this manner, other types of commingling should be investigated by those who know the aesthetic flavor (*rasajña*) within the compositions of great poets, as far as they occur.
Thus, having examined the definition according to tradition,
poetry fashioned by imagination shall shine as long as the moon and sun endure.
Let this treatise be examined with discernment by those whose intellects have been refined through the knowledge of the characterized, the characteristics, and their manifestation. Ckc 8.65.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Moonlight of Marvels," in the *Camatkāracandrikā*—cooled by the essence of the nectar of the fame of the illustrious King Siṅgha—and composed by the moon among poets, Viśveśvara, who is preeminent in the art of elegant literature. All is auspicious.
This treatise is completed.
